In Wolfram, Trevrizent plays the role Hermes plays in the Corpus Hermeticum (Treatises III, IV and XIII), initiating Parsifal into the knowledge of the stars with the authority of Hermes, founder of astrological science. What, then, lies behind his curious name, distorted like so many names of Latin origin in Wolfram's poem? Here the Kahanes had a fortunate insight that casts a sudden light upon the way forward.

By a chain of careful philological deductions, they propose that Trevrizent conceals the Old French Trible Escient—“threefold wisdom,” or “threefold knowledge.”239 Trevrizent, the sage of threefold wisdom, would then be none other than the Hermes of the entire Hermetic tradition: in Latin, triplex sapientia vel triplex scientia; in Arabic, as Suhrawardi's commentators also know, mothalleth bi'l-hikmat. This Arabic expression translates the Greek Trismegistos, “thrice-great,” the epithet that makes Hermes Trismegistus the “Hermes of Hermes.”

Yet Hermes is not only a teacher and initiator. He is also the supposed author of the Hermetic treatises, the sage whose knowledge embraces the whole range of learning: the natural world, the stars and the invisible worlds.

And it is in these two capacities, the Kahanes argue, that Hermes appears in Wolfram: as Trevrizent, the sage of threefold wisdom, and as Flegetanis.240 The latter name has so far resisted every attempt at explanation. That should not surprise us when we recall the extraordinary changes Greek names underwent in being written in Arabic and then transcribed back into Latin, especially in alchemical texts (Hippocrates becoming Picatrix, Empedocles becoming Pandolfus, and so on). It seems plausible that the beginning of the name preserves something like Arabic falak, “celestial sphere” or “heaven.”

More importantly, the Kahanes have assembled a cluster of traits that allow them to compare Hermes as portrayed in Arabic sources—particularly his expertise in astrology and its associated sciences—with Wolfram's Flegetanis, who explains how the Grail came to earth. Among the Arabic works attributed to Hermes was a major treatise on astronomy, al-falakîyat al-kobrâ. Our scholars suggest that falakîyat may help explain the name Flegetanis.

Admittedly, something remains unresolved in this explanation, and its completion may have to come through Persian.241 Whatever the final answer, the Kahanes make a perceptive observation. In Islamic teachings about the prophets, Hermes is identified with Enoch, who is himself identified with Idris. Wolfram, meanwhile, describes Flegetanis as a pagan through his father, a Jew through his mother, and a descendant of Solomon. Such a double ancestry could well reflect the merging of Hermes and Enoch into a single figure.

Wolfram also has Flegetanis insist that anyone who hopes to see the Grail must be baptised—a demand entirely consistent with baptism in the Hermetic “Mixing Bowl.” All this suggests that Trevrizent and Flegetanis may conceal two aspects of the same Hermes: Trevrizent, the sage of threefold knowledge, is Hermes the initiator; Flegetanis is Hermes the author of the Hermetic treatises.

If we accept both identifications, one problem remains: how the Arabic Hermetic material reached the West, and who transmitted it to Wolfram. This brings us to the third name, Kyot the Provençal. The debate seems hopeless so long as we assume that Kyot gave Wolfram a complete Urparzival—an already composed, fully told story of Parsifal—for no trace survives of such a work in Provençal. Here again I can only refer to the evidence by which the Kahanes identify Kyot the Provençal with William of Tudela, a contemporary of Wolfram (Kyot being Guillot, a Catalan-Aragonese diminutive of William).242

William was a Jewish convert whose native language was then so close to Provençal that he could reasonably be called, on linguistic grounds, “Kyot (Guillot) the Provençal.” He knew Latin, Hebrew and Arabic, and understood the abc—in Arabic, the abjad, the philosophical alphabet and the mystical science of letters. He was skilled in astrological geomancy, a practice whose symbolism was then regarded as part of theology itself.243 The astrological passages in Wolfram's Parzival, which clearly display a direct familiarity with Arabic terminology, have precisely this character: their chief concern is less with any particular event in the sky than with its symbolic meaning and the interpretation it demands.

We cannot linger further over the Kahanes' fine book, though we hope that the brevity of our account has not diminished the force of its argument. Their comparative table244 sets out a striking series of correspondences between the stages of Hermetic initiation and the journey of Wolfram's initiate, embodied by Parsifal. This is not merely a novel of education (Erziehungsroman), but a poem of initiation. The same mystical vessel—the mixing-bowl Grail—stands at the centre of both the fourth treatise of the Corpus Hermeticum and Wolfram's Parzival.

The Monad in the Hermetic text and the Grail in Wolfram are alike the beginning and root of all things. “Nothing exists without a beginning. As for the beginning itself, it arose from nothing but itself, since it is the beginning of everything else. Being the beginning, therefore, the Monad contains every number without itself being contained in any of them.”245 The procession of the Grail—twenty-four maidens appearing in succession and carrying seventeen lights between them, until the Grail queen appears—is thus “a representation of the soul's mystical journey toward the Monad, itself symbolised by the Grail.”246

How, then, should we imagine the Urparzival? Kyot-Guillot found the original version of the story Wolfram tells in Tudela (previously read as Toledo), “written in pagan script”—that is, in Arabic. The details of its origin remain mysterious.

But according to Wolfram's own testimony, Kyot-Guillot gave him access to it. What he provided, however, was not a finished book, an already coherent and complete tale that Wolfram needed only to copy out. Wolfram himself says that he worked with no model before him—“without a book.” The Hermetic elements he used are scattered throughout the whole body of Hermetic writings.

The Kahanes therefore propose that the Urparzival was the body of teachings and symbols gathered by Kyot-Guillot and Wolfram, which Wolfram himself then shaped into the story of an initiate: the story of Parsifal.247

It seems to us that the Hermetic elements in Suhrawardi's work point to a similar process. (Let us recall once more the tradition that traces the origins of the Ishrâqîyûn, the philosophers of illumination, to the sister of Hermes.) Elsewhere we have translated the passage in which Suhrawardi describes Hermes' ecstatic ascent.248 Like the account of Hermes' vision of his Perfect Nature, this story bears the marks of an Arabic-language Hermetic tradition that may have anticipated the initiate's journey as Suhrawardi would later shape it in his own stories of initiation.

Hermes prays at night in the Temple of Light: he is gathered into himself, in the presence of the “sun” of his soul, hidden within the material body. When “the column of dawn burst forth, he saw a land sinking away”—his physical being consumed, like the phoenix, in the fire of “Eastern” Light as his soul blazes beyond the boundaries of the body, kindled by the Light of Lights. Hermes cries out to his “father” for help: the Nous, his agathos daimôn, or Perfect Nature.

The reply comes: “Take the ray of light as your rope; grasp it and climb to the battlements of the Throne.” Hermes is carried up to Heaven, like Enoch, with whom Islamic teachings about the prophets identify him, or like Elijah in his chariot of fire. The ray of light that he grasps as a rope, drawing him upward toward the “battlements of the Throne,” plays the role of the magnetic stone, the Grail, in Wolfram.

We know that, for “Eastern” theosophy, the bursting forth of dawn is the appearance, in the mystical “East,” of the splendour of the Light of Glory, the Xvarnah. For the initiate, the return to this “East” is the morning of his glorification. At the coming of that morning—or that spring—we shall encounter Suhrawardi's mysterious bird, the Simorgh. Insofar as we can identify the Simorgh with the phoenix, we see in Suhrawardi the return of the phoenix image evoked by Wolfram.249

But the fire here is mystical: it is the soul becoming incandescent in “Eastern” Light, the light of the Xvarnah or the Grail. If, during the early Middle Ages, certain people of Harran or even of India, inspired by the story of Hermes, gave themselves to actual flames, that was one of the tragedies of taking the literal meaning (sensus litteralis) literally.250

Hermes' ascent is his arrival at the source of Light and Life—the source reached by Suhrawardi's initiate on the mystical Sinai, at the Emerald Rock (Mount Qaf, Mount Salvat), at the end of the Tale of the Western Exile. For the shaykh al-Ishrâq, it is the same event in the world of the Malakût, the spiritual realm, as the ecstasies of Kay Khosraw and Zoroaster, who are carried into the presence of the “sources of the Light of Glory” (Xvarnah).

Dawn breaking forth, the soul rising in the “East” on the horizon of the world of pure Light—this is precisely what the vision of the Xvarnah means to Suhrawardi. (The connection between dawn and the Xvarnah is already marked in the Avesta by the name “mountain of dawns.”) The “Eastern” hero is transferred into the mystical world of Hurqalya. He becomes hidden from this world while still alive, as Kay Khosraw did, as the Twelfth Imam of the Shiites did, and as the Holy Grail itself now is.

Whether we say that Parsifal takes the Holy Grail back to the East, or that Galahad carries it to Sarras, from where it is taken up to Heaven, the event these images express is the same, as we shall have occasion to say again. For “East” and “Sarras,” like Hurqalya, are places in the “eighth clime,” invisible to the senses of those who have not been “baptised in the Mixing Bowl.” This passage into another realm is the initiate's transfiguration, anticipating what will be fulfilled at the end of his own spiritual destiny. Suhrawardi will express it in a magnificent “Grail story” with Kay Khosraw as its hero (see below, § 5).

Thus, on one side, the research we have just examined takes us from the Holy Grail of Wolfram's Parzival back to Hermeticism. We find a corresponding witness to the purpose of Hermetic gnosis in Suhrawardi's account of Hermes' ascent, whose mystical meaning he understands to be the same as that of the visions of Kay Khosraw and the prophet Zoroaster.

All are heroes of the spiritual epic that leads them back to the “East”: to the splendour of Light, to Ishrâq, which the ancient Persians called the Xvarnah. And now, on the other side, the Xvarnah, the Light of Glory, will lead us back to the Holy Grail, if we follow the second investigation announced earlier. The circle closes—a circle whose centre and circumference are both Suhrawardi's “Eastern theosophy,” as can happen with spiritual circles, unlike those of the physical world.

This second investigation, as we have said, is the work of a Zoroastrian scholar, Sir Jahangir C. Coyajee, and dates from some thirty years ago.251 Unfortunately, he knew nothing of the work of the shaykh al-Ishrâq, which at the time was still unpublished.

Yet if Coyajee's proposed link between the Xvarnah and the Holy Grail, and between Kay Khosraw's Iranian knighthood and the knights of the Grail, proves plausible, then the appearance of the heroes of Iranian epic in Suhrawardi's mystical tales gives that link, to our mind, an entirely different kind of evidence. In those tales, heroic action is fulfilled as a spiritual epic. The earlier study followed traces within the texts themselves from Wolfram back to Arabic-language Hermeticism. The path from Xvarnah to Grail, unfortunately, offers no equally precise signposts.

Yet we already know that Suhrawardi crossed this distance effortlessly: within his own work it lies between the vision of the Xvarnah granted to Kay Khosraw and the “Grail story” whose hero is Kay Khosraw. From Suhrawardi onward, at any rate, the connection is made, and its effects reach backward into the entire past. That is why we speak of evidence “of another order”: the evidence of spiritual events that make up the soul's history, always present, breaking through the one-way passage of time. Such evidence is not simply a conjecture drawn from reconstructing the fading material traces of a vanished past.

The connecting link through which Coyajee suggests that Iranian knighthood met the knighthood of the Grail is not Hermeticism but another religion: Mithraism. In fact, these two initiatory traditions had already influenced one another before the time of those we call the “Platonists of Persia.”

We can outline the problem Coyajee sets himself, following his account as faithfully as possible.252 Much ingenuity and effort have gone into explaining the legend of the Holy Grail—through the cult of Adonis, the Eleusinian mysteries, those of Samothrace, and so forth. By drawing attention to Iranian parallels, however, Coyajee proposes a hypothesis that could explain several otherwise puzzling features.

As he reminds us, it has remained difficult to explain how the theme and legend of the Grail in their Christian form became linked with the whole Celtic cycle that includes the Grail motif, the saga of King Arthur and the knights of the Round Table. Some have attributed the connection to Robert de Boron; others believe that he found it already established in an earlier Latin source; still others credit Chrétien de Troyes.253 In the German cycle represented by Wolfram's work, another event enters the picture—the very one that led the first study we examined toward Hermeticism.

According to Coyajee, the Iranian parallels ultimately form a body of clues suggesting that the Grail cycle contains elements derived from the Iranian epic tradition. Above all, they would allow us to recognise one underlying image in the Holy Grail and the Xvarnah, the Light of Glory. The idea of the Xvarnah is organically bound to that of a company of knights gathered around a line of people who bear its power.

We encountered the same theme in Suhrawardi, inspired by sayings of the First Imam of Shiism. Prominent among these bearers is Kay Khosraw, a central figure for Suhrawardi because he gives his name to the Khosrawânîyûn, the “Eastern” sages or theosophers, the ishrâqîyûn. Coyajee will compare Kay Khosraw with Parsifal and King Arthur.

But if we are seeking an actual historical route by which these traditions met, we must find some material trace of contact between the Celtic and Iranian worlds. Coyajee believes that, on the Iranian side, the contact came through the religion of Mithra: Mithraism.

There is, first, the special link established by the hymns of the Avesta between Mithra and the Xvarnah (see the Zamyad Yasht and the Mihr Yasht). Wherever the worship of Mithra appears, reverence for the Xvarnah accompanies it. As we have recalled, Xvarnah means both Glory and Destiny; the Greek translation of “royal Xvarnah” was Tykhê Basileos, the king's fortune or destiny.

Consider, too, the details of Mithraic imagery: the vessels, dishes and mixing bowls shown in sculptures of Mithra slaying the bull, calling to mind the rites of his mysteries and Mithraic communion feasts. Mithra himself appears as a young figure armed with sword and spear; on coins from Bactria, the Xvarnah is represented as a god carrying a spear. Bowl, sword, spear: all are characteristic objects in Grail literature.

Second, Coyajee finds a common ideal linking Mithraic fellowship to the brotherhood of the Grail: the quest for the Source of Life, moral and physical purity, and the close bond between companions. Perhaps Mithraism has too often been described as a religion of “soldiers.” It was not so much that professional soldiers were especially drawn to it; rather, initiates themselves received the title miles or milites, “soldier” or “soldiers,” by virtue of their initiation. That is not quite the same thing.

And it is worth noting that in medieval Latin miles means precisely “knight.” The bond of brotherhood is formed in the service of a cause that invites comparison between the Iranian tradition underlying Mithraism and the chivalry of the Round Table. There is certainly much to reflect upon here. Unfortunately, so much has been destroyed that we shall never know more than a little about Mithraic rites and initiation. We have referred several times to the document known as the “Liturgy of Mithras.”

Yet what matters most is the direction of the mystical journey held out by each tradition. The initiate of Mithra was introduced to the soul's journey toward the Islands of Light, across the ocean of stars and beyond the planetary spheres.

Perhaps the paths that lead our knights to Avalon or Sarras converge there too, as do those leading to the Green Island, the dwelling place of the Twelfth Imam, or to the “Western Paradise” of Amitabha, the Buddha of Infinite Light in Japanese Pure Land Buddhism. For in every case we are concerned with the “world of Hurqalya,” the “eighth clime,” and that intermediate “East” itself still lies to the west of the “greater East” of the Jabarût, the higher world of divine powers.

Let us return from these distant realms and glance at our maps—on which, of course, the cities of the “eighth clime” cannot appear. There is nevertheless an interesting geographical question: where might the Mithraic priesthood and the Celtic priesthood have met? Coyajee recalls the enormous spread of Mithraism through Gaul, Italy, Britain and Roman Germany. Remains of mithraea, temples dedicated to Mithra, have been found in great numbers.

Conversely, Druidism can be spoken of as extending from Ireland to Asia Minor, in Galatia. And in Asia Minor itself, communities of Magi had been established since the Achaemenid period. We have already had occasion to recall the connection between those Magi and the worship of Mithra. A meeting of Iranian and Celtic traditions, of Magi and Druids, thus seems more than plausible. Mithraic traditions may have entered Celtic beliefs long before the rise of the Roman Empire.

Certainly, there is no objection in principle to this broad picture.

Yet without texts, plausibility cannot rise to the certainty possible when a teaching has been explicitly set down. Here scholarship can do little more than identify analogies. Its position is less favourable than in the case of Wolfram and Hermeticism, where the texts themselves can be closely compared. For our purposes, then, it seems better to remain faithful to the phenomenological approach to the end: to seek above all to understand what shows itself to Suhrawardi, and how and why it shows itself to him in precisely that way.

We must begin with the spiritual event—an event that has truly taken place, but has taken place spiritually: his vision and his decisive commitment, in which the visions of Hermes and Zoroaster, the Light of Glory and the Holy Grail, come together.

From this starting point we must seek to understand the secret—the bâtin, the inner meaning—that he reveals to us, and how and why he reveals it. This is why we have preferred not to speak here of the migration of symbols, the history of ideas, great historical “currents,” or the recurring archetypes of the unconscious. Such explanations are all acceptable, provided one accepts the more or less agnostic assumption that the only interesting and knowable thing is, so to speak, the “gesture” made by a thinker or a doctrine—not what that gesture is actually trying to show us.

But what Suhrawardi is trying to show us is the direction of Ishrâq, of the Malakût, the spiritual world. It is there that all the events of importance to the “Oriental” philosophy of divine wisdom take place—the events whose heroes are Hermes, Kay Khosraw, and Zoroaster. The Malakût belongs neither to the past nor to the future. It is neither something that has been left behind nor something that “still remains to be done.” In itself it is Present, with an absolute presence: a presence freed from every condition we impose when we define something as past or future.

Can we bring this world into view by pursuing phenomenology to its ultimate conclusion? This “unveiling of what is hidden” (kashf al-mahjûb) is precisely what Suhrawardi and his companions accomplish when they show us what they see: an “Orient” that appears on none of our maps, where the deeds of heroes continue and reach their fulfilment as a mystical epic, and where Iranian chivalry and the chivalry of the Grail thereby meet. Once Suhrawardi, the shaykh al-Ishrâq, has taught us how to make this “orientation” a reality, the parallels identified by Mr Coyajee—particularly those concerning the Xvarnah and Kay Khosraw—can begin to bear fruit.254

2. The Forms of Manifestation and the Lineage of the Xvarnah and the Holy Grail

Here again, we can touch on only a few of the many comparisons proposed by the Zoroastrian scholar, and only in broad outline. At the same time, we shall indicate what we believe is the direction these comparisons must take if observations about the forms in which the Xvarnah and the Grail appear, and about the sacred lineages of those who possess or guard them, are to become genuinely meaningful.

As has rightly been observed,255 neither the Xvarnah nor the Holy Grail is described as possessing any single, fixed form.

Yet both appear in similar forms, from which certain shared qualities emerge. The Holy Grail, we are told, was “neither of wood, nor of metal, nor of stone, nor of horn, nor of bone.”

Nevertheless, it could take on material appearances—a vessel, a cup, a bowl, a stone—alongside the other “Wondrous Objects,” the lance and the sword. The Xvarnah, too, is spiritual in its essence: so much so that it is, before anything else, the object of a struggle between heavenly powers and the opposing forces of Ahriman.

But it, too, can appear as a cup, a stone, a lance, a flame, even a bird (when it deserts King Yima), or a stretch of sea (when it escapes Afrasyab the Turanian).

In the Iranian epic tradition, one form in which the Xvarnah became “material” was a stone: a talisman, a sacred object charged with supernatural power. Kay Khosraw had inherited it from his distant ancestors. It possessed extraordinary healing powers: it could restore reason to the deranged and bring the dead back to life. (We have already seen that the Xvarnah is also the energy that holds a being's existence together—its “light” and its “destiny.”) This talisman bestowed courage and all the qualities of the spiritual strength that ensures victory.

Likewise, in Wolfram von Eschenbach's epic, the Stone “which is also called the Grail,” brought down from heaven by angels and entrusted to the guardianship of a mystical order of knights, grants those who contemplate it long life, even immortality, because the Grail is the source of Life.

The form of the cup is no less celebrated. We need only recall the central object of the Christian Grail cycle. Identified with the chalice of the Last Supper, entrusted to Joseph of Arimathea, who had collected Christ's blood in it, the holy Vessel is brought to the White Island—that is, Great Britain—by a company of mysterious messengers. Their leader varies with the version of the story: in Robert de Boron's account it is Bron, Joseph of Arimathea's brother-in-law, who becomes the first king of the sacred Lineage; in the prose Lancelot, for example, it is Joseph's son Josephé, the mystical figure of the first and only Christian bishop.

In either case, the journey is not one whose route and stages we could plot on a map. It is a passage of an altogether different order. The supernatural powers of this cup, and the many themes of the “quest for the Grail,” fill the whole body of Grail literature. One can only wish that the complete “canon of Grail writings” might someday be assembled in a single edition, in a modern language accessible to any willing reader.

The cup is also one of the forms in which the Xvarnah manifests itself. In the Iranian epic cycle it is called the Jâm-gîtî-nemâ, “the cup (the Grail) that reveals the universe,” or the “mirror of the universe.” At the spring equinox the whole cosmos can be contemplated within it—not so much the affairs of the “seven climes” of the earthly world as those of an invisible world, of which the planets and constellations are merely signs.

But to attain this vision one must be a consecrated figure, a hieratic person such as Kay Khosraw, invested with the royal Xvarnah. The poem by Suhrawardi that we shall examine later, with Kay Khosraw as its hero, is among the finest expressions of the mystical meaning of this Iranian Grail. The cup became a recurring theme throughout Persian mystical literature: the Jâm-e Jam, the Grail of Jamshid.

The lance and the sword provide further parallels. Armed with the supernatural lance, Kay Khosraw attacks the magician's evil fortress. The lance strikes the wall; the dark stronghold vanishes; the demons occupying it scatter. In its place a different castle appears, splendid and bathed in light and flowers.

By this deed Kay Khosraw reveals himself as bearer of the Xvarnah and successor to Kay Kâûs. He is “the one who knows the meaning of the lance.” Likewise, it is only when Parsifal finally asks about the meaning of the lance and the Grail that the spell is broken—the magical prohibition that had held nature in desolation, barrenness, and deprivation. Once more the earth comes alive with the brilliance of flowers and the songs of birds.256

But the Iranian epic, like our Grail cycle, also knows the knight who fails: Fariborz. “He in whose hand the sword breaks” is the image of a knight whose quest ends in defeat. As for the “castle of the Grail,” Kay Khosraw's story will allow us to return to it shortly.

To sum up, very broadly: in both traditions there is a mysterious virtue or power which manifests itself through a Wondrous Object—a talisman or sacred instrument—surrounded by an aura of holiness like the most sacred relic.257 Whether the object is a form of the Xvarnah or the Grail itself, it offers the nourishment of immortality and the illumination of knowledge.

Whoever possesses the Xvarnah in its fullness possesses not only the gifts associated with spiritual consecration but also the victorious strength of the knight. The Xvarnah passes from one hero to the next without any visible intermediary. This is what leads Mr Coyajee to compare the royal succession of those who bear the Xvarnah with the lineage of the guardians of the Grail.

Just as the Grail is brought to earth by angels and entrusted to knights who are the purest of men, so the Xvarnah originates among the powers of Light. It belongs at first to Ohrmazd, to his archangels, to the Yazatas, and to all beings of light, both those of the invisible spiritual world (mênôk) and those of the material earthly world (gêtîk). It passes from sovereign to sovereign through the first two legendary dynasties of the Iranian epic: the Pishdadians (the “lawgivers”) and the Kayanids, from Kay Qobad to Kay Khosraw.

It passes to Zarathustra, or Zoroaster, prophet of the religion of Ohrmazd (Ahura Mazda, the “Lord-Wisdom”), and to King Vishtaspa, his protector. It passes to Zoroaster's last son, who is to be born at the end of our Aeon: a Zarathustra redivivus, a Zoroaster returned—the final Saoshyant, whose relationship to Zoroaster is analogous to that of the Twelfth Imam to the Prophet Muhammad. The Light of Glory “will accompany the victorious Saoshyant and his friends when he makes a new world, free from old age, death, and decay; eternally living, eternally growing.”258

We should notice that this vision of the last things, characteristic of Iranian spirituality as a whole, necessarily entails the present concealment of the Xvarnah. It entails the present concealment of the Twelfth Imam in the same way, just as it entails the concealment of the Grail. Here, where these ideas meet, we might find what all those whom Suhrawardi calls the Khosrawanians (Khosrawâniyûn) have in common with the chivalry of the Grail. We might also find the foundation of a shared ethic, through which both groups devote themselves, incognito, to the same struggle. For each, their strength remains sacred and invincible so long as their hidden identity is preserved.

The struggle for the Xvarnah “began in Heaven.” The Holy Spirit of Ohrmazd (Spenta Mainyu) and Ahriman (Angra Mainyu) contend for it (Yasht XIX, 46). The sacred history of the Xvarnah on earth is the manifestation and continuation, in the visible material world, of the struggle between Ohrmazd's powers of Light and Ahriman's opposing powers of Darkness. From this perspective, too, we ought to consider what the Iranian dynasty of the Kayanids may have in common with the dynasty of the Grail's guardians.

But we have the impression that Mr Coyajee, as a comparative historian, intends to go much further. (It is strange that, on the shifting ground of material facts and surviving remains, the critical historian is willing to venture much further than the phenomenologist, whereas the phenomenologist is the one who ventures forward as soon as the task is to acknowledge spiritual facts as spiritual facts and establish their standing.) The Zoroastrian scholar identifies parallels that allow him to set the old King Kay Kâûs beside Titurel; Kay Kâûs's son Siyavakhsh beside Amfortas, the “wounded king”; and Kay Khosraw beside Parsifal.

The aged Kay Kâûs longs for the arrival of the hero of his line—his grandson—to whom the Xvarnah will pass. Because his son Siyavakhsh has been killed on the orders of the king of Turan, the land of Iran lies desolate and devastated. A heavenly voice tells the Iranians that if they wish this ruin and desolation to end, they must set out to seek the future bearer of the Xvarnah. When Kay Khosraw succeeds in killing the evil Turanian, the land of Iran bursts into flower again,259 just as the domain of the Grail does upon Parsifal's return.

Thus, according to our author, an Iranian royal line would correspond to the Grail lineage of the German cycle.

Yet, as we know, the lineage of the Grail's guardians is not the same in Wolfram's account—the German cycle—as it is, for example, in Robert de Boron's Joseph and the cycle that grew out of it. This has given rise to no shortage of difficulties and debate.

We shall consider only the aspect that interests Mr Coyajee. Joseph of Arimathea prays that guardianship of the Grail may remain with his descendants. Are these descendants to be understood as a family line by blood, or as a succession of mystical initiates? Now, the Zamyad-Yasht (the hymn to the Dea terrestris, the goddess of the earth)260 describes how the Xvarnah became attached to, and passed in succession through, eight kings in a line beginning with Kavi Kavata (Kay Qobad) and ending with Kavi Husravah (Kay Khosraw). This is the line of the Kayanids as later told in Ferdowsi's Shâh-Nâmeh. Other texts, meanwhile, make it possible to identify eight guardians of the Grail between Joseph of Arimathea and King Pelles.

But fitting these traditions into such a scheme is far from straightforward. Mr Coyajee nevertheless believes that if we agree to identify the eight Kayanids, guardians of the Xvarnah, with the sacred Lineage of the Grail, all the difficulties posed by different versions of the family relationship between the Grail's guardian and the knight who completes the Quest disappear. The desolation of the Grail Domain can then be explained by the murder of Siyavakhsh, son of Kay Kâûs and bearer of the Xvarnah, treacherously killed by Afrasiyab the Turanian, whose son-in-law he had become.261 Ultimately Kay Khosraw and Parsifal shine through one another as heroes who win, or win back, the Xvarnah or the Grail.

The consequence of such a proposal would be to derive the Arthurian epic of the Grail directly and entirely from the Iranian epic of the Xvarnah, as from the source with which it must therefore have been identical at the beginning.

Perhaps this proposal is too quickly satisfied with outward, material facts, as though we were tracing the antecedents of Corneille's Le Cid among its Spanish predecessors, or showing that one Gallic tribe descended from another. That is why, from the phenomenologist's standpoint, the proposal seems at once to go too far and yet to stop short of the real issue. It goes too far because its claim of actual historical identity is extremely vulnerable; and in defending that claim we risk losing everything we have gained from the parallels themselves.

Yet in doing so it still stops short of what those parallels imply: they allow us to glimpse an entire sphere of spirituality shared by the idea of the Xvarnah and the idea of the Grail. It is one thing to say that the Kayanids stand in relation to the Xvarnah as the sacred Lineage does to the Grail. It is quite another to say that the second lineage is historically identical with the first. To doubt this material identification is in no way to abandon the parallels already discerned.

Rather, we must bring out their full significance in the way Suhrawardi himself would have done: by understanding the kind of bond he establishes between the Khosrawâniyûn, the sages of divine wisdom in ancient Persia, and the Ishrâqîyûn, the philosophers of light in Islamic Iran. The historian, who can pronounce only on material facts, naturally shakes his head at something that escapes the categories of empirical science and cannot be explained by tracing one instance of the same thing back to another.

When a philosopher recognizes his spiritual ancestors and claims descent from them, however, this is not a succession of legal heirs whose rights can be established by archival documents. It is an innovating event, one that takes place in the history of the soul. Its effects can reach backward into that soul's past and reshape it, so that the event cannot be “explained” merely by reducing it to an earlier occurrence. Or rather, its true “antecedent” lies elsewhere, on the level of a world of which historical reality here below is only a passing manifestation.

One thing shared by the Kayanid dynasty and the dynasty of the Grail is that both escape the chronological classifications of our history books. Attempts to identify the Kayanids with the Achaemenids known to the Greeks have failed. Here, then, is a lineage of heroes whose deeds and attributes are distinct and whose tradition continues from the Avesta to the Shâh-Nâmeh, yet to whom we cannot assign dates. (The same is true of Zoroaster, for whom the various proposed dates remain approximations.) The Kayanids enter history only through the resonant invocation of the hymn that celebrates them or the epic that tells their story.

And yet the events of their epic are perfectly real—real in a dimension different from that of the history Julius Caesar recounts, for example, in his Commentaries. That is why we prefer to speak not of a “mythical prehistory” but of an archehistory: a history of origins that stands in relation to ordinary history as an archetype stands to its particular expression.

Likewise, the Grail lineage enters history only as the light of a sanctuary shines through a stained-glass window into the darkness outside. What common measure could there be between that light and Caesar's Commentaries? But rather than diminish the claim, let us say that the sacred history of the Grail is projected onto the historical scene as nothing less than such a light—and cannot even be fixed in place there, since nothing on that scene foretold its coming or offers a measure for it.

The lineage of the Holy Grail has no place in official Church history. It does not even compete with the succession to the Apostolic See; it simply knows nothing of it. Instead of Peter or James, it speaks of Joseph of Arimathea and the mysterious Josephé. References to the Norman-Angevin Plantagenet dynasty in certain works of the Grail cycle belong to the transformation of Glastonbury, Arthur's sanctuary, into a holy place. Within that transformation lived the aspirations of a Celtic Church that had earlier been abolished by force, now rising again as a secret Church of the Grail, to endure incognito in this world.

How many other facts lead us directly into a history that is metahistory, and therefore also archehistory! We might also compare the transmission of the Light of Glory from Ohrmazd's heaven to Kay Khosraw with the transmission of the “Muhammadan Light” (Nûr mohammadî), created at the beginning of all things: from the heavenly Adam through prophet after prophet to Muhammad, and from Imam to Imam until the Twelfth.

The lineage of the Twelve Imams does not compete with some worldly dynasty on the same plane. As we have already observed, it is the esoteric line that guards the “Muhammadan Light” and the walâyat, the spiritual authority and bond of devotion; from the beginning, the number of these “upholders” was fixed in advance at twelve. Its concern is something quite different from what people today call “doing history.”

With all this in mind, what do we mean when we speak of a “meeting” between the Iranian chivalry of the Xvarnah and the Celtic chivalry of the Grail? Is it a fact that can be “explained,” causally deduced, because Druids and Magi may have met in Asia Minor, or Druids and initiates of Mithraic mysteries in Celtic lands and Britain? We need not even mention the scarcity of documents on the matter. The essential point is simply this: Druids and Magi, Druids and Mithraic initiates, could have stood side by side for centuries, and the meeting we are concerned with might never have taken place.

Indeed, why should there not have been hostility, reserve, or rivalry? If a researcher with “open eyes” can now discern the event of this meeting, it matters that the researcher discern where the event took place, and at what level of knowledge and plane of being it has meaning.

In the same way, the Gospel of Nicodemus, containing the sacred history of Joseph of Arimathea, and the entire Celtic saga of King Arthur and his Round Table could have coexisted materially in the Western world—in libraries, for instance—without a single knight ever setting out on the Quest for the Grail revealed at the Last Supper, and hidden from the world again since Galahad's ecstatic death. For that quest to begin, the event of their meeting had to occur. Where, and how? Precisely where the Gospel of Nicodemus ceased to be an “apocryphal” book and became a book brought fully into the light.

Suhrawardi speaks to us of events that take place: that is, events that have their place in the Malakût. A spiritual event indeed “happens” somewhere other than in social history, literary history, the history of ideas, and so on. In certain periods, this is perhaps the hardest kind of event to imagine or grasp—if it can be grasped at all.

We shall have reason to return to this when discussing the idea of hikâyat, or mystical narrative. There is no history of a particular spirituality other than that spirituality itself, alive and at work. Otherwise it is no longer its history. We meet again the situation we encountered in the preceding book when trying to understand the events of Shiism. The dilemma was already before us: either acknowledge that some events belong to a history different from the one examined by empirical science, or impose upon them from outside categories that are not their own. In the latter case, the events elude us at the very moment we think we have grasped them.

By contrast, the researcher who has somehow become capable of “receiving” these events, having adjusted the powers of perception to their true nature, has much to learn from the parallel Mr Coyajee draws between the deeds of Kay Khosraw and those of Parsifal. We have just as much to learn when Suhrawardi claims Kay Khosraw—the figure from whom the mystical sages called Khosrawâniyûn take their name—as a spiritual ancestor of his Ishrâqîyûn. What Kay Khosraw's saga teaches us about the ecstatic sovereign already prepares the way for the spiritual lineage formed within the Malakût, the setting of every event in sacred history. For we can never be mere spectators of such events.

Suhrawardi himself becomes an active witness to them, as he does in his psalms and mystical tales. He can do so because his entire spirituality is eschatological—concerned with the ultimate destiny of existence—just as Kay Khosraw, King Arthur, and Parsifal are figures of that destiny, and just as the meaning of the “Orient,” of the “return to the Orient,” is eschatological. It means becoming hidden from the world of sensory appearances, in a quest that can be completed only beyond this world, in the universes upon which the very appearance of this world depends. This is why Suhrawardi's tales mark, above all, the passage from the Iranian heroic epic to the mystical epic.

3. Kay Khosraw and Parsifal

Even the brief comparison we have sketched will help bring into focus the prince to whom Suhrawardi, in agreement with tradition, assigns an exceptional place among the sages of ancient Persia: Kay Khosraw, son of Siyavakhsh and Ferangiz, the daughter of Afrasiyab the Turanian.

Every text celebrates him as an extraordinary man, and Zoroastrian tradition honours him as one who understood and practised the Mazdaean religion even before Zoroaster's prophetic mission.262 He was the eighth and last sovereign of the Kayanid line, king of Xvaniratha: the central keshvar, or clime, of the seven regions that make up the Mazdaean Imago Terrae, the spiritual image of the earth.263 He is “one of the seven immortal princes of Xvaniratha”264—one of those who, now withdrawn to a refuge invisible to the inhabitants of this world, will accompany the Saoshyant, together with some of their knights, when he prepares the transfiguration of the world (frashkart) at the end of our Aeon. This same theme reappears in Twelver Shiism in the companions of the Twelfth Imam.

We have noted this already, and shall have occasion to recall it again, for the entire spirit of Iranian religious life seems to vibrate to the same underlying note. Kay Khosraw's person, his role, and his epic are eschatological through and through: his story continues and reaches its end in a world beyond ours, at once very close and very far away.

An essential feature of this vision of the last things is the mystical fortress. Its location cannot be plotted on any map, and it invites certain comparisons with the castle of the Grail. It remains on the horizon throughout the tragedies in which the fates of Kay Khosraw's grandfather and father—Kay Kâûs and Siyavakhsh—are bound together. In the end, it becomes the hidden place where Kay Khosraw's own exaltation reaches fulfilment.

Having completed his mission and his reign, Kay Khosraw withdraws to the mystical castle of Kang-Dêz. To withdraw there is to become hidden from the eyes of this world. A few heroes and prophets have entered it without first crossing the threshold of death. That is what the final scene—one of the most beautiful in Ferdowsi's Shâh-Nâmeh—will show us.

The fortress of Kang-Dêz belongs to the theme of the Mysterious Dwellings built by kings and heroes, whose significance for the destiny of the world is fundamental. Where is this mysterious castle? People have sought it sometimes in the east, sometimes in the far north. All these locations can be true, because particular geographical places correspond to particular visionary experiences.

But to verify those experiences, we must leave our maps behind. The far north is the celestial Pole, the “Emerald Rock,” and there, as Suhrawardi knows, the “intermediate Orient” begins. Whether the castle is said to stand in the heart or on the summit of Mount Alborz, or of Mount Qâf, the meaning is the same: it belongs to the “eighth clime.” To reach it, one must pass through the centre of the central clime, through Erân-Vêj in medio mundi, at the world's centre. We thus have the two poles of the axis joining soul and cosmos.265

Perhaps the best indication, then, is the one tradition itself gives us: “On the border of Erân-Vêj.” It is precisely at that “border” that the hero's destiny and that of his fortress are decided. This is why the castle has so many counterparts. There is the var, the enclosed refuge of Yima (Jamshid), which generates its own light. Within it, the chosen preserve eternal youth so that, after the world's destruction, they may one day repopulate it with a higher humanity.266 Kay Kâûs builds his own castle on the same model.

But Yima and Kay Kâûs are “wounded” sovereigns, made “mortal” through their own fault. It will fall to Kay Khosraw to establish the fortress securely and withdraw into it to await the appointed time. There are also the dwellings of the powers of Darkness: Afrasiyab's underground stronghold, for example, where he is protected by an iron enclosure.267 We are greatly simplifying this whole account.268 What chiefly concerns us is the contrast it presents, parallel to that between the Grail castle and the evil castle of the magician Klingschor (Klingsor), the “Castle of Wonders.”

The fortress of Kay Kâûs, Kay Khosraw's grandfather, is also the scene of his own tragedy. At the heart or summit of Alborz—that is, of Mount Qâf269 (the place to which Suhrawardi's mystical tales likewise lead us back)—Kay Kâûs, still sovereign of the seven keshvars, has an immense palace built with seven dwellings: one of gold, two of silver, two of steel, and two of crystal.270

From this fortress he holds at bay all the demons Ahriman has unleashed upon the world. The seven palaces have a magical virtue: if a person weakened by age and threatened by approaching death enters through one gate of the enclosure, that person comes out through the other looking like a fifteen-year-old youth. Kay Kâûs himself had undergone this transformation.271 Its symbolic meaning is transparent, like everything associated with the approaches to the “Source of Life.”

But then Kay Kâûs is seized by the dizzying desire for power. For at this “border” a human being faces a choice: either understand that the only passage beyond it is the way Kay Khosraw will take, or imagine that weapons and machines can still be of some use. This is the tragic mistake: what kind of “heavenly” space are we speaking of? The world of Light is not a world one can enter with machines and weapons, however “modern” they may be.

Yet Kay Kâûs's mistake has been repeated down to our own day. And now Kay Kâûs, at the head of an army made up of the very demons he once fought, assaults heaven. Of course he cannot cross the boundary between Darkness and heavenly Light—that is, he cannot escape the world of becoming and death. His army perishes; he falls back to earth, wounded forever and deprived of his Xvarnah. In later traditions, such as Ferdowsi's, the flying device—already familiar from an episode of the Greek Romance of Alexander—is absurd but no less significant: a basket carried aloft by eagles, enticed by pieces of meat hung from the lances to which the birds are fastened.272

However high he had risen, Kay Kâûs had never truly left this world. Now wounded and powerless before the demon of death, he can only await the one whom the Xvarnah—or the Grail—will make a victorious hero.

From this moment the victorious hero enters “history,” but a history whose true setting is the Malakût. We do not know at what date in our historical chronology Zoroaster entered this world. We are told, however, by the Dênkart, that his Fravarti—his heavenly being—was created at the beginning of the fourth “millennium” of our Aeon in the spiritual world, the world in its mênôk state.

In the same way, we learn here that, after Kay Kâûs's defeat, as he flees, he is pursued by Neryoseng, “messenger of the gods, promoter of the worlds,” who wishes to finish him off. Neryoseng is prevented from doing so by the Fravarti of Kay Khosraw:273 the heavenly being who exists before Kay Khosraw's earthly birth, his archetypal self of light, his “angel.” Kay Khosraw's Fravarti intercedes because it knows that Kay Kâûs must live to father Siyavakhsh, so that it—the Fravarti—may itself enter this world and fulfil its mission as the hero who defeats Afrasiyab and the powers of Darkness.

Hence the terms in which Kay Khosraw's Fravarti is invoked in a hymn of the Avesta.274

After Kay Kâûs's failure, his son Siyavakhsh in turn builds the mystical fortress that will be called Kang-Dêz, in the far north, amid the highest mountains: in other words, at the heart or summit of the cosmic mountain.

But although Siyavakhsh begins the work, only Kay Khosraw will “stabilize” the fortress and give it its lasting order. Kang-Dêz is marked by two features: its astonishing architecture, that of a city in the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world; and its role in the final destiny of the world.275 The fortress has seven walls, made respectively of gold, silver, steel, bronze, iron, crystal, and precious stone. Within its enclosure rise fourteen mountains; seven navigable rivers flow through it. The land is so fertile that grass grows to the height of a man in a single night.

There are fifteen gates, each as tall as fifty men. The diagonal distance from one gate to another is seven hundred parasangs,276 a journey of twenty-two days in spring or fifteen days in summer. In this city—whose description resembles those of Jâbarsâ, Jâbalqâ, and Hûrqalyâ in the “eighth clime”—dwells Khôrshêd-Tchehr, one of Zoroaster's sons. He will lead the companions of Peshotûn, the city's ruler and another hero of the last days, son of King Vishtaspa, Zoroaster's protector,277 in the final battle against the powers of Ahriman. This is where Kay Khosraw has withdrawn as one of the seven princes who will accompany the future Saoshyant.

The inhabitants of Kang-Dêz are described in the same terms as those of Hûrqalyâ in Suhrawardi's writings: happy and glorious, faithful and devout, strangers to old age and death. (Compare below, Book VII, the inhabitants of the Green Island, home of the Hidden Imam.) They will return to the land of Iran, to Erânshahr, only to prepare the transfiguration of the world (frashkart) through the victory of Ohrmazd and the Amahraspands and the destruction of Ahriman.

But between the moment when Kay Khosraw's Fravarti interceded for Kay Kâûs and the moment when Kay Khosraw, having fulfilled his mission on earth, left this world for the mysterious fortress, a long tragedy unfolds. It is a family tragedy that drives Prince Siyavakhsh into exile; and, paradoxically, he finds refuge with the eternal enemy, Afrasiyab. He marries Afrasiyab's daughter Ferangiz. For a moment there seems to be a premonition that Afrasiyab might be redeemed through his daughter.

Yet Afrasiyab falls prey to intrigue and treacherously orders Siyavakhsh's death. The young woman, now pregnant, is saved by the wisdom of a great Turanian dignitary. It takes a dream vision, an unexpected consent, and a daring, perilous flight for mother and child to set out secretly for distant Iran. They will be found, in the solitude of forests and mountains, by a band of Iranian knights—led by the valiant Giv—who have been searching for the guardian and bearer of the Xvarnah for seven years.278

Thus begins the chapter we might call “The Childhood of Kay Khosraw,” which Mr Coyajee has compared with “The Childhood of Parsifal.”279 The son of Siyavakhsh and the son of Gahmuret have each lost his father through treachery and betrayal. Each has a princess for his mother; each is raised by her in the solitude of forests and mountains; each learns from her the secret of his origins, unknown to everyone else. Both spend their childhood in the woods, playing at being knights. When they first appear at a royal court, they astonish everyone with their ignorance of courtly manners.280 Both are “sons of a pure heart.”

Just as Parsifal comes to the court of the Fisher King, Kay Khosraw comes to that of his grandfather, King Kay Kâûs, himself a “wounded” king who lies waiting for the one who will guard the Xvarnah. Both have the same duty to set right a wrong: Kay Khosraw must avenge his father Siyavakhsh against the violator of the Xvarnah; Parsifal must defeat the Fisher King's enemy and avenge the death of his brother Goon.281 Both will restore the king's health, free the land from its magical prohibition, and bring spring bursting forth again. One will become sovereign through the royal Xvarnah; the other, king of the Grail.

According to the epic tradition, Kay Khosraw's heroic deeds begin with the episode already described: the collapse of the evil, enchanted fortress under the blow of his supernatural lance, and the appearance of the paradisal Dwelling. Religious tradition speaks instead of the destruction of a temple of idols.

In either case, it is not the light of an ordinary physical flame that disperses the Darkness gathered by demons before Kay Khosraw. It is one of the three forms of Fire corresponding to the three manifestations of the Xvarnah: Adhar Gushasp, the Fire of kings and knights.282 This royal Fire settles upon his horse's mane and drives away the darkness produced by the enchantments, enabling Kay Khosraw to make out the idol temple and destroy it. In its place he builds a temple to the royal Fire. This temple has been located in Azerbaijan, on the shores of Lake Urmia or on Mount Savalan, where Zoroaster's conversations with Ohrmazd and his archangels have also been located.

We have already discussed how the westward movement of the Zoroastrian Magi consecrated the “visionary calling” of certain geographical places. The faculty that perceives the holiness of places and knows that particular events “took place” there is a malakûti faculty: a faculty of the spiritual world, not one of empirical perception. An ancient tradition aptly reminds us that the sacred places of the Mazdaean Imago Terrae cannot be seen by ordinary eyes: “Kay Khosraw,” we are told, “concealed the entrance to the temple he had dedicated to the royal Fire, so that no one, until the Day of Resurrection, knows where the temple stands.”283

Surely it is also along the horizons of a geography beyond the senses—a “geosophy,” or wisdom of sacred places—that we must follow Kay Khosraw's quest: the extraordinary, far-ranging journeys that occupy seven years as he pursues Afrasiyab-Ahriman to destroy him. The journey extends as far as the Sphere of the Stars. Some of these regions can be identified on our maps, but many others certainly cannot. The entire route is marked chiefly by landmarks through which a long tradition suggests the soul's struggles—the struggles that “take place” in the Malakût: crossings of deserts, mysterious voyages over distant seas, and the like.

Kay Khosraw crosses Khotan and travels as far as China, then to the remote coast of Makran. There he embarks upon a mysterious sea and, after seven months' sailing, reaches Afrasiyab's fortress, the underground Kang-Dêz. He captures it and destroys it, along with its ruler. Once the one who tried to seize the Xvarnah by force has been destroyed, the task is complete, and the return to Iran retraces the journey in reverse. This journey still takes place in the dimension where two opposed poles face one another: Afrasiyab's underground fortress and Kay Khosraw's paradisal Kang-Dêz.

The hero cannot enter the latter until he has destroyed its opposite, its shadow. He must draw inward and pass through all the climes of the world and the soul before standing “on the border of Erân-Vêj,” in medio mundi—at the centre of the world—and there entering the centre that is also the origin, the “Land of Visions,” where the laws of the physical world cease to rule.284 The search for the “Source of Life” stretches across all the climes before leading back to the centre. It is the same direction the “archangel of fire” will show the ishrâqî pilgrim, who reaches his goal only at the end of the “Tale of the Western Exile.”

From the moment the Light of Glory rests upon Kay Khosraw—as the kingship of the Grail rests upon Parsifal—everything has been accomplished. The years during which their reigns continue on earth change nothing essential; the spiritual impulse simply becomes more clearly defined. The hero is already a figure of the final destiny of the world, destined to bring the heroic epic to completion as a mystical epic. The latter will be fulfilled in the “Land of Visions,” in that “Orient” where the blessed Kay Khosraw was carried into the presence of the “Wisdom (Sophia) of the Most Holy Father.”

Suhrawardi expressly referred to this vision more than once to show that the “Oriental” philosophers of divine wisdom, the ishrâqîyûn, were none other than the khosrawâniyûn of ancient Persia, whose name derives from Kay Khosraw. In the eyes of this world, King Kay Khosraw is moving toward occultation—concealment from ordinary sight, in the sense used in Shiism of the occultation of the Twelfth Imam.

The physical laws governing his presence in this world are suspended, for the relationship between the “eighth clime” and the other seven climes is not governed by physics. The “eighth clime” is at once very near and very far. This is why such a presence—in the sense of final, awaited presence expressed by the Greek word parousia—remains imminent. It is enough—or it would be enough—for human beings to see with eyes other than those of the flesh, and at last to learn how to look upon what is looking at them ...

Kay Khosraw's disappearance from the visible world unfolds in three stages.285 (a) He receives a revelation from Heaven calling on him to prepare for the “Great Renunciation.” He lives in meditation and prayer; his knights can no longer gain access to him. They become anxious. Have they offended him? When Zâl speaks to the king on their behalf, and they hear him speak of his approaching “ascent to Heaven,” they are terrified.

Has their prince fallen prey to the same dizzy madness as his grandfather Kay Kâûs, who bound his throne to flying eagles and tried to force his way into the secrets of the starry heaven? But no: one cannot storm heaven's entrance with material machines. Their prince calms them with modest, measured words. (b) Kay Khosraw sets up camp outside the city. He solemnly confirms each of his warriors in his office and rank, then appoints Lohrasp as his successor, the founder of a new dynasty.286 (c) Kay Khosraw sets out for a high mountain.

At first a lamenting crowd follows him. Eight of his knights decide to accompany him on the long journey, but their prince warns them: the path ahead leads through lands without water or vegetation; since they cannot follow him “as far as Heaven,” they should at least spare themselves the hardship of returning. Three heed his advice—Godarz, Zâl, and Rostam. The other five persist much longer, at the cost of great exhaustion.

One evening they halt beside a spring. We are undoubtedly at the mysterious boundary, the Source of Life. Kay Khosraw tells his knights that they will never see him again. He gives them a final, solemn warning: a snowstorm is about to break; they must hurry back, or they will no longer find the way to this world. He then bathes in the spring, and suddenly his companions realize that he is no longer visible.

Instead of following his advice, they search for him a long time, but cannot find him—just as the followers of the “Friend of God from the Highlands” will fail to find their master (see below, Book VII). They camp by the spring, talking of their vanished prince. Overcome with exhaustion, they fall asleep, and the storm buries them under deep drifts of snow.

Thus their souls follow their lord, who has gone before them—though he himself did not have to cross the threshold of death—to the mystical castle of Kang-Dêz. He had already withdrawn there in meditation before announcing his “Great Renunciation” to his people.287

This, then, was the traditional image of Kay Khosraw that Suhrawardi had in mind when, in his Oriental Theosophy, he gave the prince so high a place among the sages of ancient Persia, and when he made him the subject of his own “Tale of the Grail.” Iran's heroic epic reaches its completion in mystical vision. The mystical epic succeeds the heroic epic, just as in Suhrawardi's writing the mystical tale takes the place of theoretical doctrinal exposition.

As we have seen, Mr Coyajee established his comparison at the beginning of the heroic story, setting “The Childhood of Kay Khosraw” beside “The Childhood of Parsifal.” When that story reaches its fulfilment as a mystical epic, the task of comparative phenomenology seems to grow wider. The theme of concealment becomes especially important, because the mystery of that concealment can be considered at several levels.

We may note, for our part, that in one continuation of Chrétien de Troyes—the Continuation of Manessier—Parsifal reigns for seven years, then retires to a hermitage and becomes a priest. “The Grail was with him night and day.” After his funeral, the Wondrous Objects—the Grail, the Lance, and the Silver Dish—appear upon his tomb. Then they vanish, and are never seen again.288 Here the Wondrous Objects become hidden from this world in the same way as the Xvarnah.

But Parsifal himself disappears from this world by crossing the threshold of death, since the story tells us of his funeral. In the Queste del Saint-Graal, Parsifal is buried with Galahad in the “Spiritual Palace” of the mystical city of Sarras. Here we come closer to mystical concealment: to be buried in Sarras, and especially in its “Spiritual Palace,” is not to be buried in a city of this world.

Finally, in the Titurel of Albrecht von Scharfenberg, Parsifal and his knights carry the Holy Grail “to India,” and no one has seen them since.289 This time we encounter a form of the concealment of the Grail and its king that corresponds to the concealment of the Xvarnah and Kay Khosraw.

Yet there seems to be another direction in which to look for these parallels: the correspondence between Kay Khosraw and King Arthur in their respective concealments and in the roles they will play at the end of time. We might compare Kang-Dêz, the mystical castle to which Kay Khosraw withdraws, with the enchanted island of Avalon (or Avallon) in Celtic tradition, that marvellous island of the Otherworld. It is an island bearing the fruits of immortality (Avalon, Avallach: the fruit that preserves from death); a mysterious, blessed island also called Insula puellarum, the Island of Maidens.

We may note in passing that exactly the same name appears in certain Iranian traditions of the last things: shahr-e dokhtaran, the City of Maidens.290 Parsifal himself seems to pass through it during his Quest (the “Castle of Maidens” in the Continuation of Wauchier).

But the enchanted castle or island of the Otherworld is always represented as a fortified, inaccessible place, invisible except to one who is invited, called, or chosen. It lies beyond the seas. Compare the voyage described in Suhrawardi's Tale of the Western Exile, or the journey to the Green Island, home of the Hidden Imam.

We can therefore better understand why it is Water, in its supernatural state as the Source of Life, that hides Kay Khosraw from his companions after their last sight of him in this world. Similarly, after the Celts' final battle against the Saxon invader, King Arthur is mysteriously carried away to the island beyond the seas, the island of eternal youth. There his wounds are healed by the Regia Virgo, the island's queen—Morgan—whose beauty exceeds that of her divine companions.

Hidden from the inhabitants of this world, Arthur will return to help his people and lead them to victory. In the same way, Kay Khosraw, having passed through the Water of Life, now dwells unseen in Kang-Dêz among the other companions of the hero of the last days. With that hero he will appear again on the Last Day to bring about the Transfiguration of the world.

We could draw on other traditions here, were our purpose not simply to suggest the convergence of certain Celtic and Zoroastrian traditions concerning the end of time. Judged by our ordinary measures of time and space, the last things seem to lie at the end of a long delay, at an immeasurable distance.

But judged by their own time—as believers who live in the expectation of them experience them here and now, in their own Malakût—both delay and distance disappear. This fulfilment takes place with each mystical believer, as Suhrawardi's “Tale of the Grail” suggests. It transforms geographical places, whose sacred quality is then perceived by a faculty other than the senses. In the twelfth century, Avalon could be identified with the haunted ground on which Glastonbury Abbey was built.291

The same phenomenon occurs when the Grail castle is located at Montserrat, Montségur, or elsewhere, or when the site of Zoroaster's visions shifts from eastern Iran to western Iran, in the mountains of Azerbaijan.292 All these locations can be true, and true at the same time, because theirs is a different kind of truth from the one established by officials drawing up a land register.

Everywhere and always, this truth involves the “symbolism of the centre,” and what William Blake, a visionary of the highest order, knew how to express: “And if a man changes his dwelling, his heavens accompany him—wherever he goes, and all his neighbours mourn his loss. Such are the spaces called earth, and such are their dimensions.”293 The Imago Terrae, the image of the earth, does nothing but reflect the Imago Animae, the image of the soul.

And the Imago is neither an organ nor a representation that depends on empirical perceptions; on the contrary, it precedes, orders, and governs those perceptions. That is why it cannot convey its “object” to those who are indifferent, convince them of the holiness it perceives in certain places, or show them the bonds it perceives among certain events and persons. For it is the organ through which the Malakût is perceived.

And this is precisely the phenomenon that a fully developed phenomenology has the task of “saving”—of safeguarding and making intelligible. It belongs to the same whole traced by the lineage of spiritual knowledge (silsilat al-’irfân) which Suhrawardi sees joining the Khosrawâniyûn to the Ishrâqîyûn when he draws the diagram of his spiritual ancestry. To allow a spiritual fact to reveal itself to us as it reveals itself to Suhrawardi is, at the same time, to understand the faith that gives rise to that fact—the intentional direction of that faith—and the horizons of meaning which the spiritual fact, in turn, makes possible and explains.

Then Kay Khosraw's mystical castle, Kang-Dêz-behesht (Kang-Dêz Paradise), rises before us in the “eighth clime,” the same world to which the mystical city of Hûrqalyâ belongs: the “intermediate Orient.” Castle and city alike represent the “celestial pole,” in medio mundi, at the world's centre. They stand at the threshold of what Suhrawardi calls the “Orient of Lights,” the sources of the Xvarnah, where, in an eternal dawn, arise the divine manifestations contemplated by the sages of ancient Persia.

The fact that Suhrawardi's mystical tales bring the heroic epic to completion as a mystical epic implies that the hero's deeds must be oriented from the beginning: they must tend toward this “Orient,” toward their fulfilment there. This “orientation” is the Oriental goal of the mystical epic. To reach that “Orient” is to give the epic and its heroes their eschatological meaning, their significance for what lies beyond this world and at the fulfilment of time.

We may say that the mystical epic begins whenever the heroic epic—or the romantic or chivalric epic—is oriented in this way, in Suhrawardi's sense of “orient.” From that moment it has two poles, an “orient” and an “occident,” which is to say an inner meaning and an outer meaning, an esoteric and an exoteric dimension (bâtin and zâhir). This is a feature shared by the story of Kay Khosraw and the story of Parsifal.

Whatever key opens up that meaning—Zoroastrianism, Hermeticism, Neoplatonism, or Celtic Christianity—it opens onto a horizon where the Malakût takes shape in concrete spiritual forms: the world where the soul's mystical castles stand. To reveal this meaning, the true meaning, is the work of spiritual interpretation, the ta’wîl whose supreme application in Shiism we have already examined.

But we must not misunderstand. This does not mean simply reducing an imaginal event or a living vision to a few abstract theoretical propositions. That would be to turn our backs on the “Orient.” As we shall have occasion to say again, the event of the soul is itself—and is first of all—the ta’wîl that brings theoretical propositions back to the “Orient” in which they become true. This is the distinctive character of the hikâyat, the narrative that is at once history and imitation (mimesis). It is history because it imitates a higher world, and its imitation is the image (mithâl) of that world.

Here the power of images and imaginative perception to produce knowledge—their noetic function—becomes decisive. At the same time, the storyteller, the “historian,” can no longer be regarded as detached from the events narrated, without responsibility toward them. The listener or reader, for their part, can realize the meaning of those events only if this ta’wîl, this spiritual interpretation, takes place within them as well. The word ta’wîl itself carries the idea of a “passage,” a “turning back,” for it names the act of leading something back to its source, its archetype—its asl, its origin or “original.”

All those who have followed the spiritual paths of Islam have, of course, practised ta’wîl in interpreting the Quran.

What is remarkable about Suhrawardi is that he knew how to apply ta’wîl to the figures of Iran's religious epic—not only Kay Khosraw, but others as well. For him, the deeds of the Iranian heroes, from the Avesta to the Shâh-Nâmeh, thus become part of the phenomenon of the Book that we examined earlier (Book I). Drawing on the interpretive resources offered by Islam's sacred Book, Suhrawardi rose to a vantage point from which he could bring within that same phenomenon of the Book the wisdom of ancient Persia's philosophers of divine things, the wisdom of Hermes, and that of the ancient Greeks and Neoplatonists.

We cannot lightly judge—and still less dismiss, as has been done—Suhrawardi's attachment to Iran and its spiritual heritage.

We must first understand that this Iranism is in no sense racial. It is hieratic, in the Neoplatonic sense of spiritual consecration which we have used here before.

We must then understand the ta’wîl he practises, and confuse it neither with “allegory” nor with an arbitrary construction. Ta’wîl, spiritual interpretation, is not a dialectical construction. It discloses intentions and brings latent possibilities to life. It is the “unveiling of what is hidden” (kashf al-mahjûb). It can understand physical things theologically, which is quite different from “constructing” a physics.

The Neoplatonists already understood this perfectly well. Ta’wîl leads an event back to its source, its “original”—that is, to the Malakût, to the event as it occurs, and as it has its place, in the Malakût. This is how Suhrawardi “leads back” the Iranian epic to its mystical meaning, to its Orient: he recognizes in it an epic already oriented toward that destination.

Hence the importance that will be assumed by the mysterious bird Simorgh, a figure of the Holy Spirit. We see, then, that the Quest for the Orient reaches its fulfilment at the very point where the quests of Kay Khosraw and Parsifal reach theirs.

4. The “Eastern” fulfilment of the heroic epic in the mystical epic

More generally, we should speak of a passage from epic or historical narrative to mystical narrative. The works in which Suhrawardi brings this passage to completion are short prose compositions, and this is precisely what sets them apart from the mystical epics that make up so important a part of Persian literature: the works of Attar, Jami, Assar of Tabriz, Khaju-yi Kermani, Katibi, and others. To bring together what has gone before, we shall try to prepare the way for understanding these mystical narratives—for their ta’wil, the interpretation that leads them back to their spiritual source—by considering two points.

First, there is the idea of the “East” and of the “return to the East.” Here we can discern something shared by Suhrawardi’s Eastern Theosophy, which fulfils the ishraqi project, and the Grail cycle discussed earlier, in which we detected affinities both with the spiritual world of ancient Persia and with Hermeticism. The Iranian spiritual heritage and Hermeticism are both living presences in Suhrawardi’s work; meanwhile, the adventure of the Grail ends in a “return to the East,” understood as a withdrawal from the sight of this world.

Second, there comes a moment when doctrine becomes an event of the soul. This is the decisive moment in which mystical narrative—Suhrawardi’s hikayat—takes shape, and we must understand both the transition and its true interpretation. In the Grail cycle as in Suhrawardi’s, the “Eastern” destiny gives the whole narrated adventure its direction and meaning.

  1. Kang-Dez is the mystical castle at the summit of Mount Qaf, where the adventure of Kay Khosraw comes to its end. Mount Qaf, as we know, is the world of the soul, the malakut, the “eighth clime.” The ishraqi tradition names several cities there, the “emerald cities,” with Hurqalya at their summit. The cycle of the Holy Grail likewise knows of a city “in the East,” where the Grail’s adventure ends: a place higher even than all the heights (Montserrat, Monsalvat, Montsegur) and mystical sites (Corbenic) where the Grail was revealed to its chosen ones in this world. That city is called Sarras. The name may evoke Sarracena, the country from which the Saracens were said to come, and the texts may place it “on the borders of Egypt”; but it would be as futile to search for its geographical coordinates on our maps as to search there for Hurqalya or the Green Island. “On the borders of Egypt” must be understood in the light of the tradition inherited by Suhrawardi, in which the biblical departure from Egypt is interpreted by ta’wil as departure from the “land of exile.” Indeed, Sarras has exactly the significance of the cities of the “eighth clime”: it is an “intermediate East,” a threshold between this world and the other. The Holy Grail rests there twice: first, when it is brought from the mystical Jerusalem to the West (Great Britain); and then, on its return to the East. There, once it crosses the threshold, it vanishes from human sight. These two journeys of the Grail correspond to the two movements familiar throughout Islamic theosophical gnosis: the soul’s descent and its return ascent (nozul and so’ud).

On its “descent,” then, the Grail is carried by Joseph of Arimathea, his son Josephes, and their companions, who stop at Sarras.294 This has occasioned surprise, since the inhabitants are described as “pagans,” worshippers of the stars (like the Hermetic Sabians of Harran).

But Sarras is precisely where we find ourselves in the malakut, the world of the Soul; and that world contains souls in all their diversity, with their many dwelling places. It is there that the soul’s battles take place. The key to Sarras is the palace described as the “Spiritual Palace” (Palais espiriteus), where the passage from the lower malakut to the higher malakut takes place.

In this hidden world of the Soul, Joseph gives his first preaching. And in the sanctuary of the Spiritual Palace, his son Josephes is consecrated—with holy oil brought by angels—as the first Christian bishop and the first guardian of the Grail. He stands at the origin of a lineage which, as we have already seen, neither competes nor can even be compared with any worldly dynasty or canonically established succession. It knows nothing of such successions, for its “history” takes place elsewhere.

Sarras appears again on the road of “return,” when Galahad, the high prince of “celestial” knighthood, brings the Grail adventure to completion. Having healed the wounded king at Corbenic, he sets out for Sarras in the “Holy Land,” accompanied by Percival and Bors. There Josephes appears once more, although he departed this earth long ago.

But that is precisely the point: we are at Sarras now, no longer on this earth. We then hear the account of the Grail’s last Supper, in which, some centuries ago, the knighthood of the West perhaps entrusted its final secret. Surrounded by angels, Josephes celebrates the Grail liturgy in the Spiritual Palace of Sarras. He gives communion to Galahad; then, lifting the paten that covers the Grail, he invites the celestial knight to contemplate its mysteries. Galahad dies in ecstasy, and angels carry away his soul. A heavenly hand, attached to no visible body, seizes the Grail and the Lance and carries them “into heaven.” Never again are they seen in this world. Never again is the supernatural Mass of the Grail celebrated, nor the secret words of consecration spoken that Christ had entrusted to Joseph of Arimathea.

From then on, the lineage of the Grail’s guardians is hidden from this world, and with it the whole knighthood of the Grail Templars. Similarly, with the Twelfth Imam, the line of Imams—the esoteric continuation of prophecy—entered into concealment; and with the concealment of the spiritual “pole,” the entire mystical hierarchy of his Friends and faithful followers also became hidden from human sight.

Percival, too, dies at Sarras, and we are told that the bodies of Galahad and Percival are buried in the “spiritualities” of Sarras. This detail confirms what we have already observed: within the “spiritualities” of Sarras, the body in question can only be the imaginal body, the substance of the resurrection body, the jism mithali, made not of the elements of this world but of the elements of the malakut.295 “Burial” therefore takes on a supernatural meaning as well. The Spiritual Palace of Sarras is not simply a “sublimation” of the Grail Castle.

There are degrees within the world of the malakut. Some of its sacred manifestations descend into this world; others remain enclosed within the malakut, as does the Spiritual Palace of Sarras, precisely because it is the threshold to the higher malakut. The chosen person crosses that threshold; the one who is not chosen never will. Once it is crossed, the “return to the East” is complete. And only a narrative can tell of that return: a doctrinal account can do no more than point towards it. What matters, then, is the telling, because each person will either reach or miss the truth according to whether they know how to hear it.

The Grail cycle has several ways of telling this return. In works composed after Wolfram’s, the “East” is called India. But an old text by Abdias already tells us what “India” actually means: “The historians say that there are three regions bearing the name India.
