The first is the India bordering on Ethiopia; the second lies near the Medes; the third is at the ends of the world.”296 With the third, we find ourselves once more “at the summit of Mount Qaf.” Two texts belonging to the Germanic Grail cycle bear witness to this.

First, around 1300, the story of Lohengrin, the “Swan Knight,” son of Percival, brings about something like a revolution in the Arthurian cycle. Instead of withdrawing across the seas to the mysterious island of Avalon, under the care of the Virgo Regia, King Arthur takes the Grail to India, leading all his knights. Henceforth he and his companions remain its invisible guardians in a distant, unknown country of the “East.”297

Second, Titurel, by Albrecht von Scharfenberg (writing around 1270), carries further the story that Wolfram’s Parzival leaves untold. Wolfram ends with Percival’s enthronement as king of the Grail, while his brother Feirefiz, enabled by baptism to “see” the sacred Vessel, marries Repanse de Schoye, the Grail Queen and sister of Amfortas, and returns with her to his distant kingdom. There they have a son, Prester John, that famous and mysterious figure about whom so many different views have been expressed.298

But Titurel has further events to recount. The Templars of the Grail, perceiving the accumulating threats and disasters outside the Temple, decide upon the “return”—a return that will lead to the Grail’s concealment. (Their decision recalls that of the Ismaili dignitaries who resolved to “withdraw into esotericism,” thereby inaugurating our present cycle of concealment.)299 Percival accordingly carries the Grail and the holy Treasures to India, accompanied by the entire Grail knighthood, intending to join his brother Feirefiz. Here Prester John appears as the independent ruler of a marvellous kingdom, possessing every material and spiritual wealth, including the Seven Gifts and Twelve Fruits of the divine Spirit of Wisdom. Encouraged by his brother Feirefiz, Percival wishes to entrust the Holy Grail to Prester John.

But, to the contrary, it is Prester John who offers his crown and kingdom to the man who comes to him as guardian of the Grail. In the end, the decision comes from the Grail itself: Percival remains king of the Grail; he becomes Prester John’s heir and takes his name. In the Dutch Lancelot,300 on the other hand, Prester John appears as the “son of Percival.” On the mystical plane of spiritual genealogy there is neither impossibility nor contradiction here. As soon as Percival takes the name of Prester John, the Prester John he himself becomes is at once Percival’s heir, the son of his soul—just as Josephes is, for Joseph of Arimathea, the son of his soul.

Prester John’s retreat is established in the invisible realm, where the different versions of the event must be brought into relation according to principles quite unlike those we would apply to Caesar’s Commentaries. Each version tells the same essential event. At Sarras, following Galahad’s ecstatic death, a heavenly hand withdraws the Grail into the invisible. Here Percival leads it back to India, that is, “the ends of the world,” to the East that is the origin of things and has no place on our geographical maps.

Percival and Prester John merge into one another, as though Percival–Prester John had now become the pole of all the Johannites: those who believe in the Church of John, the Johannine Church, as the invisible Church of the Grail. Within this Johannine faith lives belief in the Paraclete—the very Paraclete whom, as we have seen, certain Shiite theosophers identify with the Twelfth Imam, the Imam now in concealment.

We have recalled all these features because they matter in the light of the studies whose conclusions we examined above—studies that brought Zoroastrianism, Hermeticism, and the Grail cycle into contact. In Suhrawardi’s theosophy, Zoroastrianism and Hermeticism are chiefly what determine its “Eastern” destiny. That destiny is enacted and fulfilled in the cycle of mystical narratives forming part of his work. And we have now found the same “Eastern” destiny in the Grail cycle. On either side, the mode of storytelling has a common tone.

Whether we perceive it determines whether we can perceive the order of reality to which the narrated events belong: the level of reality to which these narratives raise the doctrines that constitute their esoteric meaning. Under what conditions do those doctrines constitute the esoteric—and therefore the true—meaning of the narratives? Mystical epic and mystical narrative demand an interpretation through which we may gain access to their reality. Without it, unable to reach that reality, we shall be left speaking merely of “marvels” or the “imaginary.” In other words, whether we actually realise the “Eastern” destiny depends on how we interpret these narratives.

Why does something that can be set out perfectly well as a doctrine, in a sequence of logical propositions—as Suhrawardi has done in his major works—at a certain point escape all theoretical exposition and become a story? The answer lies in the very idea of the East professed by the Ishraqiyun, the philosophers of illumination. We need only recall it briefly. Their “East” is at once beginning and end (arche and telos), the place of origin and of return, the keystone joining the two arcs of descent (nozul) and ascent (so’ud). This entire cycle is the hidden history of a category of beings of light whom Suhrawardi calls Nur Espahbad: Lights that govern a body. His choice of the term already revealed to us a deliberate echo of the ancient Iranian knighthood.

The same code of spiritual chivalry—beautifully expressed by the word javanmardi—runs through the whole tradition. Whether we speak of the struggle of the Fravartis (foruhar), who choose to descend to earth to help Ohrmazd, or of the struggle of the Espahbad Lights against the Darkness of ignorance and forgetfulness; whether we speak of the Light of Glory (Xvarnah) or the Muhammadan Light, of the quest for the Grail or the quest for the Imam now hidden, a constant purpose gives direction to the Iranian spiritual seeker’s struggle. The seeker may aspire to be among the companions of the Saoshyant, helping him bring about the Transfiguration of the world, or among the companions of the Hidden Imam, preparing the “Great Resurrection” (Qiyamat al-Qiyamat, the Resurrection of Resurrections).

In either case the same purpose points towards the only possible victory: a triumphant return to the “Eastern Source”—the Light of Glory, the Muhammadan Light, the Light of the Grail, the Life and Light of Hermeticism. It is “Eastern” not because it is one kind of knowledge among others, or even an especially privileged knowledge, but because it is the East itself: the source and goal of all knowledge. The spiritual hero who completes this Quest possesses both the highest theosophical wisdom and the sacred, transformative experience called ta’alloh, corresponding to the apotheosis of the “Chaldean Oracles” and the Hermeticists (see Chapter II above).

The initiate must therefore travel in a direction whose constant point of orientation may bear different names: the Spiritual Palace of the mysterious city of Sarras; the mystical castle of Kang-Dez; Hurqalya—in short, a city of the “eighth clime.” This “East,” the threshold to all the other “Easts,” Suhrawardi liked to call Na-Koja-Abad, literally the “land of No-Where.” Elsewhere we have discussed at greater length this Persian expression, coined by Suhrawardi, and why it is utterly impossible to translate it as “utopia,”301 even though grammatically it is the exact Persian equivalent of the Greek ou-top(eia). It is “No-Where,” but at the same time it really is a land, a country (abad): the very country in which the events of mystical narratives occur.

One may be granted a vision of it, but no one who has seen it can point out where it is. What leads one there is not the conceptual certainty of a theoretical proof, but the power of an event actually accomplished—and that event can only be told in a narrative. Unless our metaphysics gives real existence to Hurqalya’s “third world,” neither the intellectual world nor the world of sensory perception, our interpretation cannot do justice to its reality. It will mistake this world for the “imaginary” or the “unreal,” and the narrative will offer it nothing but imaginary things. This is why we have stressed the metaphysical importance of the three-world structure in Suhrawardi and the mystical theosophers related to him.

It follows that we must recognise the genuine power to know that belongs to imaginative perception and imaginative consciousness. These are not “fantasy.” Indeed, a metaphysics that recognises their rightful place protects them from the extravagances to which they are abandoned when philosophy treats them merely as a fantasy that produces unreality. Imaginative perception is the faculty by which we enter a world that is neither imaginary nor unreal, but imaginal: the mundus imaginalis.302

We cannot say where this imaginal world is. Someone who has seen it cannot show it to another. That is why it is called “No-Where” (na-koja in Persian): one cannot find one’s bearings in relation to it by using the coordinates of the geographical or astronomical world beneath the Sphere of Spheres. When it is said to “begin at the convex surface” of that sphere, the intention is to suggest the passage beyond, to the summit of the cosmic Mount Qaf. This means passing from the outside of things (the exoteric, ta exo) to their inside (the esoteric, ta eso), from outward history to the true, inward history.

Yet there, within, we find ourselves outside things once again. The world of the Soul—the lower malakut of embodied souls and the higher malakut of liberated souls—is not “somewhere” in the world perceived by our ordinary senses, and so we cannot say where it is located.

But it is the world of the Soul that contains, surrounds, and embraces this entire universe, whose places all belong to the category of ubi, the “where.” The world of the Soul enjoys the privilege of spiritual circles, in which the centre is also the circumference. In relation to locations in the sensory universe, the malakut is an ubique, an “everywhere,” both very near and very far away.

One advances through it only by advancing in modes of being; the physical place from which one reaches it makes no difference. This arrival at, or passage into, the reality of the malakut can be pictured in many ways: the heavenly hand which, at Sarras, removes the Grail from human sight; the Grail’s return to the “East”; Kay Khosraw’s withdrawal into the castle of Kang-Dez; the voyage to the mystical Sinai, to the celestial pole at the summit of Mount Qaf (in The Tale of the Western Exile); the drop of balm which, placed in the hollow of the hand facing the sun, passes through to the back of the hand (in The Tale of the Crimson Archangel); the voyage to the Green Island, home of the Hidden Imam; the journey with the Imam upon the White Cloud; and so forth. Each is an exodus from the world governed by the laws of the external senses and of physics—an exodus accomplished through a fourth dimension, the quarta dimensio.

This exodus answers the command uttered in one of Suhrawardi’s tales: “When you are told, ‘Return!’ it implies a place where you were present before. But woe to you if by the place of return you mean Damascus, Baghdad, or some other earthly city.” It is also the command given in the Quranic verses: “O soul at peace, return to your Lord, well pleased and pleasing to Him … Enter My Paradise” (89:28, 30).

Hence Suhrawardi writes the following lines, which Mir Damad, Qazi Sa’id Qommi, and other great representative Shiite theosophers loved to quote: “The theosopher who truly possesses mystical experience is the one for whom the material body”—that is, the apparatus of the external senses—“has become like a tunic which he sometimes takes off and sometimes puts on. No one is truly a mota’allih, one who has attained this sacred state, until he has experienced taking off and putting on this garment.”303 Such “disrobing” is the condition of entry into Na-Koja-Abad, where nothing can be perceived by our ordinary faculties. A person can accumulate an immense amount of theoretical knowledge and still be incapable of shedding that garment, never reaching the “Eastern” shore. For one cannot arrive there until theoretical knowledge has given way to the event itself.

The question posed above now takes on greater force. Why, we asked, must doctrinal exposition resolve, in the musical sense of the word, into mystical narrative? Because theoretical proof alone can never bring about the “crossing” to the “Eastern” shore. Doctrine must become an actual event. And the reality of that event can only be the reality of the malakut. If we cannot acknowledge that reality, cannot recognise the events of the malakut as real, we reduce visionary narrative to allegory and begin to speak, as people do today, of the need for “demythologisation.” Such “demythologisation” amounts to surrender and incapacity.

Against it we must set what can properly be called spiritual realism, or mystical realism. For if it has been necessary to move from the doctrinal exposition of esoteric truths to a narrative in which they are transmuted into events, what relationship now holds between those truths and the narrative? To discover the story’s esoteric meaning, must we return to the level of conceptual certainty at which the esoteric doctrine stood when expressed as logical propositions? This, in essence, is what certain rational commentators on Suhrawardi’s mystical narratives have done.

But if that were simply the key to visionary mystical tales, those tales would be redundant copies of theoretical explanations, which could convey the same message just as well, or better. The narrative would be no more than an allegory. Whatever an allegory conveys can also be understood through rational exposition; it remains at the same level of knowledge. Mystical narrative, by contrast, tells what can neither be expressed nor made known except through the visionary symbols perceived by the narrator. There is a shift, a change in the level at which knowing takes place. For the narrative is theosophical doctrine become a real event in the world of the malakut. If doctrine is the esoteric meaning of this narrative, it is not doctrine as theory: it is precisely doctrine become event.

We shall see again below that this is the act of the hikayat, the telling of mystical history. The interpretation of mystical narrative therefore does not consist in “descending again,” in bringing its events back down to the level of conceptual certainties. Quite the opposite: ta’wil, spiritual interpretation, carries those certainties back to the level of the malakut, where the narrative’s events take place. Doctrine is the narrative’s esoteric meaning insofar as the telling raises it into a spiritual event, not insofar as it remains theoretical. Only then does mystical narrative fulfil the role of leading the initiate into the mysteries which Suhrawardi intended for it.

This also warns us against the misunderstanding we shall discuss below, which would cause us to miss both the event told in these narratives and their “Eastern” destiny. To make the point clearer, let us use the traditional terminology of the three degrees of certainty. A) There is theoretical certainty (’ilm al-yaqin): knowing, for example, that fire exists, having been told what fire is. B) There is the certainty of direct sight (’ayn al-yaqin): seeing the fire with one’s own eyes, witnessing it. C) There is certainty personally realised (haqq al-yaqin): being burned by the flame, becoming fire oneself.

The distance between A and B is the distance between theoretical doctrine and doctrine become a personal event. In our present case, A means learning from Suhrawardi’s book Eastern Theosophy what the “East” is. B is the level at which doctrine becomes event: one is made a witness of that “East,” because one is “caught up” in the story, in something that only a narrative can tell.

But C emphatically does not mean simply returning to A to uncover the narrative’s theoretical esoteric meaning. It means, on the contrary, taking everything said at A and raising it to B, so that when doctrine has become event, the pilgrim awakens to the awareness that this event is happening to him, and that in his very person he is its reality and its truth.

That, at its highest point, is “Eastern” knowledge. It is why mystical narratives so often speak in the first person. They are the story of the initiate being led back to his “East.” He does not have to prove the event; he has to tell it, recounting what he witnessed and the world in which he witnessed it. In this way, through his own story, he leads the deeds of the heroes back to the “East,” because their story has now become his. His own story is their ta’wil, their mystical interpretation. This is what happened for Suhrawardi with the heroes of the Iranian epic: Kay Khosraw, Zal, Esfandiyar. The heroic adventure comes to completion in the mystical adventure that is its “Eastern” destiny.304

  1. The misunderstanding we mentioned above could prevent us from grasping not only Suhrawardi’s mystical narratives but also the spiritual movement that inspires the whole Persian-language mystical epic, from Attar to Jami. Its roots lie deep in our supposedly “modern” habits of mind, which are fundamentally alien to the “concrete spiritual” reality of the mundus imaginalis, to everything involved in entering the malakut, and hence to the meaning of the real events that take place there. We can see this misunderstanding weighing upon the fine study mentioned earlier, whose authors compared Greek and Middle High German texts in detail and identified Hermetic elements in Wolfram von Eschenbach’s Parzival. Why is it that, when they try to explain the “passage” from the Hermetic doctrine of the Mixing Bowl (Crater) to the action of the Grail poem, we feel as though the explanation has run aground?

The authors305 tend to explain the transition in which “doctrine becomes narrative” as an application of the technique of sensus litteralis, familiar from medieval interpretation and rhetoric. They mean that the poet, having learned a Hermetic doctrine, would have started with these teachings as a secondary, mystical meaning and worked towards a narrative as their primary, concrete meaning—the literal sense. The poet would thus have moved from the analogical meaning to the literal meaning; from the sublime teaching of the Crater, Wolfram would have fashioned something “real,” a sequence of events enacted by a cast of characters. Such an explanation seems to neglect everything involved in prophetic inspiration, poetic creation, visionary feeling and perception, and the sudden opening of a new dimension. Would everything, then, depend on a particular “technique”? But how could any technique make doctrine become event? Wolfram should have produced no more than a laboriously constructed allegory, an elaborate fable.

Yet his Parzival is certainly not that: it is a real story. The question is, what order of reality does it belong to? The misunderstanding underlying this explanation is, above all, the unfortunate and all too common confusion of symbol, or symbolic history, with allegory. We have already identified the source of the confusion: people invoke reality as though it had been established once and for all that only one level of reality exists. This is precisely what a comprehensive phenomenology cannot accept. It must preserve the reality proper to the malakut, the “eighth clime,” and the events that take place there.

A great deal is at stake: narratives such as Suhrawardi’s have more than once suffered from explanations whose ultimate effect is to make them unnecessary. If they merely duplicate a more directly intelligible form of exposition, they can simply disappear once they have been “explained”! Clearly, everything turns on what we mean by the words literal, real, and event. Our preceding pages were intended to confront exactly this problem.

To begin with, the Greek word anagoge means the act of raising or leading upwards (we encountered it earlier in Chapter II, section 2, in connection with the theurgic or sacred ascent of the soul). One rises from the literal meaning to the anagogical meaning, transfiguring the world of things into the world of the Soul. The anagogical meaning presupposes the literal meaning that supports it and of which it is the hidden meaning.

But it is difficult to see why, if we already possess the anagogical meaning, we would need to construct a literal meaning, or “descend” to one—and how the anagogical meaning could be both the starting point and the secondary sense, while the literal meaning would be both the destination and the primary sense. Interpretation is not a technique, although it can certainly establish techniques, such as the various methods of exegesis. Interpretation is the very act of understanding. Understanding takes place at different levels—or, more exactly, in the experience of the spiritual thinkers we are considering, its very act brings several levels to light and unveils them. These levels correspond to one another: they symbolise one another.

The so-called literal meaning is no more primary than the anagogical, mystical, or spiritual meaning is secondary (see also Book I above). Both—and indeed every possible meaning—are forms in which the same Ineffable manifests itself (mazahir), or symbols of it at different levels. At each level they are acts of interpretation, ways of understanding the Ineffable, whether through concepts, lived events, or some other form. They are symbols because, at any given level, the Ineffable can reveal itself only as it reveals itself there, and at that level it is impossible to say it otherwise. An allegory, by contrast, merely repeats something already known in another form, without changing the level at which it is known.

Let us return to the different degrees of certainty, corresponding to the levels of understanding, that we sketched a few pages ago (above, p. 191). The transition from A to B is the passage from doctrinal exposition to something actually accomplished and told in a narrative.

However sublime and esoteric, doctrinal exposition points only to a possibility. It tells us what will really happen if the initiate sets out on the journey. This explains the urgent command Suhrawardi addresses to the initiate at one point or another in his stories of initiation. As soon as that command is heard, we reach something actual, something enacted: an event. In itself this event is already a ta’wil, leading back to the “East.” It is not merely an event of outward history, such as the history in Caesar’s Commentaries or in a social novel. Precisely because it is an event with an esoteric meaning, it is an event of the Soul. It takes place in the malakut, the world that is the Soul’s “East.”

There lies its full reality; there is no need to look for it elsewhere, in outward history. Places—castles, lakes, forests—are states of the soul; its battles are battles of the soul, and so on. Nor should we look for the meaning of this accomplished spiritual event in a theoretical teaching alone, even an esoteric theosophy: the event is what puts that teaching into action and gives it reality. The meaning of this enactment is a transmutation of doctrine: the transformation of ’ilm al-yaqin into haqq al-yaqin, certainty through knowledge into certainty through personal realisation.

We said above that reaching C, the level of personal realisation, does not mean descending from B back to A. Unfortunately, that is what people do today when they speak of “demythologisation,” and they do so only because they cannot reach C: the event is no longer understood. One reaches C insofar as one has risen from A to B and grasped the secret of that passage—insofar as theoretical teaching, having been transmuted into event, is lived as personal fulfilment, an event one experiences oneself. This is not a question of psychology; it is an event in the very order of being, something like an ascent to a new level of existence. Certainly, B, the level at which the event is narrated, will then appear as a sensus litteralis.

But this literal sense belongs not to the world of objects given in ordinary experience and sensory perception, but to the imaginal world: a sensus litteralis in mundo imaginali. There is a principle of Shiite theosophical interpretation: what is esoteric at the level of one world is exoteric at the level of the world immediately above it.

Thus a “literal sense in the imaginal world” is esoteric in relation to what is real in ordinary sensory perception, where objects and events are apprehended in the material world. Mystical narrative is the esoteric meaning of doctrinal teaching or outward history because it leads them onward, transferring them to the “East.” At the same time, that same mystical narrative is the outward, exoteric appearance of the event that puts doctrine into action and transforms it into reality. Its esoteric meaning is therefore not simply that doctrine in its theoretical content, which indicated only a possibility. (This is the decisive point at which commonplace interpretation fails, reducing symbol to allegory.) Its esoteric meaning is the very same doctrine realised in existence, become an event of the soul and therefore told in the narrative.

Accordingly, the words literal, real, and event must always be used with rigorous attention to the level to which they apply. Only then can interpretation preserve the “Eastern” destiny of the mystical adventure. This is certainly a difficult and delicate task. It is not simply a matter of drawing up tables matching established figures to ready-made symbols, but of grasping the progressive transformation of all those figures into symbols.

Let us illustrate the process we have just described—and the misunderstanding to which it is vulnerable—with a series of examples. Once again we take them from the fine study referred to above. Its authors draw parallels between a number of themes in Hermetic teaching and corresponding events in Wolfram’s poem. To connect these comparisons with our analysis, we shall mark each term with a letter, A or B, indicating the respective levels described above.

A) In Hermeticism,306 the Nous (Intelligence), as the power of salvation contained in the Crater, is brought to earth as “life and light.” B) In Wolfram’s poem, an actual dove of dazzling whiteness descends upon the Grail bearing a life-giving host. — A) In Hermeticism, the Crater satisfies its initiates’ thirst for knowledge and promises them life after death.

B) In Wolfram, the community of the Grail receives real food and drink from it, and eternal youth is promised to those who contemplate it. (Yet Wolfram does not tell us the actual form of the Grail thus contemplated. As for the real food, though it is named after foods of this world, its form in reality is shaped each time by the desire, whatever it may be, of the person who receives it. This is a particular feature of the reality of the imaginal world.) — A) Advancing along the path to salvation, the Hermetic initiate reaches a door beyond which shines the symbolic light of gnosis.

B) In Wolfram, this is an actual light: the Grail procession emerges through an actual door and passes through the hall where the Grail community is assembled. (Yet twenty-five maidens carry seventeen lights corresponding to the soul’s stages and spiritual constituents;307 the symbolism of these numbers goes beyond the merely real. The maidens are certainly not allegories. They are indeed real, but their reality is the same as that of the Grail Castle, which belongs to the “eighth clime.”) — A) Among the Hermetic community, initiation establishes a mystical bond of parentage between “father” and “son.”

B) In Wolfram, this relationship becomes a real dynasty within the Grail community. (Real, certainly, but not in the sense of a dynasty belonging to this world. It does not enter history in the ordinary meaning of the word. Its history is real, but it takes place elsewhere.) — A) Hermetic initiates are “brothers” through their religious association. B) Percival and Feirefiz are brothers by actual birth. (But this kinship belongs to the same order of reality as the Grail dynasty.) — A) The person who lacks gnosis looks without seeing: eyes of flesh cannot perceive what Hermeticism calls God.

B) Before his baptism, Feirefiz cannot see the Grail. (But this is itself an indication that the actual vision of the Grail is sacramental in nature.) — A) Hermeticism speaks of the spiritual beauty of the ecstatic and of absorption into divine silence. B) In Wolfram, the ecstatic is Titurel, who remains alone with the Grail behind a closed door and whose physical beauty is extraordinary. — A) Hermetic initiation brings knowledge of Joy. B) During the Grail procession, Percival notices that he has been clothed in a mantle like that worn by Repanse de Schoye,308 the beautiful princess who carries the Grail. (Here, especially, the real can be seen to correspond to what we called level C above.)

We could easily draw the same parallels between themes of “Eastern Theosophy” and events filling Suhrawardi’s mystical tales (The Tale of the Crimson Archangel, The Tale of the Western Exile, The Rustling of Gabriel’s Wings, and so on), as well as Persian mystical epics more generally.

In short, we are left with the impression that when these authors describe as real the event in Wolfram corresponding to the teachings of the Crater, they mean to suggest that the Grail poem brings Hermeticism’s sublime teaching back down to the level of ordinary “reality.”

But would that mean that, before the poem, Hermetic teaching stood on the level of the “unreal”? Certainly not. Here we feel the ambiguity of the word real, and this is why we firmly retain the distinction between the levels established above. Wolfram’s poem does indeed confer reality on a teaching which, considered simply as teaching, had indicated only a possibility, a direction.

The poem enacts the “Eastern” destiny of that teaching, carrying it from A to B. When the word real is applied to B, then, it must not refer to “reality” in the ordinary sense of the term. It must be used according to the demands of spiritual realism: we must admit the full reality, both spiritual and concrete, of the malakut, the “eighth clime,” where all the events of the Grail occur. This is why, as we reviewed the correspondences identified by these authors, we added a slight qualification wherever they called something at B real: to suggest that this reality was, by that very fact, more than what is real in the everyday sense.

The esoteric meaning of the poem does not lie in the bare wording of the Crater’s teaching. The narrative is certainly the outward, exoteric appearance of the event that takes place when one passes from A to B. But its esoteric meaning is not simply to be found back at A, where the doctrine was still a possibility. It does not consist in returning there. Its esoteric meaning lies precisely in the passage from A—the spiritual possibility contained in doctrine—to B, where doctrine flowers into a spiritual event.

Awakening to the secret of that completed passage is what we described above as C. Nothing expresses it better than the final detail: Percival discovers that he is wearing the same mantle as the Grail Queen, the woman who carries the Grail. Only when A has thus been raised to C is it fitting to speak of the anagogical meaning. This assumes that we read Wolfram’s whole poem as a narrative of initiation, which it indeed is, as the magnificent ninth book shows, when the hermit Trevrizent initiates Percival into the Grail’s secret.

Doctrine has been raised into a real event of the soul, something accomplished in the world of the malakut. At this level, doctrine is no longer the esoteric meaning of the event; the event is the esoteric meaning of doctrine. Otherwise, if we needed only to return to theoretical certainty to unlock the esoteric meaning of the poem, the question would arise once more: what use would there be for Wolfram’s epic, or for any similar mystical epic, if they merely duplicated teachings that could be understood without them? Then the Grail cycle, too, would have to be “demythologised.”

But we know that anyone who speaks of “demythologising” is simply in Feirefiz’s condition before his baptism.

These reflections on Suhrawardi’s mystical tales and the Persian mystical epic generally have a wider significance. They bring us back to what we said earlier (Book I) about interpreting the Holy Book. We rejected the word “technique” because it would imply that the inspired prophet and the creative poet alike laboriously consult a catalogue of correspondences. Neither the Persian mystical epic nor the Grail cycle results from an effort resembling the encryption of official documents or the transposition of an orchestral score from one key into another. Nor, in the heat of inspiration, does a composer follow a textbook of harmony page by page. The biblical writers, whether writing “history” or prophecy, wrote under the fire of divine inspiration. The Prophet Muhammad merely “recited” what the Angel of Revelation communicated to him.

Yet beneath the words of biblical and Quranic narratives, spiritual interpreters have discovered a wealth of meanings extending across several worlds. Certainly, someone who “looks without seeing” can regard these many meanings only as later insertions.

But the distinction between A, B, and C can help anyone capable of seeing set that objection aside once and for all. Inspired writings did not even have to begin at what we called A: A is absent from them. Through visionary inspiration, through hierognosis, they stand at B from the outset. The interpreter seeking their spiritual or esoteric meaning does not “descend again” to anything corresponding to A. Certainly, the interpreter must uncover correspondences and reveal the doctrinal contents spontaneously “encoded” by inspiration beneath the text of the narratives.

But if the work ended there, it would all be a simple matter of technique. To discover the gnosis hidden beneath the outward form of the narrative is to discover that gnosis from the outset not as theory, but as something enacted (see also Chapter V, section 1, below).

That is why esoteric interpretation, ta’wil, neither destroys nor abolishes the outward, exoteric appearance. Its task is not to “explain away” that appearance, but to illuminate its depths so that we see through it. The outward form must therefore remain. Esoteric interpretation knows that every concrete detail is a genuine form of appearance (apparentiae reales). Spiritual realism can recognise these appearances as real because it possesses an account of the being of the imaginal world. Without that world, as our authors have repeatedly observed, neither the visions of prophets and mystics nor events such as the resurrection would have a proper place in which to occur. And it is precisely this joining of A and B at C that distinguishes all esoteric interpretation grounded in the “phenomenon of the Book” from a purely theoretical esoteric philosophy.

We must keep this firmly in mind if we are to understand the interpretations of Swedenborg, who finds in the biblical narrative the spiritual history of the spiritual human being, or those of Shiite thinkers, who find in Quranic verses the hidden history of the Imam and the Imamate from the beginning.309

When we speak of joining A and B at C, we mean, in brief, that the narrative’s esoteric meaning is not simply located at A: it is A raised into an event at B. At C, the situation is similar whether the narrative comes from the Bible or the Quran, or from the epic traditions of the Avesta or Ferdowsi. Outward history has become inward history, a history whose events are perceived in the reality of the imaginal world. At C a new “dimension” breaks through, one entirely absent from A on its own.

Suhrawardi gives us the key to esoteric meaning at C—the key to faithful interpretation—on two especially important occasions: in his “Tale of the Grail,” at the instant when his own person suddenly becomes the place where that history happens; and at the conclusion of The Tale of the Western Exile, when he cries out: “This story is about me.” No technique can bring this fulfilment about. It is the unexpected, the unheard-of, imposing itself with the authority of a creative act of divine grace. So it is expressed in the magnificent closing scene of the second part of Goethe’s Faust: “The Unfulfilled—Here becomes an event—The Indescribable—Here is accomplished.”310

The “return to the East” is indeed the Indescribable Event. As soon as one attempts to tell it, the telling inevitably takes on the outward appearance of a sensus litteralis.

But the esoteric meaning of that telling does not lie in some earlier theoretical certainty that continues to exist independently. It lies where every intelligible certainty is transmuted into an accomplished event: “between Heaven and Earth,” as the ending of the second Faust puts it; in the “intermediate East,” the “eighth clime,” as Suhrawardi would say. There lie the place and the secret of the narrative, the hikayat, in which the “Eastern” destiny is brought into action.

5. The “Tale of the Grail” by a Khosrawani mystic

Suhrawardi attempted to tell the Unsayable—the accomplished “return to the East” for which his entire Eastern Theosophy prepares us—in a brief and extraordinary “Tale of the Grail.” All the themes we have explored in the preceding pages were brought together with this tale in view, for its reverberations spread outward in many different tones. We have seen that Kay Khosraw exerted a kind of fascination on Suhrawardi’s thought. He recognised in him the exemplary figure of the sages of ancient Persia, even before Zoroaster, and called those sages the Khosrawaniyun—a name derived from Khosraw—placing them as the predecessors of the Ishraqiyun, since both belong to a single spiritual family. Now, seeing Kay Khosraw appear in this tale as “king of the Grail,” we understand still better the hidden motives of the Shaykh al-Ishraq, the Master of Illumination.

That is why it was appropriate to bring Kay Khosraw’s adventure into resonance with Percival’s, the Light of Glory (Xvarnah) with the Holy Grail. This “Tale of the Grail” could only have been composed by a Khosrawani mystic; it arrives almost as a climax. Just as its challenge to the unsayable awakens something of the spirit of Faust in us, so its very title inevitably sets off distant echoes of Wagner.

The Event it tries to tell must be grasped at the level of reality where it is literally true. That level is not our world, but the world “between Heaven and Earth,” between the “greater East” and the earthly “West.” Neither Kay Khosraw nor Percival nor Galahad has left traces in archival records; Kang-Dez, Hurqalya, and the Spiritual Palace of Sarras lie beyond the reach of archaeological excavation.

Yet their characters are no less real than those regarded as real by history in its ordinary sense, and the places of their adventures are no less real than the ground dug by the archaeologist’s pick. They belong, however, to another order of reality: the order that the preceding pages have sought to locate and establish, in keeping with the very premises of Suhrawardi’s Eastern Theosophy.

The mystic must therefore attempt to tell this Event. But to succeed in telling it means succeeding in making it appear to the listener or reader. Both listener and reader become involved in the same process. Each bears a different responsibility, yet both are joined in the same adventure. Under what conditions can the author try to tell? Under what conditions can the listener or reader understand what the author has tried to say? The hikayat answers both questions, because the conditions of telling for one person and of understanding for the other are identical: they are the very conditions that make the hikayat possible.

We have referred more than once to the hikayat in the preceding pages and discussed it at greater length elsewhere.311 Here let us recall simply that this word, used in both Arabic and Persian, carries the sense of reciting and also of imitating (mimesis). It is a narrative that imitates, a story that re-enacts: the active repetition, here and now, of the Event.

We shall see that this kind of narrative exceeds every technique and everything a technique could anticipate. If technique were enough, anyone who had read the Corpus Hermeticum could have produced a Percival, and anyone who had read Eastern Theosophy could have produced Suhrawardi’s cycle of tales. Even if we cannot create such works, we must still understand them, and recognise something more in them than a technique. For anyone who sees nothing but technique, the Event will certainly never occur. Here, too, the listener or reader bears responsibility: the responsibility of understanding. No one will understand the Event that the story seeks to tell unless that Event has at least begun to take place within them.

Hence Suhrawardi’s commands to “return” (to the place where you were before), to board Noah’s vessel, and to say with him: “May it sail and come to port!”

Through such commands, Suhrawardi divides responsibility for the hikayat between author and listener. He confronts the listener with the very demand that he, as author, had to meet in order to become, in his own person, the place where the Unsayable Event occurs—the Event his narrative attempts to tell. We know well that for Suhrawardi an “Eastern” philosopher can “make the history” of philosophy only by acting as a philosopher. And to act as a philosopher is not to stand by and watch philosophy; it is to put philosophy into action.

Suhrawardi has shown us that, for him, “making the history” of the Ishraqiyun meant practising Eastern Theosophy while claiming for it the ancestry of the Khosrawaniyun, the sages of ancient Persia. The Event takes place by its own authority and thereby summons up the past which the Master of Illumination claims as his own when he calls himself the “reviver of the theosophy of ancient Persia.” In doing so, he “makes the history” of the Ishraqiyun. Henceforth the Event remains, because Suhrawardi does not merely describe or recount a history: he is that history.

I believe I have found the clearest definition of what the hikayat involves in a text which, unfortunately, is still unpublished, like so many others.312 In it, Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa’i explains that in the act of narration or “recital” (hikayat), three things become one: the storyteller, the deeds being told, and the hero to whom the story refers—or from whom it is reported. Likewise, the witness (shahid, one who is present and contemplates), the thing contemplated and present to the witness, and what the witness testifies about it: in the act of testimony (shahadat), these three become one and the same.

Multiplicity and difference arise only from the standpoint adopted. This is because mystical recital becomes real only when the mountain of selfhood, closed in upon itself, has been levelled. “Then it is correct to say that the storyteller, the deeds narrated, and the hero of the story”—the exemplary hero who is “imitated”—“form one and the same reality.” And the Shaykh concludes: “This takes place in every being, according to the measure of each. Meditate, and meditate again!”

Those final words, “in every being,” are decisive. They mean that the threefold unity of the hikayat is formed anew in each person who in turn becomes its living repetition. Such people are not merely “disinterested” readers; they take its full responsibility upon themselves. That is why we can speak of a history that breaks into the course of ordinary history. In the act of re-enactment, time becomes reversible: the event rescues the past from being merely past. Between what we called A—the doctrinal or historical account, still a possibility awaiting fulfilment as a spiritual fact—and C, the completed passage from outward to inward history, there was a gap.

The act of the hikayat crosses it. This history breaks through the history we usually regard as the only real one, the only history “that counts.” This is what led us earlier to say that the only history of a spiritual tradition is that spiritual tradition itself, because the only person who truly “makes its history” is someone whose own history, in one measure or another, is that spirituality. It always is, to some degree; but it may also be so in a disastrous way.

By this we mean that every interpretation of history itself entails a historiosophical position, to use Schelling’s apt expression: a philosophical understanding of what history means. The historian may or may not be conscious of this position, may acknowledge it or remain silent about it. Nevertheless, according to the view of history that the historian inevitably holds, that historian “makes the history” being discussed.

However “objective” the historian tries to be, the very act of turning history into an object will mark the final moment in the “history” undertaken and made in one way or another. It is a “final moment” because so-called historical consciousness rules out any absolute significance for a philosophy or doctrine. Since, from its perspective, the meaning of a philosophy or doctrine is defined essentially by its relation to moments in the past, historical consciousness can only lead everything into the museum of history—at best a “dialectical” museum.

How can such meaning be freed from the whirlpool of historicism? How can we find an absolute meaning in a philosophy or doctrine? The answer lies in the conditions of the hikayat, which Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa’i summed up in a few lines. They are simply another aspect of what we have called spiritual realism. Some will say that this is a demand running counter to our present conception of the humanities and social sciences. Perhaps so.

But our purpose here is not to reform their methods and outlook. It is to show how Suhrawardi brings Kay Khosraw’s heroic adventure to fulfilment in his own mystical adventure, and to enter into what happens in his Tale of the Grail and his other mystical tales.

Now Shaykh Ahmad told us that “this happens in every being.” But one line earlier he had specified: “Every being in whom the mountain of selfhood closed upon itself has been levelled”—in other words, the mountain of subjectivity (ana’iya). Two paradoxes confront each other here. On the one hand, the “objectivity” of the methods employed by historical consciousness goes hand in hand, where the meaning of doctrines is concerned, with a “sceptical subjectivism.” On the other, the hikayat as we have described it may prompt the Western philosopher to exclaim that this is pure “mystical subjectivism.”

Yet precisely in order to establish the threefold unity that rescues the past from its death in the past, the hikayat presupposes the abolition of subjectivity or subjectivism. The objection therefore misses its mark. If it is raised, it will be through ignorance of the human being’s “polar dimension,” a dimension that breaks through the “latitudinal” dimension of historical consciousness. This “polar dimension”—vertical, longitudinal—is established by the apophatic theology of Shiism and Sufism, the theology that speaks of God by acknowledging what cannot be said of God. It affirms that what we call God remains forever the Unknowable, the Abyss, the Silence. God can make himself known to us only by taking on qualities and modes of manifestation corresponding, in each case, to what we ourselves are. God reveals himself to us only within us and through us. Rationalist criticism can hear such an admission only as a confession of “absolute subjectivism.” Perhaps.

But apophatic theosophy can go further and ask: what frees this absolute subjectivity from itself? Nothing other than its own relation to the Ineffable that reveals itself to it. For within this relation the Face-to-Face is formed. The Face through which God reveals and shows himself to a human being is also, in each instance, the Face through which that human being, as they know themselves, shows and presents themselves to God.

Hence the celebrated saying: “Whoever knows himself knows his God.” The Face through which a person knows their God is, by that very fact, the Face through which their God knows them. In Shiite theology (see Book I above), this is the theme of the Imam as God’s Face turned towards humanity and as the human Face upon which God looks. The Imam is thus the pole of a reciprocal relation that is answerable to no condition outside itself. This is precisely what it means to know God only through God himself.

We can now understand why, in the threefold unity of the hikayat, the storyteller is at once the active agent of the deeds recounted and the one who receives and undergoes their action. It is the very paradox we have tried to describe. Our spiritual thinkers can express it in a language and tone uniquely their own, drawn from the mysticism of love. We shall see it wonderfully developed in Ruzbihan (Book III below).

Thus, even in a context of the highest speculative theosophy, Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa’i refers to what poets have said about Majnun and Layla—the Tristan and Isolde of Arabic and Persian poetry. Majnun cannot contemplate Layla’s beauty, which overwhelms and blinds his sight. Only Layla’s own gaze, working within him, can perceive Layla. In the same way, our vision of God can only be the vision through which God, within us, sees himself: “We know God only through a gaze which, within us, is a gaze from Him and towards Him, as the poet says: When the Lover longs to gaze upon the Beloved—Though he has no strength to do so—The Beloved, in her mercy, lends him her own gaze—So that the Lover’s gaze, beholding the Beloved—Is the Beloved’s own gaze, beholding herself.”313

Thus the threefold unity of the hikayat is fulfilled “in every being in whom the mountain of selfhood,” or subjectivism, “has been levelled.” In being levelled, this subjectivity is freed from itself and thereby established as absolute subjectivity by the very act that works within it and sets it free. These distinctions prepare us to hear Suhrawardi’s hikayat of the Grail, all the way to the declaration in which its mounting tension finds release: he himself is the Grail of Kay Khosraw.

As we know it from a very small number of manuscripts, this “Tale of the Grail” forms a chapter in one of Suhrawardi’s mystical treatises written in Persian. The work is composed as a rhapsodic sequence of twelve parables or mystical tales, the first of which gives the collection its title, The Language of the Ants (Loghat-e Muran).314 The fourth is the hikayat, the mystical recital of Kay Khosraw’s Grail. We can distinguish four moments in it: three episodes and a conclusion.

  1. A prelude introduces the theme: the mysterious Cup possessed by Kay Khosraw, one of the forms in which the Light of Glory manifests itself. Because of its origin, the cup is traditionally known as the “Grail of Jam” (Jam-e Jam), that is, of Jamshid (Yima), the primordial sovereign who was commanded to build, in Eran-Vej, in medio mundi, at the centre of the world, the var, the paradisal enclosure so similar to Kang-Dez and to the cities of the “eighth clime.” This Grail, belonging first to Jamshid and then to Kay Khosraw, possesses the powers of a microcosm: it is the “mirror of the universe.” Whoever holds it can contemplate within it the mysteries of the visible and invisible worlds, just as Galahad was allowed, in the Spiritual Palace of Sarras, to contemplate the highest divine mysteries in the Grail.
  2. There follows a brief account of the Grail’s mysteries, whose spiritual meaning is already apparent in the prelude describing its powers. The tale suggests that the Grail is the spiritual microcosm, the human being of Light within the human being (the Espahbad Light), enclosed in a “sheath of skin” or “leather scabbard”—that is, in the material body of flesh. But sometimes this Light loosens its bonds and slips out of its sheath; at that moment the Grail becomes invisible. This is the moment when Kay Khosraw, like Titurel alone with the Grail behind the symbolic door, is absorbed in contemplation, united with the beings of light. (This disappearance corresponds to the pilgrim’s arrival at the summit of Mount Qaf in The Tale of the Western Exile; made permanent, it is Kay Khosraw’s vanishing from his knights’ sight near the Fountain of Life, or the Grail’s removal when Percival takes it back to the “East.”) The Grail is visible only when the leather scabbard—the physical body—binds it again. But what becomes visible is merely what shines through that form “fashioned on the lathe,” the ten “joints” symbolising the five external senses and the five inner senses.
  3. When the bonds are loosened, the soul of light (Nur Espahbad) rises towards its “East” in an ecstatic moment that anticipates its exitus, its departure from this world. This “East,” this hour of ishraq, of illumination, is called the “spring equinox”: the moment when Day and Night come into balance and the victory of Light over Darkness is decided. The same feature recurs throughout the tradition of Jamshid’s Grail. Kay Khosraw then holds the Grail facing the sun, so that the impressions of all visible and invisible worlds appear within it. This recalls the symbolism of the drop of balm placed in the hollow of the hand which, when the hand is held towards the sun, passes through to the other side (at the beginning of The Tale of the Crimson Archangel). From this moment, Eastern Theosophy is no longer simply a doctrine over which the intellect labours. Its “Eastern” destiny is enacted through the anticipation of an end of time experienced personally. The transposition of eschatology into personal experience is announced by the appearance of three Quranic verses. Through ta’wil, their resonance travels into the mystic’s innermost being. That is why we have translated these three verses in the present tense, as the grammar permits and spiritual interpretation requires.
  4. Finally comes the concluding declaration, a quatrain proclaiming who—or what—the Grail is. The revelation of the Grail breaks forth as the revelation of the human being of light who has attained self-knowledge. Here is an attempt to translate this Tale of the Grail:

“I. Kay Khosraw possessed the Grail, the mirror of the universe. Whatever his heart desired, he could contemplate in that Grail. Through it he learned of the invisible worlds; within it he surveyed the whole of existence.

“II. This Grail was enclosed in a leather scabbard, shaped on a lathe and fitted with ten joints. Whenever Kay Khosraw wished to learn some further mystery of the Invisible, he set this scabbard turning again (to undo it). When he had loosened every bond, the Grail was no longer visible. But when the turning bound all the joints together once more, the Grail appeared.

“III. At the spring equinox,315 Kay Khosraw held the Grail directly facing the Sun. When the star’s radiance struck the Grail, all the lines and impressions of all the worlds could be contemplated there, made manifest.

“When the Earth is spread out flat, casts forth what it contains and remains empty, when it listens to its Lord and becomes worthy of Him—then you, O human being, you who strive on your way towards your Lord, behold, you meet Him (84:3–5). — Nothing hidden within you will remain concealed (69:18). — Every soul will know what it has sent ahead of itself and what it has left behind (82:5).

“IV. When I heard my master tell the Tale of the Grail of Jam,
I myself became the Grail of Jam, the mirror of the universe.
Let my own Grail, the mirror of the universe, be drawn from its sheath;
This buried Grail is the burning Flame that feeds upon our death.”316

In this brief and astonishing “Tale of the Grail,” all the conditions we have examined in the preceding pages are enacted, brought together, and confirmed. The content of the doctrine that leads towards self-knowledge flowers into the image of Kay Khosraw’s Grail, at once a real object and a real event. The Unsayable which Eastern Theosophy has struggled to express is accomplished as the “return to the East.” The event becomes the hidden meaning of doctrine, and the fulfilment of that hidden meaning. At the same time, the tale expresses it beneath the outward appearance of a sensus litteralis.

Yet the hidden meaning of this “literal sense” is not a return to the theoretical certainty of the doctrine that explains what the “East” is. It lies on the higher level where doctrine, having become event, brings the initiate to awareness of the Event whose very place of occurrence is his own person: “I was—I became—the Grail of Jam, the mirror of the universe.” The Grail is a real object, but real in the way that objects of the supersensible world are real. It is a real event, although it does not occur in our world and breaks the course of its history.

Indeed, it is so real that it is never “superseded,” because it is always waiting to “take place.” What makes the Word true is not that it belonged to “its own time,” as historical consciousness understands the phrase, but that it becomes the time of every faithful initiate in whom the Event is accomplished.

Thus the ta’wil practised by Suhrawardi in his Tale of the Grail and his other mystical stories is in perfect accord with his own ta’wil of the Holy Book. He sets out its rule as follows: “Recite the Quran in ecstasy (wajd), with inward emotion and subtle reflection. Recite the Quran as though it had been revealed for your own case alone.”317 This brings us back to the “phenomenon of the Holy Book,” as expressed in the saying of the Fifth Imam, Muhammad al-Baqir (see Book I above). If the Quranic verses had meaning only in relation to the circumstances and people for whom they were revealed, the entire Quran would have been dead long ago!

But ta’wil, the interpretation that makes it the hikayat, the story of each believer who recites it in Suhrawardi’s manner, keeps it alive “until the Day of Resurrection.”

The two mystical tales by Suhrawardi which we shall now translate will offer further examples. In The Tale of the Western Exile, the stages of the exile’s “return journey” are marked by Quranic verses which ta’wil applies to the mystic’s personal situation. These verses mark the successive stages of his spiritual state until he reaches the “East,” the “celestial pole.” At the conclusion we shall encounter a figure recognisable as the one whom Suhrawardi’s Hermeticism has already introduced to us as “Perfect Nature.” Before that, we shall read The Tale of the Crimson Archangel.

At two decisive moments in the initiation the archangel gives his earthly companion, two episodes from the Iranian mystical epic will enter the story. Once more we shall see that the heroic adventure finds its fulfilment in the mystical adventure, which enacts its “Eastern” destiny. This is how Suhrawardi proceeds throughout his Eastern Theosophy: he leads the sages of ancient Persia forward into Islam and back to the “Eastern Source,” bringing forth the Ishraqiyun, the Neoplatonists of Islamic Persia, as the spiritual heirs of the Khosrawaniyun of ancient Persia.

PreviousIII. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and AngelologyNextV. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic

Chapter V “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic

1. The Purpose of the Tale

The “Tale of the Grail” has just shown us, in living action, the “Eastern” goal of the “Eastern theosophy”—the wisdom of the spiritual East. We have seen at work the threefold unity implied by the hikâyat, the mystical recital: the person telling the tale, the heroic story being told, and the hero whose deeds are retold merge into a single reality, different in each individual case.

The ishrâqî mystic, a seeker of illumination, speaks in the first person as a khosrawânî, a sage of ancient Iran; he himself is the Grail of Kay Khosrow. In the same movement, the Ishrâqîyûn (the Illuminationists) become the living hikâyat of the Khosrawânîyûn, the sages of ancient Iran. Through them, the deeds of their predecessors are enacted again, made present even in Islamic Persia, by means of ta’wîl, the spiritual interpretation whose secret is preserved and extended by the inner tradition of Islam.

When the Grail is unveiled—and its true identity is disclosed—the Eastern adventure reaches its end in an anticipation of the soul’s final departure, its exitus. It fulfils the Prophet of Islam’s injunction: “Learn to die spiritually before physical death overtakes you.” The fear and darkness of ignorance that make us dread death are now dispelled. The initiate knows that he is going home, and knows the way. “The indescribable has become real.” What had not yet been accomplished has happened; it has become an event, an accomplished fact.

For an Illuminationist, this indescribable reality is precisely what the Book of Eastern Theosophy attempts to describe, along with the major works that prepare the way for it.

Yet Suhrawardi and the Illuminationists said repeatedly that reading books is not enough to make one a member of the family of the “hieratic” sages, those who have themselves attained spiritual knowledge. Books can set the reader on the path and guide him toward fulfilment, but in themselves they remain no more than a possibility.

One must acquire the ability, as a settled habit, to slip out of the physical senses as though taking off a garment—the leather sheath that concealed the Grail of Kay Khosrow—and enter the “eighth clime,” the Middle Orient of the spirit, the mundus imaginalis, or imaginal world, which stands at the threshold of the greater spiritual Easts. To a historian accustomed to the usual categories of the outward history of religions, what seems inconceivable may be the sudden, compelling reappearance, at the heart of the Sufism of Islamic Persia, of figures from the Zoroastrian tradition of ancient Persia.

Yet here that apparent impossibility has become a spiritual fact, embodied and made intelligible in the person of the Shaykh al-Ishrâq, the Master of Illumination. Before him, we could certainly search for traces that would establish a passage and continuity between the two Persias. Such traces are plentiful, but they can always be disputed, as traces are disputed when the person who left them is no longer present. From the time of the Master of Illumination onward, we are no longer dealing merely with remnants to be collected. We confront the compelling presence of a spiritual event that will itself leave its mark on everything that follows: the Illuminationist tradition of Islamic Iran.

The figure of Kay Khosrow, the king who attains ecstasy, dominates the spiritual horizon of ancient Iran as Suhrawardi sees it. We already know the principle that governs our master’s practice of ta’wîl: “Recite the Quran as though it had been revealed for your own case alone.” His “case” is that of a seeker of spiritual knowledge whose vision opens onto many spiritual universes. They hold the secret of his own story, because it is from them that he came, and to them that he returns. His story is a metahistory: it breaks free of the straight line imposed by outward history, for neither its origin nor its future has its place on that level of reality.

To become contemporary with that past and that future—to meet them together in the present—requires a critical understanding of time. Such an understanding would later be developed by other thinkers, notably, as we have mentioned, the great Shia philosopher Qazi Sa'id Qommi.

Suhrawardi could apply this principle of interpretation not only when reciting the Quran but also when reading the book that, for Islamic Persia, serves almost as a Bible of ancient Iran’s heroic deeds: Ferdowsi’s tenth-century Shâh-Nâmeh, the Book of Kings.

We can imagine him reading the Shâh-Nâmeh as we read the Bible, or as he himself read the Quran: as though it had been written for his own case alone. We have just recalled what that case involves. Read in this way, the Shâh-Nâmeh could become the history—or rather the metahistory—of the soul as it lives in the heart of the spiritual seeker.

Suhrawardi could therefore perceive, woven into the very fabric of the Shâh-Nâmeh, the whole history of the soul and its world. This is the level on which the poem becomes readable once we keep in mind the fullness of being and all its worlds. It is much as the distinguished Neoplatonist Proclus knew how to read the story of mysterious Atlantis: as a true history and, at the same time, as the “image of a certain reality existing within the Whole.”318

A commentary on the Shâh-Nâmeh along these lines would be fascinating. It would show the poem interpreted in a way comparable to the reading of Homer’s Odyssey in Hellenistic religious devotion. Unfortunately, apart from the exceptional figure of Kay Khosrow, the Master of Illumination has left us indications of a spiritual interpretation for only three other heroes of the Shâh-Nâmeh: Zal, Rostam, and Esfandiyar. Yet those indications are of enormous significance.

We shall see the meaning of these three figures emerge at the heart of the work translated here as the “Tale of the Crimson Archangel.” This is precisely why, having to choose among Suhrawardi’s mystical tales, we gave this one precedence over the others.319

Following the example of Kay Khosrow, this tale allows us to understand particularly well how Suhrawardi’s spiritual interpretation discovers the Eastern fulfilment of the heroic epic: the history of the soul encoded within it. It shows how the Iranian heroic epic reaches its resolution as a mystical adventure. This is certainly not a matter of abstract speculation or a table of correspondences from which one can produce automatic translations of one thing into another.

The meaning of Zal’s story and of Rostam’s is suggested to us only as something learned in “conversation with the Angel.” That conversation, too, takes place “between Heaven and Earth.” In following the outline of the Shâh-Nâmeh, the story of the soul awakened to spiritual knowledge descending into this world and its ascent in an ecstatic exitus, made possible by the powers of the higher worlds, is distributed between the figures of Zal and Esfandiyar.

But this arrangement is not something whose meaning can be proved by logical argument. The certainty disclosed by spiritual interpretation belongs to a level beyond both the senses’ perception of the heroes’ outward exploits and the grasp of ordinary reason.

Indeed, the hidden meaning of the stories of Zal and Rostam is revealed only in enigmatic phrases, almost in passing.

Yet their connection with the mystical bird Simorgh tells us that this is the secret of the whole tale. Understanding that secret determines whether the Angel’s disciple can answer the Angel’s veiled challenge: “If you are Khezr, you too can pass through.”

Through its paired episodes concerning Zal and Esfandiyar, the “Tale of the Crimson Archangel” is thus immediately linked to the Iranian heroic epic, now destined to find its fulfilment as a mystical epic.

Another of the Master of Illumination’s tales, by contrast, is more directly connected through its imagery with ancient gnosis and Hermeticism: the “Tale of the Western Exile.” This is the second tale we have chosen to translate here. We chose the pair not only because together they bring to life the dominant elements of Eastern theosophy—Neoplatonically interpreted Zoroastrianism and Hermeticism—but also because the two tales have a special relationship to one another. They stand in much the same relation as two works in Avicenna’s cycle of visionary tales: the “Tale of Hayy ibn Yaqzan” and the “Tale of the Bird.”

The first describes the terrain; it maps the universes that the mystic must cross to escape the “cosmic crypt.” The “Tale of the Bird” is the actual flight, carrying the pilgrim all the way to the end of his spiritual ascent.320 In just this way, the two tales of Suhrawardi translated here complete and answer one another, forming a single whole.

We said earlier that someone gifted with the vision can see the “eighth clime,” but cannot show it to someone else—not even point out the landmarks of the way in any effective manner. Only an Angel can attempt to do that. The “Tale of the Crimson Archangel” shows the direction, indicates the road, and hints at how one may “pass through,” culminating in the final invitation: “If you are Khezr…” The “Tale of the Western Exile,” for its part, returns to the very beginning, as the first tale does.

But the exile then answers the invitation he has received: he sets out. His road is full of adventures, until at last he reaches the “Emerald Rock.” He must come back, for until the final exitus every ecstasy is fleeting.

But at least he now knows the road he himself must travel. He tries, in turn, to indicate its stages. He does so, however, by encoding them in Quranic verses that must be deciphered with the aid of ta’wîl. And to use that key of interpretation, one must oneself set out upon the road.

Here again we must avoid a misunderstanding. The few indications we give in our introductions to these tales are justified only if we remember what was said earlier (Chapter IV, section 4) about this kind of explanation. It would be a paradox—indeed an illusion—to suppose that one had explained the meaning of a mystical or initiatory tale by reducing the events it recounts or evokes to a set of theoretical doctrines, however sublime those doctrines might be. For the very purpose of the tale, as a mystical tale, is to pass beyond them. Suhrawardi’s earliest commentators, writing in Arabic or Persian, certainly tried to provide the keys to his tales by proceeding in just this way.

Yet when we have finished reading their explanations, we see that, if we stopped there, we would have missed everything that makes the tale a drama. Taken instead as guides to orientation, their commentaries are extremely useful. They are ductus lectionis, guides to reading, and nothing more. If they alone could give us the “inner meaning” of an action whose narrative form supplied merely its “literal meaning,” Suhrawardi would have had no reason to write his cycle of tales at all. He wrote them because his great teaching treatises, and the form he had adopted in those works, still fell short of what he needed to say.

What he needed to express was no longer only the coherent body of theosophical teaching, but that same teaching transformed into an event of his own soul. Each stage of the doctrine became a stage of the journey: a state actually lived and realized by a soul making, in reality, the pilgrimage described by the teaching. Exposition became story. The story, then, is not the starting point from which the doctrine is derived.

Nor does it speak of events taking place in our phenomenal world, the world of outward history. It is already the elevation of the doctrine to the level of events occurring in the world of the Soul, the malakût. This is why, from the standpoint of teaching, the doctrine may be called the tale’s inner or esoteric meaning; yet from the standpoint of spiritual realization, it is the tale that reveals the inner meaning of the doctrine.

Whenever we refer to a point of cosmology, psychology, or angelology to “clarify” a particular phase of the narrated event, we must not forget that the cosmological theory, for example, is not in itself the tale’s esoteric meaning. It becomes that meaning only when it is raised to the level of the tale and transformed by it into an event. Then, indeed, the theory is the tale’s meaning, precisely because the tale is the theory’s happening, its fulfilment. This “circle of interpretation” simply reflects Suhrawardi’s fundamental conviction: philosophy that does not culminate in mystical experience, in a “hieratic” ascent, is barren and meaningless. Conversely, mystical experience without prior philosophical training runs a serious risk of going astray.

But brought together, the two attain a level higher than either could reach on its own.

We have stressed this point before (Chapter IV, section 4, levels A, B, and C), because it seems to us that the most serious misunderstandings about interpretation lie hidden here. The “Tale of the Western Exile” will provide a further, exact confirmation. In that tale, particular stages of the “return” are represented by particular Quranic verses. The journey of return is therefore the esoteric meaning of those verses.

It follows that the fulfilment of the event cannot be sought in the mere words of the Quranic verse, but in what those words mean when they are lived and realized—made present again through action, in accordance with Suhrawardi’s interpretation and that of the Fifth Imam. The meanings of the Quranic verses then unfold across several levels of the universe.

At each level, the literal meaning proper to that level is true and is at the same time a spiritual meaning; that literal-and-spiritual meaning is, in turn, the esoteric meaning relative to the level immediately below it. The visionary landscapes that open before the soul in the mundus imaginalis, and the figures who appear within them, are therefore real with the reality proper to supersensible beings.

But this reality is far more than the reality of a mere literal narrative whose esoteric meaning would be supplied by theoretical doctrine.

We can now understand why a theosophy expressed through dramatic action passes beyond the level at which it could, or should, furnish the “dialectical proofs” available to theoretical reason. Its grounds of certainty and its proofs are essentially those of directly tasted wisdom: dhawq, related here to the Latin sapere, knowledge that actually savours what it knows.321 And this knowing, a spiritual knowledge that saves, is inseparable from the movement of faith; it is that movement itself.

We can only be astonished by certain sweeping, categorical claims made today against gnosis—for instance, the assertion that it tries to provide faith with a second set of truths carrying the same kind of certainty as the exact sciences. Such a claim betrays a very limited acquaintance with gnosis. We have expressly rejected any idea of knowledge running alongside faith as a duplicate of it.

But if one begins by separating pistis (îmân, fides), faith, from gnôsis (’irfân), spiritual knowledge, one will obviously never succeed in bringing them together again in the unity of theosophia (hikmat ilâhîya), divine wisdom.

Let us now use these principles to examine the themes of the “Tale of the Crimson Archangel.” The tale begins with an important prologue. At its close, seven themes are announced, which the Angel will then develop in the teaching through which he initiates his disciple.

2. The Prologue to the Tale

The prologue itself unfolds in several stages.

a) A question put to the author by a friend provides the opening: the pre-existence of the soul. Here the reader will recall the magnificent image in Plato’s Phaedrus of souls following the gods in a heavenly procession, and of the fall of some among them.322 The soul’s wings naturally suggest the form of a bird.

Hence the first motif: the “language of the birds” (Mantiq al-tayr). The Quran speaks of this language (27:16), saying that Solomon, as a prophet, had received the gift of understanding it. To understand the language of birds is to understand the language of all created beings as they speak through their very existence. Each thing is then alive and has a voice; each reveals its secret. To understand that language is to possess the key to symbols. This precious gift is therefore associated with the state of the soul before its fall into our world.

Moreover, Mantiq al-Tayr, The Language of the Birds, is the title of one of the best-known Persian mystical epics, by Farid al-Din Attar (twelfth century), whose culmination is the episode of Simorgh. We have already encountered that name here, and shall meet it again, for Simorgh is of great importance in Suhrawardi’s tales.

b) The soul’s pre-existence leads naturally to the next theme: its fall into captivity. We hear of the hunters called “Decree and Destiny, spreading the net of predestination.” Proclus, too, speaks of hunters, those who “together with the daimones, pursue souls and imprison them in bodies.”323 More immediately, Suhrawardi’s theme here closely resembles Avicenna’s visionary tales.

The “Tale of the Bird,” originally written in Arabic by Avicenna and translated into Persian by Suhrawardi, begins in a similar way. It speaks of searching for a friend to whom one might entrust a secret, and makes a moving appeal to the “Brothers of Truth.” Then the narrative begins: “When the hunters caught sight of us, they gave a whistle so pleasing that it lured us into uncertainty […] and suddenly we fell into the nets.”324

Suhrawardi develops the same theme in the mystical rhapsody called “The Language of the Ants,” from which we earlier drew his “Tale of the Grail.” Elsewhere in that work, in its eighth chapter, he returns to the image of a captive bird. This time it is not a falcon, but a bird whose plumage reflects the colours of paradise: a peacock. “A king had a garden that was never, in any of the four seasons, without sweet herbs, greenery, and places of delight […]. Every joy the mind could conceive, every beauty the imagination could picture, was present in that garden.

“Moreover, a flock of peacocks of the utmost grace, beauty, and delicacy had settled there, and the garden had become their homeland. One day the king took a peacock from among them and ordered it to be sewn inside a skin, so that none of the colours of its plumage remained visible and, try as it might, it could no longer see its own beauty […]. The peacock lost all memory of itself; it forgot the king, the garden, and the other peacocks.”

Thereafter the bird’s whole horizon was reduced to the slit in a little basket through which food was passed to it, “and the conviction took root in its heart that no country could be larger than the bottom of the basket.”325 Once again, the peacock sewn into a covering of skin recalls the Grail buried inside its leather sheath. For the Grail to appear, or for the bird’s true form to become visible, each must be freed from the covering that conceals it.

In either case, its reappearance means reappearing in its own world, the world from which it descended only to be hidden here under an enclosing skin. To become visible again in its own world is to become invisible to this one. This is one of the ruling themes of Illuminationist gnosis, and indeed of spiritual gnosis in general.

We shall encounter another version at the beginning of the “Tale of the Western Exile.”

c) Captivity and the fall are followed by escape. This theme recurs in the other mystical tales. Each time, the author evokes a state in which the senses are “bound,” thereby releasing the person from subjection to the world of sensory perception.
