  11. Then I took the two burdens together with the spheres and placed them, along with the jinn, inside a flask I had made round, with lines drawn upon it in the form of circles.
  12. I cut off the streams of living water from the middle of heaven.
  13. When the water stopped flowing to the mill, the building collapsed, and the air escaped into the air.
  14. I hurled the Sphere of Spheres against the heavens, crushing the sun, moon and stars.
  15. Then I escaped from the fourteen coffins and the ten tombs, from which the shadow of God rises again, to be “drawn little by little” (25:48) towards the sacred world, after “the sun has been appointed its guide” (25:47).
  16. I found the path of God. Then I understood: “This is My path, the straight path” (6:154).
  17. As for my sister, during the night she was “enveloped in divine punishment” (12:107). She remained in darkness for part of the night, after fever and nightmare had brought her to a state of complete prostration.
  18. I saw a lamp filled with oil. Light streamed from it and spread through every part of the house. Even the lamp's niche caught fire, and the inhabitants blazed beneath the light of the sun rising upon them.
  19. I placed the lamp in the mouth of a Dragon that lived in the castle of the Waterwheel. Beneath it lay a certain Red Sea; above it were stars whose places of radiance are known to none but their Creator and “those firmly grounded in Knowledge” (3:5).
  20. I saw that the Lion and the Bull had both disappeared. Sagittarius and Cancer had folded back upon themselves through the turning of the Spheres. The Scales remained in balance when the Star of Yemen (Suhayl, or Canopus) rose beyond certain fine clouds woven by the spiders at the corners of the elemental World, in the realm of generation and dissolution.
  21. We also had a sheep with us. We left it in the desert, where earthquakes killed it as lightning struck it.
  22. And when the whole distance had been covered and the road had come to its end, while “the furnace boiled over” (al-tannūr, the “athanor,” 11:42 and 23:27) in the conical form (of the heart), I saw the heavenly bodies. I joined myself to them and heard their music and melodies. I was initiated into their song. Its sounds struck my ears like the rumbling of a chain dragged over hard rock. My muscles seemed about to tear apart, my joints to come undone, so intense was the delight I felt. The experience kept returning until at last the white cloud dispersed and the veil was torn.

III

  1. I emerged from the grottos and caves and left the antechambers behind me. I went straight towards the Spring of Life. There I saw the Great Rock on the summit of a mountain resembling the Sublime Mountain. I questioned the fish gathered in the Spring of Life, resting peacefully in the gentle shade of the sublime Summit. “What is that high mountain?” I asked. “And what is that Great Rock?”
  2. One of the fish then “took a certain current as its path through the sea” (18:60). It said to me: “That is what you have longed for so deeply. The mountain is Mount Sinai, and the Rock is your father's place of prayer.” “But who,” I asked, “are these fish?” “They are beings like yourself. You are children of the same father. The same ordeal that struck you struck them. They are your brothers.”
  3. When I heard this answer and felt its truth, I embraced them. I rejoiced to see them, as they rejoiced to see me. Then I climbed the mountain. There I saw our father, like a Great Sage, so immense that Heaven and Earth seemed about to split apart beneath the radiance of his light. I stood amazed, overcome with wonder. I went towards him, and he was the first to greet me. I bowed down before him to the ground, almost annihilated in the light that poured from him.
  4. I wept for a while, then told him of my suffering in the prison of Qayrawān. He said to me: “Take heart! You are safe now. Yet you must return to the western prison, for you have not entirely cast off your bonds.” At these words my reason deserted me. I groaned and cried out like someone on the point of death, and begged him to spare me.
  5. He said: “For now, your return is unavoidable. But I have two pieces of good news. First, once you are back in prison, you will be able to come to us again, and ascend easily to our paradise whenever you wish. Second, the day will come when you are wholly freed. You will join us, leaving the western land completely and forever.”
  6. His words filled me with joy. He went on: “Know that this mountain is Mount Sinai (23:20, Ṭūr Saynāʾ). But above it lies another mountain: the Sinai (95:2, Ṭūr Sīnīnā) of the one who is my father and your grandfather. My relation to him is no different from your relation to me.
  7. “And we have other ancestors besides, our lineage reaching at last to a king who is the Supreme Ancestor, himself without ancestor or father. We are his servants. We owe him our light; we kindle our fire from his fire. His is the greatest beauty of all beauties, the highest majesty, the most overwhelming light. He is above what is above. He is the Light of Light, and beyond Light, from eternity to eternity. He reveals himself in all things, ‘and all things perish except His Face’ (28:88).”
  8. Postlude. I am the one spoken of in this Tale, for I have lived through the catastrophe. From the upper reaches I fell into the abyss of Hell, among people who do not believe. I am held prisoner in the land of the West. Yet I still feel a certain sweetness I cannot describe. I have sobbed and pleaded and sighed with grief at our separation. That brief reprieve was one of those dreams that swiftly fade.
  9. Save us, O my God, from the prison of Nature and the fetters of Matter. “And say: Glory be to God! He will show you His Signs, and then you will recognise them. Your Lord is not heedless of what you do” (27:95). “Say: Glory be to God! Yet most of them remain unaware” (31:24).

4. The Gnostic's Encounter with the Angel

I. Who is the personal Angel? Anyone who has read, and perhaps carefully reflected upon, this tale by Suhrawardī will gradually have recognised and confirmed all the themes we examined at the beginning of this chapter as making up the “history of the gnostic.” The theme of the self as an “objective reality” involved in self-knowledge—in the act by which the knowing subject comes to know himself—has found its final resolution, in the musical sense of the word, in the encounter with the Angel on the mystical Sinai.

More precisely, the self now appears to us as our essential, authentic “I,” but as an “I” addressed as you: an alter ego so real that the earthly “I,” its reflection and exiled image, can enter into dialogue with it. That it is the gnostic's eternal archetype; that it reveals his origin and what he was before being manifested, projected and exiled into this world; that, in order to find it again and be reunited with it, the gnostic must undertake the search for self-knowledge whose stages Suhrawardī has just shown us, all the way to the passage through the Spring of Life—all this is attested by the Angel's declarations to the gnostic who is its “child,” just as the Angel itself is the “child” of the Angel before it.

The names most characteristic of this being in Islamic gnosis are equivalents of those used for the Angel in gnosis more generally 417: the essential or real human being (al-insān al-ḥaqīqī—ho ontōs anthrōpos), the Perfect Human Being (al-insān al-kāmil—anthrōpos teleios), Perfect Nature, the luminous self, the human being of light (shakhs nūrānī), and so on. We have already noted the close affinity between the form of light that unites with the Ismaili initiate and the luminous self of Manichaean gnosis 418.

In short, through many different approaches and variations, we are brought back to a conception of the Angel very close to the angelos of Valentinian gnosis: the Angel of which “we are a portion.” Similarly, in the “Tale of the Exile,” the Angel on Sinai contains the gnostic, who is its child, and is itself contained within the Angel before it. As the gnostic's heavenly counterpart, the Angel expresses his whole being, his being in its fullness—his pleroma.

An expanded commentary on the entire cycle of Suhrawardī's tales could be built around this theme.

Yet the variations on it within his work present one final difficulty that we cannot simply ignore. Without examining it further, we would leave our treatment of the Angel in Illuminationist (ishrāqī) gnosis unfinished. The difficulty can be stated as follows.

Earlier (chapter III, section 5), we read the beautiful psalm Suhrawardī dedicated to his “Perfect Nature,” whom he greeted as his personal Angel. He addressed this Angel as the one who, on the level of the spiritual world, is both his “father” and his “child.” We immediately think of Fāṭima, the Prophet's daughter, who is called “the mother of her father” (Umm abīhā). The gnostic's soul would therefore also be the “mother” of the one whose “child” it is in its spiritual reality of light.

On the other hand, we have just read the initiation received by the exile when he meets the Angel on the mystical Sinai. We have recognised who this Angel is. Here the gnostic calls him his “father,” but not also his “child.”

Suhrawardī's commentators faced this difficulty without resolving it. Dawwānī, for example, tends to identify the angel Gabriel—the Angel of the human species (rabb al-nawʿ)—with the Perfect Nature of Hermes' vision and Suhrawardī's psalm. Conversely, Maybodī, a pupil of Dawwānī himself, tends to raise this Perfect Nature to the rank of the archetypal Angel in person. In truth, neither seems even to regard the matter as a question, though they arrive at the same identification by opposite routes.

We must try to see why. We are not dealing with the kind of dilemma posed by logical concepts, and we should avoid imposing an unnecessarily heavy dialectic upon it.

Still, the question cannot be escaped: must we distinguish the gnostic's Perfect Nature from the Angel of humanity? If so, if it really is the personal Angel who appears as Perfect Nature, how does the individual soul relate, on the one hand, to Perfect Nature as its personal Angel and, on the other, to the Angel on the mystical Sinai as the Angel of humanity? Put differently, how does the pair formed by Perfect Nature and the earthly self, of which Perfect Nature is the Angel, relate to the archetypal Angel of the Human Being, or of human reality itself?

Suhrawardī himself seems to provide the elements of an answer. If we read his explanations of Gabriel's nature as the Angel of humanity alongside his Hermetic writings and the texts of the Hermetic tradition concerning Perfect Nature, a coherent conception begins to emerge.

Listening closely to the “rustling of Gabriel's wings” in the initiatory tale of that name, we can see how Suhrawardī brings Avicenna's angelology to flower in its Illuminationist form. In doing so, he brings out the very symbol of a two-in-one unity—the Angel's two wings—formed by Perfect Nature as the luminous self and by the soul, the earthly self, darkened by its descent. Their two-in-one unity is the “icon” of the archetypal Angel.

He is the Angel of this union because from his right and left wings proceed, respectively, Nous and Psyche, ʿaql and nafs, Perfect Nature and the earthly soul. He is the Angel of their pairing, their two-in-one unity, just as Perfect Nature is the Angel of the earthly self. Here we may recall Esfandyār's final vision as he was dying: the two wings of Sīmurgh.

When we speak of the “angel” here, then, we do not simply mean the familiar image of a guardian angel. We mean the gnostic conception of a “heavenly self” belonging to the Angel's world. More precisely, the way Suhrawardī speaks confirms that the idea of a guardian angel derives from the image of a heavenly Double 419. We may also express it this way: “The Angel-spirit fell and was imprisoned. It is this angel that is the soul of man.

“Thus one divine element is within man and another outside him. Originally they formed a unity which the fall divided. Because of that original unity, either part can stand for the other” 420. Precisely because Perfect Nature is both “father” and “child,” Hermes himself can finally be invoked as Perfect Nature.

The meeting of Avicenna's angelological tradition with the Hermetic tradition in Suhrawardī leads us towards an understanding of this reversible relationship. Taken together, these texts provide every element of an understanding of the human being grounded in angelology. At a still deeper level, they point to a structure of being—an ontology—from which emerges the twofold pattern that we find throughout related forms of gnosis.

We shall conclude by recalling its forms in Mandaeism, Mazdaism and Manichaeism.

II. “Perfect Nature” as the Hermetic conception of the personal Angel. In the tale of the “Rustling,” the angelic order is divided into three hierarchies, as it is in Avicennian angelology.

But the Shaykh al-Ishrāq, the Master of Illumination, prefers the term Kalimāt, “Words” or “Verbs” (the Greek Logoi 421).

First come the greater or perfect Words: the pure cherubic Intelligences (Angeli intellectuales), the tenth of whom is Gabriel. He is the Holy Spirit sent to Mary, the Angel who communicates Revelation to the prophets, and the one in whom philosophers recognise their Active Intelligence. Ultimately, he is the Angel whom the exile meets on the mystical Sinai. Next come the intermediate Words: the hierarchy of angels who move the heavenly Spheres (Angeli caelestes).

Finally come the lesser Words: the souls of light. “From my light I created those who burn with longing,” we are told. That Light is the Holy Spirit, the archangel Gabriel.

In the tale this archangel appears with two wings (other angels have more). His right wing is pure light; his left wing is by no means the Ahrimanian Darkness, but is “tinged with a reddish brown,” like the colour sometimes seen on the Moon's surface. (We may think again of the explanation of the “Crimson” Archangel, whose colour is the red glow of twilight.) We are told that the archangel has two aspects, two intelligible “dimensions.”

Considered in his act of existing through his Principle, his being is necessary and contains no element of non-being. This is what the right wing of absolute light signifies.

But considered in his essence, his quiddity—what he is in himself—he is contingent: he harbours the possibility of not existing. This is what the left wing, dark with a reddish glow, signifies. In Avicenna, each Intelligence or archangel has three intelligible “dimensions,” corresponding to an act of threefold contemplation: contemplation of its Principle, of its being as made necessary by that Principle, and of its being as merely possible in itself. From these proceed, respectively, a new Intelligence, a Soul, and a heaven made of subtle matter 422.

Here only two “dimensions” are retained, those found in the archangel Gabriel, tenth in the hierarchy of perfect Words. These two dimensions also exist in the Intelligences above him—the ones whom the Angel of Sinai describes to the visionary as occupying other Sinais higher than his own. From these two dimensions proceed, each time, a new Intelligence (ʿaql) and a new Soul (nafs), a Nous and a Psyche.

But when the unfolding of being reaches the tenth archangel, it bursts, so to speak, into a multitude: the intelligences and souls of human beings. Suhrawardī's visionary perception gives this angelology a more dramatic character, one concerned with salvation. Since Gabriel is the archetypal Angel of humanity, his “two wings” represent the paired structure of the human being—or at least of the gnostic—a pair whose two members have been separated by their earthly adventure.

From his right wing proceeds Nous, Perfect Nature. From his left proceeds the soul that descends, immersed in the lower world. The joined wings truly represent both the “heavenly twin” of Manichaean gnosis and its “earthly twin,” and therefore the relation between the fallen angel and its heavenly counterpart, the angel of light who comes as messenger and saviour: the one whom its earthly “twin” comes to know, or recognise again, in knowing itself.

We might call this the “Sophianic couple,” since some of the “Faithful of Love” greeted the Angel of the Active Intelligence as Madonna Intelligenza, the heavenly Sophia, and what the Angel reveals in this image is the restored unity of the Sophianic pair. His two wings are the image, the “icon,” of the Nous–Psyche pair, just as that pair is his image. There are as many images of Gabriel as there are Nous–Psyche pairs.

Here visionary imagination introduces the element of drama. To restore the pair is to make the “reddish shadow” that dims the left wing disappear, for whenever the exiled self finds its Perfect Nature again, it recovers its being of light, what it was at the beginning. The two wings are then both wings of light, each illuminating and reflecting the other.

Thus takes place the “return of the Angel,” whose origin and purpose Ismaili sacred drama has, in its own way, expressed with such depth 423.

Put briefly, all this helps us understand how Illuminationist gnosis can take a pattern derived from Avicenna and join it to a quite different gnostic tradition, that of Hermeticism, in order to express its own vision.

We can already see a bridge between them in a philosopher who preceded Suhrawardī: Abū'l-Barakāt al-Baghdādī (died around 560/1164), who devoted particular attention to the Active Intelligence. Why, he asked, should there be only one such Intelligence for all humanity, as Avicennian philosophers maintained (and as the Averroists maintained too, though with a different understanding)? The answer will differ depending on whether we hold that all human souls are identical in species and essential nature, that each soul differs specifically from every other, or that souls are grouped into spiritual families, each forming a different species.

The second and third possibilities lead us to acknowledge a plurality of Active Intelligences. “This is why,” Abū'l-Barakāt writes, “the ancient Sages ... who were initiated into things beyond the reach of the senses, held that for every individual soul—or perhaps for several souls sharing the same nature and affinity—there is a being of the spiritual world who throughout their lives watches over that soul or group of souls with special care and tenderness. It is this being who initiates them into knowledge, protects them, guides them, defends them, consoles them and brings them victory. They called this being Perfect Nature.

“And this friend, defender and protector is what theological language calls the Angel.” He adds another statement rich in spiritual implications: “Some souls learn nothing except from human teachers; others have learned everything from invisible guides known to themselves alone” 424.

This remarkable passage already brings us to the transition we need. The philosophers' Active Intelligence becomes the gnostic's personal Angel, and this Angel is what Hermeticism calls Perfect Nature (al-Ṭibāʿ al-tāmm). This is precisely the movement of thought made by Suhrawardī himself, and it will leave its mark on his entire spiritual vision.

Instead of an impersonal, collective relationship between all human beings and one Active Intelligence common to everyone, Perfect Nature gives each gnostic's relation to the Angel its individual character. Their two-in-one unity constitutes their being in its fullness, their own pleroma. From this point of view, Suhrawardī's Hermetic texts and those of the wider Islamic Hermetic tradition confirm one another.

We are thinking here not only of the passages in which Suhrawardī exalts Hermes as the “father of the Sages,” but also of those in which Hermes appears as the central figure in an ecstasy revealing the world beyond death, the man to whom the secret of Perfect Nature is disclosed. Almost all these passages have already been quoted in this book.

Let us recall them.

First is the account of the vision in which Hermes questions the mysterious, beautiful being of light who appears to him. “Who are you?” he asks. “I am your Perfect Nature” 425. Every later Illuminationist would return to this text. Elsewhere we have the account of Hermes' nocturnal ecstasy in the Temple of Light (above, chapter II, section 3, and chapter IV, section 2).

We noted certain parallels between it and the “Tale of the Exile”: the “midnight sun” (the full daylight of spiritual Imagination amid the night of the senses), and the collapse of the “city of oppressors.” Hermes cries out, “Save me, you who are my father!” and hears the reply, “Seize the cord of the ray of light and climb to the battlements of the Throne.” He climbs, and beneath his feet there is an Earth, while above him there is a Heaven—the Earth and Heaven of the Malakūt, the spiritual world 426.

Earlier we quoted in full the beautiful psalm in which Suhrawardī invokes his Perfect Nature as both his “father” and his “child” (above, chapter III, section 5). Elsewhere, in a still unpublished text, the “Psalm of the Great Testament,” he cries: “I borrowed the fires of the meteors and set the shore ablaze with them. I drove off the hordes of demons, lest they see me ascending towards the hosts of light.

“I called upon my father, saying: O Angel of perfect theurgy! You who are near to God, you most noble one! Take me to yourself, so that my being may expand into a splendour of the divine Light.” After a kind of mystical pilgrimage, passing from height to height through the temples of the invisible, he concludes: “Such is the divine commandment, in accordance with which the sacred sign of Hermes was engraved” 427.

Let us now bring together four Arabic texts from the Hermetic tradition in which Perfect Nature is mentioned.

First come two accounts, one attributed to Hermes himself, the other to Socrates; then two invocations. They all appear in a famous work of theurgy known in Latin as the Picatrix (a corruption of the name Hippocrates), whose Arabic original is entitled Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm (The Goal of the Sage). It was wrongly attributed to Abū'l-Qāsim Maslama of Madrid (al-Majrīṭī), a Spanish scholar and mathematician who lived in the fourth/tenth century.

The book contains a long passage quoted from a work called al-Istamākhīs, in which Aristotle supposedly advises Alexander and teaches him how to invoke Perfect Nature and ask it to appear. The passage describes in detail the famous vision to which the Illuminationists, following Suhrawardī, returned again and again.

We learn that Perfect Nature is “the secret hidden within philosophy itself,” a secret which philosophers believed they could disclose only to disciples who had reached the degree of wisdom. It is a spiritual being (rūḥānīya) in which philosophers participate to differing degrees, and to which they have given various names—so badly distorted in Arabic script that no well-grounded identification of them is yet possible.

“We are then told what Hermes relates: When I wished to bring to light the knowledge of the mystery and the manner of Creation, I came upon a dark underground chamber, filled with darkness and winds. I could see nothing because of the darkness, nor could I keep a lamp burning because of the violence of the winds.

“Then, while I slept, a being of extraordinary beauty appeared to me. He said: Take a light and place it inside a glass vessel to shield it from the wind; then it will illuminate the chamber despite the winds. Next enter the underground room, dig at its centre and bring out a certain theurgic image made according to the rules of the Art. Once you have brought out that image, the winds in the chamber will cease.

“Then dig at its four corners: you will uncover the knowledge of the mysteries of Creation, the causes of Nature, and the origins and ways of things. I said to him: Who are you? He answered: I am your Perfect Nature. If you wish to see me, call me by my name” 428.

This tale, also taken up by Balīnās—Apollonius of Tyana—in the Arabic book attributed to him 429, contains all the characteristic themes of an initiatory vision: the descent into the depths of the darkened Psyche; the light of conscious awareness, like a lamp, sufficient to “break the spell”; the secrets of Creation discovered at the very sources from which the soul projects the forms that shape its universe. All this unfolds under the inspiration of Nous: Perfect Nature, or the Angel.

As examples of this kind of tale—the discovery of a book of revelation in an underground chamber, or a vision accompanied by spoken instruction 430—we may recall the openings of Suhrawardī's tales and the prologue of “Poimandres” in the Corpus Hermeticum; the Shepherd of Hermas; the initiation of Zoroaster before the Agathos Daimōn, as mentioned in the scholium on the first Alcibiades 431; and finally the vision of Kay Khosrow as interpreted by Suhrawardī.

Nous, the Angel or Perfect Nature, calls forth within the conscious soul a sequence of images—which may take the form of an imagined journey—through which the soul, like Hermes placing his flame within a glass vessel, beholds the archetypal form that has been there from the beginning.

That the Angel, or Perfect Nature, possesses this power and privilege is confirmed by a second testimony. This one is attributed to Socrates, although it too appeals to the authority of Hermes. “The wise Socrates,” we read, “declared: Perfect Nature is called the philosopher's sun, his root and his branch. Hermes was asked: How does one come to know wisdom? (Variants: How does one share in it? How does one bring it down into this world?) He replied: Through Perfect Nature. He was asked: What is the root of wisdom? He replied: Perfect Nature. He was asked: What is the key to wisdom? He replied: Perfect Nature.

“Then he was asked: What, then, is Perfect Nature? He replied: It is the philosopher's spiritual (or heavenly, angelic) being (rūḥānīya), the one joined to his star, the one who governs him, unlocks the doors of wisdom for him, teaches him what he finds difficult, reveals to him what is right, and shows him which keys will open the doors, whether he is asleep or awake” 432. It hardly needs saying that any interpretation reducing Perfect Nature to an allegory or metaphor would be a complete misunderstanding. Its subtle personhood, its beauty and light, make it a distinct apparition.

Above all, no one invokes a mere allegory with such fervour, grants it such authority, or expects such a revelation from it. The two accounts just quoted frame Suhrawardī's own texts remarkably well. The fervour shown by the Shaykh al-Ishrāq in his psalm to Perfect Nature reappears in the conversation between Hermes and his Perfect Nature, again related in the Arabic work of the pseudo-Majrīṭī. In that conversation, Perfect Nature itself teaches Hermes how to pray to it and invoke it.

Far from being a theoretical image, devotion to the Angel develops into a liturgy whose regular repetition—at least twice a year—ensures the Angel's continuing presence. It amounts to an intimate celebration of a deeply personal religion, with its own rites, performed in the privacy of an individual's place of prayer: the preparation of mystical foods, culminating in something like a communion.

Here is the central portion of this liturgy, addressed to the four Natures envisioned as distinct embodiments of Perfect Nature (rather like the four archangels of the cosmic Throne): “I invoke you, O powerful and sublime spiritual Angels, you who are the wisdom of the wise, the insight of those who understand, the knowledge of those who know. Answer me; appear to me; bring me close to your mastery; guide me by your wisdom; protect me by your strength.

“Teach me to understand what I do not understand, to know what I do not know, to see what I do not see. Turn away from me the harms concealed in ignorance, forgetfulness and hardness of heart, so that I may attain the rank of the ancient Sages, in whose hearts wisdom, insight, vigilance, discernment and understanding made their home. Dwell also in my heart, and never leave me” 433.

Later, in the chapter describing the astral liturgies practised by the Sabians of Harran, we find a second invocation. Strangely, but significantly, this one is addressed to Hermes. It asks him for a share of the power of his own Perfect Nature, while repeating word for word part of the invocation that Perfect Nature had taught Hermes to address to it.

The invocation to Hermes runs as follows: “You are so hidden that your nature is unknown; you are so subtle that no description can define you. For ... with the masculine you are masculine, with the feminine you are feminine; with the light of day you have the nature of Day, with the shadow of night you have the nature of Night.

“You rival them all in their Natures and make yourself like them in their ways of being. Such are you. I invoke you by all your names: in Arabic, O ʿUṭārid! In Persian, O Tīr! In the Roman tongue, O Hārūs! In Greek, O Hermes! In Indian, O Buddha! ... Send me a power from your spiritual being (that is, from your Perfect Nature), to strengthen my arm, guide me, and make the search for every kind of knowledge easier.

“By Haraqiel 434, the Angel appointed over your realm, may you answer my prayer and hear my call ...” Then follow formulas corresponding word for word to those we have already read, but now in the singular: “May you guide me by your wisdom, protect me by your strength, teach me to understand what I do not understand,” and so on. The prayer ends: “Dwell also in my heart, through a power issuing from your noble spiritual being (that is, from your Perfect Nature), a power that will never part from me, and through a light to guide me in all that I say” 435.

When we place these two invocations side by side, after the accounts quoted earlier, we find ourselves watching a transition: from the Hermetic liturgy of Perfect Nature, which Hermes had learned from his own Perfect Nature, to the Harranian liturgy of Hermes, which addresses Hermes in the very words he had used to invoke Perfect Nature, asking him to bestow a spiritual power flowing from it. It is as though, in passing from one liturgy to the other, Hermes and his Perfect Nature—the soul and the Angel—were joined in a sacred marriage, a union or hierogamy.

A communicatio idiomatum, an exchange of attributes, then takes place between Hermes, formerly the one who invoked, and Perfect Nature, formerly the one invoked: the invoker has now become the one invoked. The prayer of Astrampychos likewise bears witness to this unio mystica, this mystical union of invoker and invoked: “Come to me, Lord Hermes ... I am you and you are I” 436.

Once again we find confirmed the situation noted above (p. 296): because of their original unity—or, more exactly, their unity as two—each member of the pair can also stand for the other. That is what happens when Hermes, invoked in the same words with which he invoked his Perfect Nature, takes its place, or is invoked as one who has its power at his disposal.

Perhaps this simply illustrates the situation described by Suhrawardī when he invokes his Perfect Nature as at once his “father” and his “child”—the “root” and the “branch,” as the earlier text put it. In this twofold aspect, Perfect Nature is simultaneously the one invoked and the one invoking.

We can also see the practical significance of the symbolism of Gabriel's two wings, which comes to full expression in Suhrawardī as Avicennian angelology reaches its Illuminationist fulfilment. What the symbol reveals is a structure within the being of the archetypal Angel that repeats itself in the beings who express that archetype: a pair formed by Perfect Nature and the darkened soul. That is why this symbol, above all, sets the gnostic on the way to “the encounter with his Angel.”

Every Angel above Gabriel in the celestial hierarchy likewise has its “two wings”: the Intelligence and the Soul, Nous and Psyche, which proceed from it. In every Angel higher than himself, Gabriel can in turn recognise his own image. There is, however, one difference. In each of the higher “Cherubim,” the left wing is a single heavenly Soul that moves a heaven; and the shadow that darkens Gabriel's left wing diminishes and disappears as we ascend through the higher degrees.

The questions raised earlier (p. 295)—questions which the commentators seem never to have asked, for understandable reasons—now answer themselves.

What is the relation between Perfect Nature and the archetypal Angel, the lord of the species (rabb al-nawʿ)? Perfect Nature is itself the Angel, considered as the Angel's right wing, the wing of light. And the self sent on its mission to earth, the self that knows its own “self” as its Angel, is also that Angel, considered as the left wing, the darkened wing of the archetypal Angel. Gabriel's “two wings” beautifully express the situation we analysed at the beginning of the “history of the gnostic” (above, section 1). In the very act of self-knowledge, darkness begins to leave the “left wing.”

Yet if, in knowing himself, the “I” comes to know its “self,” just as the invocation says “I am you and you are I,” you and I must still remain. The joy of rediscovering unity as two requires that the two should not be confused with one another (compare the theme of the robe in the “Song of the Pearl”). When two become one, there must still be two for them to “become one.” Just as the Greek prosōpon carries the sense of a person, a face, a presence, so too the word wajh, “face,” implies ḥuḍūr, presence.

Indeed, the whole spirituality of Illuminationism is a spirituality of this Presence, just as Shiite spirituality is a spirituality of the Face—of the Imam as the divine Face shown to humanity. This is what distinguishes this mysticism from every kind of intoxication that dissolves into formlessness or inflates the solitary self. The same truth is expressed in the reciprocal relation of the child who brings forth the one who brought that child forth. We may recall Angelus Silesius's couplet: “What good is it to me, Gabriel, that you greet Mary, if you have no such message for me?”

We shall see later that alchemical symbolism is especially well suited to suggesting these things.

When, then, the earthly self “meets” its Perfect Nature, its Angel, it thereby “sees” its whole being, its pleroma. It thus sees the archetypal Angel of that fullness. That is why there is no logical dilemma here: Is this Perfect Nature? Is it the Angel Gabriel? (See also, below, the individual Nous in Manichaean gnosis.) The pair formed by the earthly self and its heavenly Double, or Perfect Nature, is precisely the individual form taken by its relation to the Angel. Within that individual relationship, the Angel is its Perfect Nature, and the earthly self is the earthly self of that Perfect Nature.

Through Perfect Nature, which it comes to know in knowing itself, the earthly self sees the Angel with “two wings,” because it is seeing its own paired being. Their pair is the image, the icon, of the Angel, just as the Angel is the image, the icon, of their pair. The Angel of human nature in its wholeness becomes visible only in and through the restored unity of Nous and Psyche, of the human being and the angel—just as the reality of love becomes visible only in the unity of lover and beloved.

Then the “two wings” reflect back and forth the splendour of a single light. In ethical terms, this means answering for the Angel in this world while the Angel answers for you in the world beyond. In terms of the soul's final destiny, it is the definitive ascent of Sinai promised at the end of the “Tale of the Exile.”

We can sum up by saying that this entire vision assumes that the soul's true existence is not one of solitude, but of duality-in-unity—what we shall call dualitude. The soul is the second member of a twofold whole, whose heavenly Double or “Twin” is the first. This presupposes an account of being—an ontology—that explains the distance and separation involved in the soul's presence in the earthly world, while already pointing towards their resolution. It presupposes the “history of the gnostic”: the soul did not begin to exist when it entered this world, but originated elsewhere and “descended” to earth.

Yet it is not enough to say that the soul is embodied here because of a fall or a choice made before earthly existence. In gnostic terms, we must stress that this descent results from the division, the rending apart, of an original whole, and that the possibility of this rift must already be rooted in that whole's enduring structure. It is this enduring structure that we propose to call dualitude, to distinguish it from the division forcibly imposed by the “western exile.”

The embodied soul has a “companion of its own kind,” a heavenly Double—the Angel—who comes to its aid and whom it must rejoin, or else lose forever after death, according to whether its earthly life has made possible or impossible the return to the heavenly condition of their twofold unity. This understanding of the soul extends far beyond Iran. A similar “Sophianic” vision took hold among the neo-Manichaean Cathars and among thinkers such as Novalis and Böhme. It may be the fundamental idea of gnostic religion, ubique et semper—everywhere and always. That is why Suhrawardī's tales awaken so many resonances.

We can hear them already in the Christian gnostic Gospels, in all the forms of gnosis bearing an Iranian imprint—Mandaeism, Mazdaism and Manichaeism—and even in times close to our own. These are the stages of an ideal journey which has already brought us here from the discourse of “Poimandres” to the “Grail tale” of a Khusrawānī gnostic.

III. Gnostic variations on the theme of the encounter: (a) Gnostic Gospels and Acts. As for the Christian gnostic writings—the scriptures, so to speak, of a religion in which the theme of the Angel is fundamental—we shall merely call a few examples to mind. Once again we draw on the profound research of H.-C. Puech, to whom every student of gnosis owes a particular debt of gratitude 437.

The theme of the “Image” is expressed with precision in the “Gospel according to Thomas” (saying 84): “When you see your images, which existed before you, which neither die nor appear, how great will be what you must bear.” The text distinguishes two experiences. One is possible now and concerns only a “likeness”: the purely outward appearance one sees in a mirror.

The other is still to come and concerns the image—or more exactly, the “icon” (eikōn). This icon is described as pre-existing, eternal, unmanifested: in short, it is what the person whose icon it is was before that person appeared in the existence of this world. It is the person's complete being and belongs to the intelligible or heavenly world—what we would call the Malakūt. It is Light, the image in which “the light of the Father has been revealed.” It is the “human being of light,” literally equivalent, as we noted, to shakhs nūrānī, shakhs min nūr.

In short, everything called “image” or “icon” in the “Gospel according to Thomas” corresponds to what Valentinian gnostics mean by the angel.

If we bring the two uses of this vocabulary together, we can say equally that the gnostics are the images, the “icons,” of their angels, and that their angels are their images, their “icons”: “the beings, the realities in whose image we were produced here below.” (This also agrees with the idea of the ʿālam al-mithāl, the “imaginal world,” since mithāl may mean both the image that reproduces something and the archetype that is reproduced. We suggested this earlier in discussing Gabriel's two wings.) Thus, when the gnostic goes to meet the Angel, he goes to meet a concrete reality: the Angel “who represents him and presents him to himself as he is in himself,” his heavenly Double, his alter ego, “more real and more true than what he currently is or appears to be.” (The same applies to the encounter with the Angel on the mystical Sinai, with one further point: it is not only an encounter awaiting us after death. For the mystic it can happen in this life, since ecstatic vision, or even visionary meditation, is a foretaste of the eschaton, the final fulfilment.)

In the “Acts of Andrew” (chapters 5–6) 438, Maximilla, Andrew's disciple, is taught that “she will perceive her true face, the face that is hers ... in a form that is immaterial, luminous, transparent, pure, heavenly—like light, pure spirit, pure Nous.” “You will have seen your face in your own being, in your essence.”

The “Acts of Thomas” (chapters 108–113) 439 contain the jewel commonly called the “Song of the Pearl,” or “Hymn of the Soul,” to which we have already referred at length. The young prince of the East has been awakened from the sleep of unawareness by the heavenly message. He has recovered the pearl and is returning to his Father's kingdom when, suddenly, on the road home, he sees coming towards him the wonderful, splendid robe the colour of light, carried out to him by two treasurers. It is the robe made for him in the very place of his origin, the robe he had to leave behind when he was sent on his mission into this world.

The robe is his exact likeness, his mirror—“a mirror reflecting back to him an absolutely faithful image of himself.” The whole robe is within him, and he sees himself entirely within the garment. They are two, distinct from one another, yet together they are one (compare the two wings of the same Angel). More than that, not only are they of identical stature: they have grown together, at the same time, in solidarity with one another. This is what is meant by Perfect Nature's being both the “father” and the “child” of the one whose Perfect Nature it is.

Nor is the robe an inert object. The tale shows it as “alive,” stirred by the “movements of gnosis.” Both the prince and the robe hurry to meet each other, until they touch and flow into one another. The robe spreads over the prince. He wraps himself entirely in it and rises to the “Gate” of the palace of the “King of Kings.” Here again we find an attempt to express what the Sīmurgh symbol also seeks to suggest: unity within dualitude, dualitude within unity, with the two still necessary to the oneness of the two who have become one.

We must also mention at least the Valentinian Heracleon's interpretation of the episode of the Samaritan woman in the “Gospel of John” (chapter 4), as preserved by Origen in his commentary on that Gospel (book XIII) 440. The Samaritan woman's personal angel—her “spiritual nature,” the partner with whom she forms a pair or syzygy—is the “husband” whose existence Jesus reveals to her, who is not “in the world” but “outside the world.” He is her pleroma, her fullness. He is the Samaritan woman herself in the fullness of her being—or, more precisely, her own eternal image, with which she must unite “to become again what she truly is.”

Nor can we omit a certain saying of Mary Magdalene in the Pistis Sophia, spoken during her conversations with the Risen One, in which, as we know, she plays a leading role. She speaks of “the power that came forth from the Saviour and is now the human being of light within us”: “The human being of light within me has guided me; he rejoiced and surged within me, as though longing to come out of me and pass into you” 441.

b) Mandaean Gnosis. We find this same theme of the Image, in all its precision, in Mandaean gnosis: it appears as “the image (dmutâ) which each believer has of himself in the hereafter, in the Kingdom of Light and Life, and with which his soul is reunited after death.” It is the divine image, the heavenly counterpart, the mystical archetype that exists for every created or manifested thing—and above all for every human soul—in the world of Mshunia Kushta, the “paradise of the Mandaeans.”

On the testimony of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa’i, we can say with certainty that this world, at least in respect of the mystical city of Hurqalya, is the equivalent of the ‘âlam al-mithâl, the mundus imaginalis, or imaginal world 442. This Heavenly Double, this “guardian angel,” plays for the human being to whom it is joined the same role in the destiny of the soul after death as the Fravarti or Daena does in Zoroastrianism (see below).

Here, as in the “Hymn of the Pearl,” the encounter is described as “putting off the bodily tunic and receiving the garment of light”; here too, two “guides” take part. A hymn from the Ginza ends with this beautiful stanza: “I go to meet my image—and my image comes to meet me. It speaks to me tenderly and embraces me—upon my return from captivity” 443.

This brings to mind many other examples. The Simurgh, too, appears in Mandaean legends, where ancient Iranian motifs have developed along lines parallel to the visionary meditations of Suhrawardi and Attar. One especially lovely legend, collected by Mrs. E. S. Drower, shows Hirmiz Shah gazing upon the bird Simurgh. “The spring was as clear as a block of ice; the water rose into the air in a single jet, white and pure, then spread out like a tree. Hirmiz sat before the Simurgh, and when he saw her gazing steadily at the spring, he fixed his eyes on it as well.

“Then he saw in the water something resembling a being of light” 444 ... For Attar, the Simurgh is above all the mystery of divinity as a mirror. It is worth noting, then, that as early as the third century Zosimos of Panopolis mentions a mirror made of electrum, apparently used in the rites of a particular Gnostic religious cult to represent the divine Spirit (to theion pneuma). “When the soul gazes at itself in the mirror, it sees the shameful things within it and casts them away ... When purified, it imitates the Holy Spirit and takes it as its model ... What does the philosopher’s maxim say? Know yourself. It thus points to the spiritual and intellectual mirror. And what is this mirror, if not the divine and primordial Spirit?” 445

c) Mithraic Liturgy. We have already mentioned the alchemist Zosimos (p. 278) in connection with the symbolism of “the sun’s position at the meridian,” and with the fundamental secret of alchemy “as identical with the most deeply hidden mystery of the religion of Mithra” (above, p. 286). What concerns us here is the invocation of the “Perfect Body” at the beginning of the Mithraic rite known as the “Liturgy of Mithra” (see above, p. 157).

The initiate is instructed to say: “O primordial genesis of my genesis, primordial origin of my origin!” Then come the four subtle, primordial Elements, each in turn embodying that origin: “Breath of breath, first breath of the breath within me; Fire ... first fire of the fire within me; Water of water, first Water of the water within me; Earthly substance, prototype of the earthly substance within me; my Perfect Body, fashioned by a glorious arm and an imperishable right hand ...”

All these subtle elements that make up the Perfect Body are invoked as the organs through which the initiate will behold the immortal Principle, following the temporary death that precedes the new birth symbolized by the initiation rite 446. The “Perfect Body” is invoked in the same way as Perfect Nature. Like Perfect Nature, or the “light-colored” robe in the “Hymn of the Pearl,” it gives symbolic form to the primordial self, the heavenly I.

d) Alchemy. To complete this further appearance of Zosimos the alchemist 447, we should also mention the final chapter of an unpublished short work by the fourteenth-century alchemist Jildaki 448. Its title, “The Priest’s Dream,” clearly recalls a vision of Zosimos: that of Ion, the priest of the innermost and most hidden sanctuaries, standing before the altar with fifteen steps 449. What makes this brief chapter so fascinating is that its two central figures in the alchemical Work are Perfect Nature and Hermes 450. Their presence brings the meaning of that Work into sharp relief by contrasting it with the helplessness of those whom Jildaki calls the Ignoramuses (jâhilîyûn). These are the false alchemists, who handle only material things. Their imagination is so profoundly impaired that they cannot grasp the being or reality of a symbol.

All their frantic activity accomplishes is the murder of Hermes and the disappearance of Perfect Nature, whom they had first succeeded in separating from him. Jildaki could hardly make it clearer that the true goal of alchemy is the mystery of an inner, psychic transformation, and that only an apprehensio aurea—a “golden apprehension”—can meet its “liturgical” conditions (see above, p. 286).

This transformation is perceived and experienced in the mystical union of Hermes and Perfect Nature, made visible through their alchemical counterparts, Red Sulfur and White Sulfur. It is the union of Eros and Logos, of love and spiritual reason, celebrated by the priest in the Temple of Venus after he turns away from the Ignoramuses and follows the instructions engraved on the temple idol.

The mystery then takes a new form, which Jildaki calls the New Child (al-walad al-jadîd), the Child of Renewal. (In Ismaili Shiism, the last Imam of a cycle, who prepares the resurrection, is called al-walad al-tâmm, the Perfect Child.) Thus, in the union of Hermes and Perfect Nature, we see the emergence in Jildaki of the symbol for alchemy’s ultimate goal: what the Latin texts call Infans noster, filius sapientiae, filius philosophorum—“our Child, son of Wisdom, son of the philosophers.”

The image of the Child, the Puer aeternus or Eternal Child, is especially suited to expressing both the unity of the new being and the two poles that give it structure. More precisely, this is the renovatus in novam infantiam, the one “renewed into a new childhood.” The figure holds two opposites together at once: beginning and end, preexistence and existence beyond this life, what is already here and what is yet to come. It joins into one the stages through which the mystical Stone passes, like a child-hero: from the lapis exilis et vilis, the humble and lowly stone, through the servus rubeus et fugitivus, the red and fugitive servant, to the exaltation of the Deus terrenus, the earthly god, light above all light, when the Stone becomes the corpus glorificatum, the glorified body.

Jildaki suggests both the beginning of these stages and their anticipated final fulfillment in the very name he gives the “Child of Renewal”—the child he, the alchemist, already is. He calls him ‘Abd al-Karim, the servant of the Noble (Stone). At the first dawning of his new birth, he is indeed the servant of the Noble Stone, which he must serve until the triumphant end, when he takes on the form of the filius regius, the royal son invested with divine power. Here is the whole Aenigma regis, the riddle of the king: the sacred marriage of heaven and earth, to be consummated in novissimo die hujus artis, on the Last Day that brings the Work to completion.

Expressed in the language of mystical alchemy, Suhrawardi’s theme of Hermes and Perfect Nature thus carries to their furthest reach the meanings we have already drawn from the symbolism of the archangel Gabriel’s “two wings.” In this Hermetic tradition we glimpse in advance the union of Lover and Beloved, the longing for which fills all Persian poetry. And if Suhrawardi’s psalm addresses Perfect Nature as the One-Who-Gives-Birth-and-Is-Born, it is because Perfect Nature gives birth to herself in Hermes precisely as Hermes (or the priest in Zosimos’s dream) is brought to birth in himself. Likewise, the Beloved, though grammatically the one who receives love, is at the same time the one who brings love into being within the Lover, giving birth to herself there as Beloved precisely by giving birth to him as Lover.

We might say that the alchemical expression of Perfect Nature’s secret makes one thing clearer than any other: for the Gnostic in this world there are two “guardian angels,” the “root” and the “branch.” There is the angel who is his parens, his heavenly father or mother before he comes into this world; and there is the angel who is his child—his own future self, born into his Perfect Nature for a life beyond this world. When he has become this “Child” entirely (when the hoopoe has become the Simurgh), the self that belonged “to this world” has been brought home “to its own world.”

Only the pair of “two angels” remains. This is what justifies Suhrawardi’s invocation of Perfect Nature as both the one who gives birth and the one who is born. It is also why Latin alchemy was so fond of the symbol of the Virgin Mother. Here, once again, we may quote a couplet by Angelus Silesius: “If God’s Spirit touches you with its being, the Child of Eternity is born in you.”

e) Manichaean Gnosis and Zoroastrianism. In the preceding pages we have assembled the themes of the image and the mirror as variations on the theme of the angel. Passing through Mithraic material and alchemy, we have returned to Perfect Nature—the supreme expression of the personal angel in Suhrawardi’s spiritual philosophy. All this now comes to a head in the search for analogies, if not direct precedents, within the spirituality of ancient Persia, which the Shaykh al-Ishraq sought to revive.

Manichaean gnosis, in fact, knows of a luminous primordial Nature, a divine being whom one of the fragments recovered at Turfan praises as “our father and our mother, our magnificence, our Self of Splendor”—that is, our Nature of Light, our primordial Self. “Hail to you, with whom our soul has been identical from the first beginning” 451.

We are brought back to the questions Suhrawardi’s writings had led us to ask (above, p. 295). Who is the personal Angel? What is the relation between Perfect Nature as personal Angel and the Angel encountered on Sinai, since both are called the mystic’s “father”? We saw how the vision itself, and the symbol in which it finds expression, dissolved the apparent dilemma: is it one angel or the other? That insight opens the path we must now follow.

Scholars have devoted particular attention to the nature and powers of the being of light known in Manichaeism as “Great Vahman,” or in Parthian as “Great Manuhmed” or “Manvahmed.” The name derives from the Avestan Vohu Manah (Persian Bahman). As we recalled earlier (p. 112), Zoroastrianism uses this name for the first of the “Holy Immortals” (Amahraspands), the archangels. Broadly, it means Good Spirit, Luminous Thought, or Nous of Light—the luminous spiritual Intellect. We have also seen it occupying the highest rank in Suhrawardi’s angelology.

But what is the relation between this Nous of Light and the individual “Manvahmeds” or “Vahmanans”?

One may see in “Great Manvahmed” the Perfect Man, identifying it with the “Column of Glory,” the “Column of Light” formed by the ascending procession of all souls freed from Darkness and returning to the kingdom of Light. From this, one might conclude that all the Vahmanans together constitute Great Vahman or Great Manvahmed.

But that reduces Great Manvahmed to a merely collective being and, in doing so, abolishes the very relationship and function essential to it: the relationship between the saving Angel and the individual soul it saves. Their unity as two does not disappear when the salvation brought by the savior restores it to its original state. The collective interpretation replaces these twofold unities with single units. It would then have to be the “Self of Splendor” itself that was held captive by Darkness.

Yet it is precisely this “Self of Splendor” that speaks to the captive as the captive’s Angel. The situation is thus like that of Perfect Nature as the Gnostic’s angel. Perfect Nature gives an individual form to the relation between the Angel and each of the beings that together make up the whole of which the Angel is the guardian. That whole consists of all these twofold unities, each made up of a Gnostic and his Perfect Nature.

The vocabulary used by the neo-Manichaeism of the Cathars points us toward the same solution. It also helps us preserve the distinct themes and the parallel relationships between these terms.

First there is the human soul, earthly and captive: Anima. Then there is its holy or angelic spirit (Spiritus sanctus, angelicus, or paraclitus). Each elect soul has its own. This is the “guardian angel” in the Gnostic sense: the Heavenly Double, the Spirit that has “remained in heaven” and acts as protector.

Finally there is the Spiritus principalis, corresponding to the saving Primordial Man or the Nous of Light, invoked through the names of the three persons of the Trinity. The cosmic Spirit or Nous stands in relation to the totality of souls as each individual Nous, Spirit, or angel stands in relation to its own soul. We are dealing, then, with a parallel between two pairs of terms, not simply with a relation between two terms 452.

This means that Great Vahman, the cosmic Nous, has a distinct existence of its own, alongside the holy Spirits or Heavenly Doubles, each of which stands to its individual soul as Great Vahman stands to the totality of souls. It is not Great Vahman as such, but each of these holy Spirits, that is the Heavenly Double of a particular soul. Suhrawardi’s symbolism of the two wings presents the same situation. The Angel exists as a spiritual being in its own right, while its two wings are its “members.” They symbolize the multitude of pairs that together form the order of beings over which it presides as Angel or lord (rabb), each pair consisting of a soul and its Nous.

We must also remember that, according to the Iranian way of counting, a whole has a unity of its own in addition to the units that compose it; it is not simply their sum. Great Vahman must therefore have a reality distinct from its parts and from their total 453.

For their part, the philosophers of Illumination (Ishrâqîyûn) repeatedly insisted that the universality of each angel-archetype is not the universality of a logical concept. It is the metaphysical universality of an essence, subject neither to the conditions of the logical universal—which is poorest in content—nor to the conditions under which such a universal is realized in singularibus, in individual things belonging to the world of the senses. This essence is fully and unconditionally what it is. That is what they perceive in the “person” of the archetypal Angel, the lord of a species whose existence is its “theurgy,” its divine work, and whose salvation the Angel brings about.

The theme of the Heavenly Double receives its fullest force in the mystery of salvation. In Manichaeism, its development concerns Mani himself before anyone else 454. When Mani is twenty-four, the Angel appears to him as his “double” or “twin” and announces that the time has come for him to reveal himself and summon people to his teaching: “Greetings to you, O Mani, from me and from the Lord who has sent me to you ...” Some of Mani’s words as he lay dying also refer to this Heavenly Double: “I contemplated my Double with my eyes of light.”

Yet a psalm celebrating the soul’s departure from earthly existence also speaks of “your Double who never failed.” Every soul, then, truly has its Double. Mani’s Heavenly Double may be Christ in the Western Manichaean tradition, or the Virgin of Light in the Eastern tradition; but each soul likewise has its own Double, its partner in a sacred pair, its Nous: the Heavenly Double who guides it to the kingdom of Light when it dies to the Earth.

It is therefore the individual Nous that appears to its soul, its earthly child, in order to strengthen, guide, and save it. It is the Nous of this particular soul.

Yet, as a “member” of the cosmic Nous, it accomplishes the whole salvation of that soul, just as cosmic salvation is the work of the great Nous as a whole. The individual Nous is a “member” of the great Nous in the same way that the individual soul is a member of its own Nous. This pattern, repeated on two levels, clarifies the familiar theological theme of the “members.” Its gradation is beautifully expressed in a Parthian hymn: “Come, soul, do not be afraid. I am your Manvahmed, your pledge and your seal, and you are my body, a robe I have put on to frighten the powers. And I am your light, the original radiance, Great Manvahmed, the Perfect Pledge” 455.

Thus an individual Nous can also present itself, to a particular soul, as Great Manvahmed. This possibility points to a very precise kind of relationship—exactly the one taught by Valentinian Gnostic angelology. There the Angels of Christ are acknowledged to be Christ himself, in the sense that each Angel, guided or sent by Christ, is Christ himself in relation to a particular individual existence 456.

We may recall that, in the “Tale of Exile,” the Angel on Sinai reveals to the Elect that above him, on a higher Sinai, stands another Angel. His relation to that higher Angel is the same as the Elect’s relation to him: the higher Angel “contains” him just as he “contains” the Elect. At every level, the two intelligible dimensions are repeated from Angel to Angel: from the “right wing” proceeds a new Intelligence, and from the “left wing” the soul of that Intelligence. And so it continues, from one mystical Sinai to the next. The drama that befalls the Tenth Angel, the Angel of humanity, is symbolized by the darkening of his “left wing”—the souls held captive in this world.

At this level, already very far removed from the Principle, the procession of being no longer has the power to bring forth one Intelligence and one Soul. Instead, as we have said, it breaks into a multitude of pairs, and the two members of each pair are separated. On one side stands the Self of Light, or Perfect Nature; on the other, cut off from it, the “exiled” self. This is the Gnostic pattern itself. Salvation means reuniting the two, freeing the exiled self from its darkness. The reunion therefore has two forms at once: an individual reunion within each pair, and a collective reunion embracing all these pairs with their respective Nous.

But the collective depends on the individual; the salvation of the whole can take place only through the salvation of each of its “members.” The catastrophe and its resolution, recurring themes in Suhrawardi’s tales, are thus rooted in the very Iranian gnosis that the Shaykh al-Ishraq sought to bring back to life.

We have already had occasion to recall what the Fravartis (Persian Foruhar) are in Zoroastrianism. They are heavenly beings, archetypes of every creature belonging to Ohrmazd’s world of light; they exist in the subtle spiritual world before the manifested world comes into being. The relation between the Fravarti and the soul (urvân, ravân) would thus be comparable to that between the Heavenly Double and the earthly self, or between Perfect Nature and the exiled self.

But here we must take account of a dramatic episode at the heart of Zoroastrian cosmology and its teaching on the soul’s final destiny. The Fravartis—“those who have chosen”—accepted the task of descending to Earth themselves. They voluntarily left the world of light to help Ohrmazd in the struggle they would wage together against the opposing power of Ahriman. For this reason, the final reunion is not simply a reunion of the soul with its Fravarti; it is a reunion of the Fravarti-soul with its Heavenly Double, the Daena 457. Scholars have debated at length how the word Daena can mean both “religion” and a person’s “transcendent” or “heavenly self,” and how it can carry both a collective and an individual meaning.

But here we can recognize just the sort of false dilemma that Suhrawardi has helped us overcome in the preceding pages. As the “religion” of Ohrmazd, the “Lord Wisdom,” Daena is indeed what the Fravarti chose before its earthly existence. It is therefore entirely capable of representing the preexistent, heavenly, or transcendent Self of a being of light. (Shiite gnosis, too, will teach that a being’s religion, Dîn, is that being’s imperishable Face.) This is the living presence at the heart of the believer, inspiring some of the most beautiful surviving texts of Zoroastrian theology, which describe the encounter with the Angel Daena after death 458.

On the third day after death—after the exitus—the Elect, approaching the Chinvat Bridge, sees a dazzling Form coming toward him: a young woman more beautiful than any beauty he has seen on Earth. Wonderstruck, he asks, “Who are you?” She replies: “I am your Daena ... (your religion and your own self), the one whom your thoughts, your words, and your deeds have made. I was loved; you made me more loved. I was beautiful; you made me more beautiful still.”

Let us remember that Hermes, too, asks the mysterious Form of Light who reveals the higher knowledge to him: “Who are you?” The answer comes: “I am your Perfect Nature.” As his psalm to her attests, Suhrawardi knows that his Perfect Nature exists before him, for it is she who brings him to birth in the spiritual world.

But he also knows that, at the same time, he brings her to birth. Likewise Daena already existed, since the believer chose her before entering this world; yet she is also the one whom his thoughts, words, and deeds have made. They grow together, just as the light-colored robe does in the “Hymn of the Pearl” from the Acts of Thomas. If all these are variations on the same encounter, we may also say that meeting Daena is no different from meeting the Image or “icon” spoken of in the “Gospel according to Thomas,” Mandaean gnosis, and, above all, the Manichaean account of the soul’s destiny after death.

Indeed, the Manichaean vision brings the details of the scene into even sharper focus. Two passages from Mani’s Kephalaia deserve quotation. One describes the Form of Light revealed to each of the Elect as they leave their bodies, accompanied by three great and splendid Angels. The first brings the prize of victory, the second the robe of light, and the third the diadem of light 459.

Another passage describes “the moment when they depart this world, when the Form of Light comes to meet them and separates them from Darkness, leading them to the Light ... The Form of Light calms the man with a kiss and with peace, freeing him from fear of the demons that destroy his body. By her appearance and her image (icon, eikôn), the heart of the Elect who leaves his body is set at rest. Then the Angel who holds the prize of victory stretches out his right hand and receives him with a kiss and with love. Then this soul pays homage to the one who saves it, who is this Form of Light” 460.

This Form of Light, then, is indeed the Angel who comes to meet the soul after death. It is also the Angel described in Ibn al-Nadim’s Arabic Fihrist 461 as a divinity of light, sent to the soul by the Primordial Anthropos, or First Man, in the form of the “wise guide.” Three other beings of light accompany this figure, along with “the maiden who resembles the soul.” All come to help the soul resist the demons that would attack it. Who, then, is the “wise guide”? That title is especially striking because its Arabic form (al-Hakîm al-Hâdî) corresponds word for word to the title at the beginning of the “Tale of the Western Exile.” There, too, it designated the “wise guide” who would finally appear as the Angel on Sinai.

A Manichaean treatise in Sogdian gives us an answer to the question raised by the Fihrist. Where the preceding text spoke of one Form of Light, the Fihrist divides it into two figures: the wise guide and the one who resembles the soul. The Sogdian text describes the Angels descending to meet the soul of the Elect, to reassure and protect it. “Do not be afraid, righteous soul ... Go forward ... ascend to the paradise of Light, receive Joy.”

And then: “His own Action, a marvelous and divine princess, a young woman, will come to meet him, immortal, her head adorned with flowers ... She herself will set him on the road to the paradise of Light.” Other Coptic texts also describe the maiden who becomes the soul’s guide. The Sogdian fragment just quoted therefore shows more clearly than any other—as Henning wrote—that “the Manichaeans shared the Zoroastrian conception of a man’s Daena, who meets him after death in the form of a young woman” 462.

It is explicitly this maiden who is called the guide, the one who “sets the Elect on the road.” At the same time, because she is the soul’s own Action, she truly resembles the soul, just as the soul resembles her. Guide and image are therefore joined in the very “person” of the Angel Daena. She is indeed the Double of Light whose dialogue with her earthly soul we heard earlier. We have already said that this sacred pairing places a mutual responsibility upon its two members. Daena will answer for the man after death to the degree that he has answered for Daena during his earthly life.

Once again, neither metaphor nor allegory is at work here. If Daena is the Action of the earthly man, it is because that Action will have taken form in his likeness. The mystery of the sacred union after death—a union whose preparation or anticipation requires a new birth—is the mystery of the One-Who-Gives-Birth-and-Is-Born, where acting and receiving action pass into one another. Daena’s birth through and within the human soul, as that soul’s own Action, is at the same time the birth of the soul in and through the Angel Daena who is acting within it.

This is precisely the meaning already suggested to us both by the symbolism of the Angel’s “two wings” and by the psalm Suhrawardi addresses to his Perfect Nature.

We recalled earlier that the longing for this unifying reunion runs throughout Persian mysticism. It will reach one of its high points in Ruzbihan’s mysticism of love (see Book III). Each time, this reunion marks or announces the lover’s new birth. We should not accuse the images used by our mystics of logical contradictions that arise only at the level of concepts formed by the understanding. Beyond logical concepts are realities that can be expressed only in images.

The relation between two beings joined as a pair—a syzygy—can be experienced and expressed through the image of marriage, the relation of lover and beloved; it can also be expressed through the image of parenthood, the relation of father and son. Each image expresses the same process of new birth, in which the roles of the two partners become reciprocal. The figures of Perfect Nature and the Angel on Sinai, of the Form of Light and the Angel Daena, overlap and take one another’s place.

What remains is the idea of a sacred union to be fulfilled at the end of time, in novissimo die: the mystery of a new birth in which a being is brought forth in the image of its Heavenly Double, an image that the Double itself actively brings into reality within that being. It is the idea of a mystical coming-into-likeness and a shared responsibility that together announce the dawn of resurrection. These themes recur wherever the splitting apart of a primordial heavenly-earthly pair expresses the mystery of the Origin.

Restoring the pair’s unity-in-twoness, its dualitude, then becomes the measure of an inner ethic, whose fulfillment will be precisely the final encounter and mutual recognition of a human being and his Angel. This is the event that dominates the horizon of Iranian teaching about the world to come and of Gnostic spirituality: in Zoroastrianism and Manichaeism, no less than in Christian gnosis and the philosophy of Illumination. “May you reveal yourself to me at the supreme epiphany,” Suhrawardi prayed in his psalm.

In the end, all our inquiries into the Heavenly Double, the Angel, converge upon a sophiology: a spiritual understanding of divine Wisdom, Sophia, as a living figure. Elsewhere we have shown how, and in what respect, Daena and Sophia can be identified with one another 463. The vision of Perfect Nature granted to Hermes is also, in one respect, a vision of Sophia herself. As we saw earlier, Hermes teaches that Perfect Nature is the one who brings Wisdom down to Earth. She is the “philosopher’s angel,” the one who governs and guides him: the “wise guide.”

Our inquiries thus open onto a whole tradition of thought about Sophia, embracing Jacob Boehme and his school, especially Gottfried Arnold, and many others down to Vladimir Solovyov. This is not the place to pursue it; another book will be needed. That book would also have to gather the visible symbols perceived or formed in visionary meditation: a whole family of images able to express the restored dualitude brought about when the member cast into “Western exile” is transformed and transferred to the “generation beyond death.” We defined this dualitude earlier as unity of essence without confusion of persons.

Suhrawardi’s symbolism of the Angel’s “two wings” has precisely this power to make us see. The Angel of human nature in its wholeness becomes visible only when Nous and Psyche, Perfect Nature and soul, earthly human being and the Angel Sophia-Daena, are reunited. In the same way, the reality of “heavenly” love is visible only in and for the unity of lover and beloved—a unity that is dualitude, not fusion, for it takes two to know the joy of being one.

The echoes of this theme sound on in endless arpeggios. We cannot follow them here. But Swedenborg’s name must not be passed over in silence. The teachings of that great Swedish visionary and spiritual philosopher, and their influence on a whole family of minds, form the Western panel of the diptych whose Eastern panel we have just examined. A few lines must suffice as a brief reminder.

f) Swedenborgian Parallels. In one of his Memorabilia, Swedenborg tells how, during a vision, he saw a chariot approaching from the far reaches of heaven. On it stood a magnificent Angel.

But as the chariot drew closer, he realized that what had appeared from a distance to be a single Angel was in fact two angelic beings: a pair of heavenly lovers 464. Of course, the vision reveals its full meaning only when seen in the context of Swedenborg’s angelology as a whole and his teaching on heavenly love. Unfortunately, we cannot explore those teachings here.

We shall remain within Swedenborg’s sphere of influence by considering another case: Balzac. We know how deeply Balzac was affected by his reading of Swedenborg and L.-C. de Saint-Martin. In November 1833, Balzac visited the sculptor Théophile Bra (1797–1863) 465, who was himself influenced by Swedenborg’s teachings and who created in stone one of the noblest and most solemn images of the “guardian angel.” During the visit, Balzac stood in Bra’s studio contemplating a sculptural group: the Virgin holding the Child, adored by two angels.

The figures were extraordinarily beautiful. As Balzac continued looking, the image of the two angels took possession of his inner world of imagination. They became the image of two natures in one being—a being approaching its final transformation, who breaks open its outer covering and reveals to a man and a woman that it was this being whom they had loved when they loved the love that united them.

Thus arose the idea for what would become Balzac’s mystical masterpiece: Seraphitus–Seraphita, one and the same angel, yet a double being, masculine and feminine, born from the union of lover and beloved. By freeing in each person “the angelic creature imprisoned within the flesh,” this angel embodies the dualitude of their love. The book ultimately appeared under the title Seraphita, and throughout it a tribute to Swedenborg and his teachings continues to resonate.

These variations in the visible representation of the angel correspond, in their own way, to variations on the theme of the Gnostic’s encounter with the Angel. Much remains to be explored beyond what we have been able to suggest here.

But we can now sum up what these texts have taught us about the nature of the human being and the meaning of human existence. On both sides, what emerges is the Gnostic experience of self-knowledge, which discovers the self as an alter ego, an “angel”—not, certainly, in the darkness of the unconscious, but in the “superlight” of a consciousness beyond ordinary consciousness.

In that very experience the Gnostic knows he has been freed from exile, that is, from solitude. His full being is a dualitude: his ego is released from the isolation of mere egohood because, together with the heavenly alter ego of which he is the earthly counterpart, it forms a complete whole, a pleroma. This fullness is strong enough to overcome the opposing powers, whether they are called demonic or are the collective and social forces of “the city whose inhabitants are oppressors” (4:77).

The ultimate meaning of this restored dualitude appears in the vision of the soul’s destiny after death, shared by the different forms of gnosis we have considered. The Image each person brings to birth in this world, the ecstatic vision each gives form to here, determines what death will be for that person. What each has willed and anticipated in this life is precisely what each will see in the supreme vision and revelation on crossing the threshold. No one can hope, in the other world, to receive a vision that he has refused or desecrated, surrendering it to Darkness, in this one. The world of the Angel cannot answer for a human being who has refused to answer for it.

Daena-Sophia will then be nothing but the extinguished heavenly past of the person who has disowned her. The terrifying vision that Zoroastrian texts describe as appearing to the demonic man—his own Action—has become a grotesque distortion of Daena. What he sees is his own self, handed over by its own denial to the nothingness of its solitude. That denial cuts it off from its Heavenly Double and leaves it marked by the mutilation of an infernal “unpairedness,” although its true nature was one of “pairedness” and heavenly dualitude. Such, it seems to us, is the meaning of a conception of the human being whose distant origins lie in the very sources of Iranian spirituality.

5. The Secret of the “Personal City”

The preceding discussion has brought out several fundamental themes: the mirror, the image, and the idea of the human soul’s fullness, or pleroma, as a lesser Logos. The “Tale of Exile” and the “Treatise on the Rustling of Gabriel’s Wings” tell the “story” of this lesser Logos. It is the “story” of the Gnostic, whose different aspects we have just traced.

But there is more. If the Gnostic descends into this world and is taken captive in the city of which it is said, “Our Lord! Bring us out of this city whose inhabitants are oppressors” (4:77), the Gnostic’s own person is also, in a corresponding vision of the imagination, represented as a city. The “city of the oppressors” is the world of illusion in which the lesser Logos presently dwells.

But this lesser Logos is itself a city, one of those of which “God Most High has said: Of those cities We tell you their misfortune; some still stand, while others have been laid waste” (7:99 and 11:102). It is the “temple,” or dwelling place, of the lesser Logos that has been laid waste.

But all the Logoi, all the Words of God, greater and lesser, “still stand”: they are the cities that endure, because they exist beyond time and the space of the senses 466. The Gnostic’s “story,” then, is the story of the personal city that endures, while the “city of the oppressors” is at last destroyed.
