This explains the importance of the theme not only for Suhrawardi—it shapes the vision of his “Treatise of the High Towers” (Risâlat al-abrâj)—but also for the whole body of metaphysical imagery surrounding the “Tale of Exile.” We would miss something essential if we ended without examining this imaginative vision of the Personal City.

For that reason, it seems important to summarize a short treatise especially representative of Indo-Persian mystical literature. Although it is not Suhrawardi’s own work, it belongs closely to the cycle of his tales.

Indeed, the treatise not only develops, in its own way, the recurring theme of “Western Exile”; several of its pages simply incorporate a chapter found in two of Suhrawardi’s narratives: the “Treatise of the High Towers” and the tale entitled “The Lovers’ Companion” (Mu’nis al-‘oshshâq). Taken as a whole, this Indo-Persian treatise is a perfect expression of the themes that shape the Gnostic’s spiritual adventure. In especially striking symbols, it recounts the Gnostic’s “story” as a search for himself, culminating in the encounter with his alter ego.

By way of introduction to this little spiritual romance, let us say that it combines two themes: the mirror and the labyrinth. Neither word, it is true, occurs explicitly in the text.

But what they signify is unmistakably present, and that is what matters. The feeling that the earthly world is a tomb in which beings from higher worlds lie buried is a constant feature of the Gnostic experience of this world. We find it expressed even in Shaykhi gnosis, in the writings of Sarkar Agha (see Book VI). Here, however, the image of the tomb becomes more complex and expansive: it becomes a labyrinth. Human existence now has a particular meaning. A being from the higher world is sent into this tomb so that it may learn to find the way out, as one finds the way out of a labyrinth (compare the “Tale of Exile,” stanza 37). The escape comes only after reaching the labyrinth’s heart, where the “Spring of Life” is found.

But this departure can succeed only if we understand how the eternal Forms of the Malakût, the spiritual kingdom, are present in this perishable world. They do not become physically part of it. They are not inherent in it as blackness is inherent in a black object. They enter it as forms and images “enter” a mirror.

Thus, to understand what we behold in this world, and where we behold it, is to understand what happens when we look into a mirror. It is within the whole human adventure, experienced as an “initiation,” that the hidden meaning of the tomb as labyrinth comes together with the phenomenon of the mirror. Their union is so essential that we find the mirror at the very “initiatory center” of the meaning of life, when life itself is portrayed as a labyrinth of bewildering turns and unforeseen events.

We can best grasp the connection between the mirror and the labyrinth by turning to one of Leonardo da Vinci’s ingenious creations, wonderfully described by Marcel Brion 467. In the ancient myth, Theseus confronted the Minotaur at the heart of the labyrinth: the monstrous double of the human being, the man-bull. After killing it, Theseus emerged from the labyrinth as the spiritual hero of a purified humanity. In the central chamber of the labyrinth, an initiate into the mystery religions would meet the high priest, who explained the symbolic meaning of the ordeals and figures encountered along the way; the initiate emerged a new person.

In certain Christian churches, a labyrinth marked out in the pavement—called the league of Jerusalem—allowed those unable to undertake an actual pilgrimage to make the sacred journey in soul and imagination. They followed its winding paths as a rite, facing dangers represented by symbolic monsters. Perhaps they reached the goal more directly in this way, since the final destination was not so much earthly Jerusalem as heavenly Jerusalem. And now Leonardo designs his own labyrinth. After an interminable journey along twisting paths, the initiate enters the central sanctuary for the supreme revelation. Here, however, the sanctuary is “an eight-sided room of mirrors that multiplies to infinity the image of the person standing at its center” 468.

This central sanctuary is not the place where the monstrous Minotaur must be fought. Nor is it the place of divine contemplation sought by the medieval pilgrim in heavenly Jerusalem. It is the place where one contemplates oneself.

But how far should we insist on the difference between contemplating oneself and contemplating the divine? To set them against each other is to miss the true meaning of this “self.” We would then risk misunderstanding the initiation offered by the “room of mirrors.” We avoid that danger if, with the spiritual writers we have been studying, we find in the vision of the mirror an answer to the question that governs the entire theory of knowledge: the question of how the forms of knowledge and consciousness come into being. Who is the “Giver of Forms,” the Dator formarum? To know the giver is to cease being enslaved by what is given. For to know the giver is to put into practice the fundamental maxim so often recalled in this book: “Whoever knows himself knows his Lord.”

How, then, is the “self” known by one who knows himself connected with the “Giver of Forms”? The title “Giver of Forms” is bestowed in both the Latin metaphysical tradition (Dator formarum) and the Arabic (Wâhib al-Sowar) upon the spiritual being philosophers call the Active Intellect. Suhrawardi has already enabled us to recognize this being as the Angel on Sinai, who appears at the end of his “Tale of Exile.” Once again we find ourselves at the heart of questions explored at length in the preceding pages.

We can already sense that the little Indo-Persian spiritual romance, which reveals something of the secret of the “Personal City,” will describe—with its own characters and scenery—the very journey whose stages are recounted in the “Tale of the Western Exile.”

The text survives in Arabic and Persian and claims to be translated from Sanskrit. The compilation can be no later than the fourteenth century, but it includes elements already found in Suhrawardi in the twelfth century 469.

It may be an originally Iranian text that returned to Iran after migrating to India. Whatever its history, the work as a whole is a characteristic example of Sufism shaped by Indian influences. Its supposed narrator is a sage of India, who presents his spiritual autobiography in a symbolic form that closely corresponds both to Suhrawardi’s “Tale of the Western Exile” and to the adventures of the hero of the “Hymn of the Pearl,” the young Parthian prince in the Gnostic Acts of Thomas. We have already pointed out the parallels between those two journeys.

The whole treatise takes the form of a narrative recounting the stages and adventures of initiation into the hidden meaning of the saying we have just recalled: “Whoever has known himself has known his God.” Between these two acts of knowing lies the whole drama of origin and return (mabda’ and ma‘âd). Its resolution reveals why the spiritual Forms “descend” into the “labyrinth.” For when they reach its heart, they discover, in the dazzling vision of a mirror, the answer to the question: Who am I?

The sage tells the story of his quest as follows: “Once I lived in my own country, the home of my parents and ancestors.

“But one day the lord of the land summoned me and said: ‘It is fitting that you should not settle in the lofty dwellings of my kingdom until you have traveled to the land made fruitful by us, which lies at the farthest border of my realm. Do not forget our covenant of fidelity; for then you will find me there, in that distant land.

“Ask my minister, who sits at my Threshold, to describe it to you. No one enters by that Threshold unless he knows him, and no one leaves except by my permission.’ When I reached the Threshold (bâb), I found him there. I greeted him, and he returned my greeting. ‘My lord and sovereign,’ I said, ‘has ordered me to journey to the land made fruitful by us.’ ‘To make this journey and reach its end,’ he said, ‘you will have to overcome obstacles and steep passages. And the return journey to us will be harder still.

“I fear that distance and hardship will eventually cause you to forget our covenant.’ ‘Nevertheless, I must go,’ I said. ‘Describe that country to me. Describe the road that leads there.’” After warning him that the fatal act of forgetting would condemn the traveler to wander through ages upon ages, the “minister” gives the descriptions he has requested, then repeats his warning: “Do not forget our covenant. If you remember it, you will find us there—both me and my sovereign.”

What the “minister” describes are all the stages and adventures of the soul’s journey as it “descends” into this world. The pattern is common to the various forms of gnosis. The regions of the cosmos, the Spheres and the Elements, appear here as a cosmic labyrinth, through which the heavenly being—the pilgrim in this story—passes until it enters the narrow passages of the microcosm. This microcosm itself takes the form of a city, with a labyrinth of its own.

The outer senses and inner faculties are portrayed as characters, each bearing the symbolic attributes of its function. They occupy the “junctions” of the labyrinth, which is nothing other than the pilgrim’s “Personal City.” Here we find, literally, the symbolic descriptions given by Suhrawardi in two of his mystical treatises, as we noted at the outset. Within the labyrinth of the Personal City, these figures play the same role as the symbolic characters encountered by pilgrims following the labyrinth marked out on church pavements.

Turning this way and that, our pilgrim lingers and eventually forgets both his promises and the very reasons he came (the young Parthian prince of the “Hymn of the Pearl” suffers the same fate in Egypt).

Yet at last he reaches the heart of the city. There, at the heart of the labyrinth, the extraordinary encounter takes place: the mirror awakens the pilgrim to awareness of himself. He sees a shaykh, the master of the city, seated on a royal throne. “I greeted him,” the pilgrim relates, “and he returned my greeting. I spoke to him, and he spoke to me. Whatever I did, he did. Whatever I said, he said. I looked at him closely, and behold: he was myself; the shaykh was my reflected image (‘aksî). At once I awoke and remembered all the promises.

“And while I was still dazzled by this discovery, I met the minister of my sovereign, the one who had instructed me. He took my hand and said: ‘Immerse yourself in this Water, for it is the Water of Life.’ When I had immersed myself, I understood the symbols and riddles of his person. He said: ‘Welcome! You are now one of us (anta minnâ)’ 470. And he announced my return to my country of origin.” This passage accords perfectly with what we read at the end of the “Tale of the Western Exile.”

Of course, with the help of parallel narratives—especially Suhrawardi’s—it would not be difficult to suggest several interpretations of the characters in this drama. The “sovereign” may be the Lord God. His “minister” would then be the Active Intellect, traditionally called the Dator formarum, the Giver of Forms, by philosophers, and identified by Suhrawardi’s “Eastern” spiritual philosophers, the Ishrâqîyûn, with the Holy Spirit and Angel of humanity. This Angel is at once the angel of Knowledge and the angel of Revelation, the Angel on Sinai in the “Tale of Exile.”

The shaykh at the city’s heart would then be Perfect Nature, the pilgrim’s heavenly alter ego. Or, still in terms of Suhrawardi’s philosophy, the three characters could stand respectively for the Angel-Intelligence that is the Dator formarum; Perfect Nature, the Gnostic’s personal angel; and the soul-self that has “descended” into this world. Suhrawardi calls this last, borrowing a term from the old Iranian chivalric tradition, the espahbad light, corresponding in a certain sense to the Stoic hêgemonikon, the soul’s governing faculty. A Shiite mystic, on the other hand, might see in the sovereign and the minister who sits at his “threshold” the Imam and his representative (his nâ’ib or his bâb, “threshold”).

There is no need to choose between these interpretations. What matters is precisely that they do not exclude one another. They—and others besides—are all possible because, even as they assign different functions to the characters, they preserve the identity of the same dramatic element. It is this: the Dator formarum, the Giver of Forms from whom our souls and our knowledge proceed, will keep the meeting arranged with the pilgrim before he set out.

The pilgrim was sent into the earthly world for the very purpose of finding him there, and of finding him in the dazzling mirror that reflects the pilgrim’s own image. As for the meeting place, it perfectly illustrates the correspondence between spiritual perspectives—the same correspondence that enables Swedenborg to arrange the levels of his spiritual interpretation. The principle is this: what is above and at the origin, when it has come into our world and assumed a place in space, is found at the center, at the heart (see above, Book I, chapter IV, section 2).

The end of the mystical journey, in the tenth and final chapter of our treatise, reveals the ultimate secret. We must follow carefully the stages of this revelation, here expressed through the phenomenon of the mirror.

First, at the city’s heart, the pilgrim discovers that the shaykh who governs it is himself: the shaykh is his own reflected image. The shock of this discovery awakens him to self-awareness. Once awake, he sees beside him the minister of his sovereign, faithful to their appointed meeting. Two details suggest that this minister is none other than Khezr: he stands beside the Spring of Life, and he invites the pilgrim to immerse himself in it.

At the end of the “Tale of the Crimson Archangel,” we read that “if you are Khezr,” you too can pass through the defiles—the labyrinth—of Mount Qaf. And here, in our Indo-Persian tale, the pilgrim has indeed become Khezr so completely that he discovers the minister of his sovereign to be himself as well. The minister, too, is the reflection of the pilgrim’s own image.

The pilgrim is then dazzled by a second encounter with the mirror. As before, the shock of that dazzling experience discloses a presence. This time it is his sovereign himself, also faithful to the appointed meeting, for the condition has now been fulfilled.

But a momentous reversal is about to occur. Previously, the pilgrim had discovered that first the shaykh of his Personal City and then his sovereign’s wise minister were mirrors reflecting his own image. Now, at the final stage of his discovery, he realizes that he himself is the reflected image of his sovereign. He has become the mirror. His soul, his own self—the self known by the “I” that knows “itself” (recall our discussion above, chapter VI, sections 1 and 4)—is this sovereign, just as earlier it was the Gnostic’s personal angel. And he himself, the “I” that knows itself, is the sovereign’s reflected image.

We can now understand why we recalled the initiate’s final discovery on emerging from Leonardo’s labyrinth into the eight-sided chamber of mirrors, which multiplies to infinity the image of the person standing at its center. In the end, the phenomenon of these mirrors is what enables us to understand the secret of the esoteric tawhîd, the innermost meaning of divine oneness.

Here is the conclusion of our Indo-Persian initiation story: “When I had understood all these things, I discovered that the minister of my sovereign beside me was myself; the minister was my reflected image. I stood dazzled. And in that dazzling moment I met my sovereign himself. He ordered me to take a thread spun by a spider. He divided the thread in two, then joined it again into a single thread, saying to me: ‘The one multiplied by the one is the One (1 × 1 = 1).’ Then I understood his allusion: I discovered that my soul (nafsî, my ‘self’) is he himself, and that I am his reflected image.”

This symbol, 1 × 1 = 1, expresses something that is neither a vaguely mystical monism, in which everything loses its distinction, nor an abstract monotheism that isolates the personal divinity from the one to whom, and through whom, that divinity reveals itself as a person. Failure to understand this has led to many misinterpretations both of Sufi spiritual philosophy and of the experience to which it leads. The mystic first discovers images that reflect the image of his soul: the shaykh of the Personal City and the sovereign’s minister. Finally he discovers that he himself is the mirror reflecting his sovereign’s image.

We can compare this with the thirty birds (sî-morgh) standing before the eternal Simurgh. Here the eternal Simurgh is the Dator formarum. What we have is neither the confusion of all things into an undifferentiated whole nor an opposition or confrontation between one being and another, but 1 × 1. This symbol is the supreme formula of dualitude: it preserves unity of essence without confusion of persons—or, in this case, without confusion of “images.” These are not two separate ones added together (1 + 1) to make two. They are two ones that, precisely by multiplying one another (1 × 1), make only one One. This is the symbolic number, the “cipher,” of esoteric tawhîd that we shall encounter again in Ruzbihan of Shiraz (see below, Book III). If this is the secret of the Dator formarum rediscovered at the heart of the “Personal City,” it is also the secret of forms and their transformations that the mystical pilgrim has thereby won.

And perhaps it is only after reaching this level of spiritual awareness that the pilgrim can understand the true daring of transformation: a daring that saves him from the catastrophe and disintegration of Forms, from the sterile turmoil of formlessness that we ourselves witness in every sphere today. For such daring unfolds only in souls that Sufism, under various names, calls souls of desire. The story of a soul of desire, as our little Indo-Iranian romance has suggested alongside many others, begins long before the soul enters this world. In that origin lies the inner law belonging to that soul alone, together with its foreknowledge of the new form that has always been its own and no one else’s.

But to what extent can our world, having broken with faith and hope, still understand—how can we avoid asking?—that for each of us, each unique being, the only truly new being is the one who guides us, and that this being can guide us only because it existed before us? And that this being, new and yet pre-eternal, is the only one who, “if we entrust it with our thought, will at last bring to fulfillment our most secret thought—the one that no one before us ever expressed, and that we ourselves did not so much think as feel, so completely did it live within us as one with love” 471.

Chapter VII The “Eastern” Tradition

1. The Spiritual Legacy of the “Royal Road”

The preceding chapters have shown how the Shaykh al-Ishrâq put his “great idea” into practice: the creation of a complete spiritual culture, one that embraces the whole of philosophical knowledge while directing it toward the full spiritual realization of the human person. The path of Ishrâq—the “Eastern” theosophy revived from ancient Persia—turns neither right nor left.

Whoever sets out upon it is called to be neither a theoretical philosopher who forgets philosophy's true purpose nor a mystical adventurer unaware of the dangers facing anyone whom philosophy has not yet awakened to self-knowledge or protected against illusions of every kind. This is why the path may be called the “royal road” (hê basilikê hodos).

I borrow the expression here from the mystical theosophy of Philo of Alexandria. Although our “Eastern” theosophers did not know his work, it too would invite many comparisons with theirs. Such comparisons would extend those that others have already drawn between Philo's divine “Powers” and the Amahraspands, the Archangels of the Avesta.

The expression royal road comes from the Book of Numbers: “We will follow the royal road, turning neither right nor left, until we have passed through your territory” (20:17 and 21:22). This “royal road” is the path of gnosis, of knowledge attained through direct vision. It is the path of the “race of seers,” and it leads them to the highest degree: the apotheôsis that Sohrawardî calls ta’alloh, becoming godlike. It is the path that brings the “exile” back to the summit of the mystical Sinai, where the entrance to the “eighth clime” opens before him.

The royal road is also what the gnostics of Islam call the “Straight Path” (sîrât mostaqîm). It turns neither right nor left: it is a path along the mountain ridge, where the virtues cultivated on both slopes come together and reach their height. Sohrawardî's great idea left a profound mark on Iran's spiritual culture. There have certainly been theoretical philosophers, and there have been Sufis who disdained philosophy. Neither group, taken alone, embodies that spiritual culture in its fullness.

We have already heard the testimony of Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî (see below, Book V, Chapter II): “What is most fitting is for the pilgrim journeying toward God to bring the two methods together. His inner discipline should never be without philosophical meditation; and, conversely, his philosophical meditation should never be without an effort of spiritual purification. Better still, his spiritual method should be a barzakh—an intermediate realm joining the two methods. Such is the path followed by the Hokamâ’ ishrâqîyûn, the ‘Eastern’ theosophers (the ‘Platonists of Persia’).” 472 Thus the spiritual teaching intended by Sohrawardî has continued from century to century.

And the name “royal road” is all the more appropriate because its emblematic hero was Kay Khosraw, the wise and visionary king who, by taking this path, brought Iran's heroic epic to its culmination as a mystical epic. He is its emblematic hero because all the sages of ancient Persia who follow him along this “royal road” are themselves named after him: they are the khosrawânîyûn, a term that, in Sohrawardî's thought, is equivalent to Ishrâqîyûn.

We now know the importance Sohrawardî attached to this name and to the role of Kay Khosraw. The meaning he gives to Kay Khosraw's example and to the designation khosrawânîyûn confirms his most explicit statements about his purpose in reviving the mystical theosophy of the ancient Persian sages. If these sages were “Eastern”—in the sense of Ishrâqîyûn—it was because they were khosrawânîyûn. This is the meaning and significance of what we might call Sohrawardî's Iranism. Its wholly spiritual and “hieratic,” or sacred, character becomes clear.

This is the first time we have used the word Iranism here. It might have found a place in one of the great systems of the “philosophy of history” developed in the West, had Sohrawardî's work been known there. In fact, there is one such system in which Iranism appears, raised almost to the status of a metaphysical principle.

But the philosophical system in question was produced by a school little known in Western Europe except among specialists. I am thinking of the circle known as the “Slavophiles” in Russia during the first half of the nineteenth century. Perhaps it is no geographical accident that this was where the principle of Iranism bore fruit in philosophy. Unfortunately, the Iranian philosophers of the time seem to have had no opportunity to learn about it; nor have subsequent circumstances done much to draw their attention to a school whose Iranism directly concerns them.

Elsewhere we have already had occasion to suggest both the affinities and the contrasts between the Iranism of Alexis Khomiakov and that of Sohrawardî. 473 We know that a whole book would be needed to pursue the comparison: the field remains completely unexplored. Here I wish only to add briefly to the suggestions made earlier.

In the magnificent philosophy of history constructed by Alexis Khomiakov—a philosophy that owes nothing to Hegelian dialectic—two principles, two types of civilization, confront one another from humanity's first steps into history. On one side stands the principle of freedom, expressed in creation; on the other, the principle of necessity, expressed in generation. Khomiakov gives these two principles names that almost personify them. Iranism is the creative spiritual principle, the religion of moral freedom.

Kushism (Kush is the biblical name for Ethiopia) is the religion of physical as well as logical necessity. Kushism knows only the necessary sequence of logical reasoning; in this sense it finds its fullest expression in Hegel's system. Iranism, or Iranian thought, “rests upon tradition and cannot be restored by a purely logical operation, for the idea of creative freedom cannot be enclosed in formulas or deduced from them. It can be discerned only through a higher intuition, beyond the narrow limits of reasoning, or through the labor of centuries that have passed through every stage of negation.” 474

Might we not say that, in Sohrawardî's thought, Kushism is represented by the philosophy of the Peripatetics—the rule of Logic, the necessity imposed by the laws of rational understanding? What Hegel represented to Khomiakov, Peripatetic philosophy, if not Aristotle himself, represented to Sohrawardî.

And the rule of logical necessity, like that of physical necessity, is broken by the visionary theosophy of Iran's Khosrawânîyûn: by the free ascent of vision, which gives shape to what it sees; by the “higher intuition” that enters spiritual worlds barred to the dialectic of Logic. The affirmation of the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world, is thus a paradoxical act. By daring to “step outside” the constraints of empiricism and the supposed certainties of rational Logic, it overcomes the opposition between them.

Khomiakov speaks of having “passed through every stage of negation.” Sohrawardî, for his part, is as opposed to the Peripatetics as anyone could be, yet he requires his disciple first to pass through every stage of Peripatetic philosophy, through the world of Logic. He does this himself throughout the first part of the Book of Eastern Theosophy, although under a Stoic inspiration in which interpretation takes precedence over dialectic.

Logic is thereby simplified and broken open, and the book arrives at a metaphysics of vision. The Kushite principle is not overcome by simply going around it or leaving it untouched. Perhaps Khomiakov's inspired intuition would take an unexpected turn if it were examined more closely alongside the purpose of Sohrawardî, the “resurrector” of ancient Iran's theosophical wisdom.

To be sure, what mattered to Khomiakov was not geographical, historical, or even ethnic fact, but the religious principle—or rather, the struggle between two principles that makes up the drama of humanity's spiritual history.

Nevertheless, his philosophy also seeks to raise to universal significance the type concealed in the very roots of a people's life: in this case, the Russian type. Even though he and the other Slavophiles were concerned above all with the Russian people's vocation as the exemplary people of Orthodoxy, their thought may also contain a latent concern for a worldly ideal, what has been called a deep-seated “populism.”

Nothing could be further from Sohrawardî's Iranism. He has shown us that the Iranian people, simply as a people, did not thereby deserve to be called “Eastern” in his sense of the word. The knowledge of their ancient sages was not “Eastern” merely because they lived in the geographical East. The reverse is true: it was “Eastern” knowledge that made these Iranians the “Easterners” par excellence. The light of this “East” is the Light of Glory (Xvarnah), which may invest a person or withdraw from one.

The “Eastern” ancestry Sohrawardî claims for himself and his followers is not an ethnic lineage but a hieratic, or sacred, lineage—in the Neoplatonic sense of the word. It lies outside the causal relationships between peoples and states. The grounds on which this lineage rests, like those of the line of guardians of the Grail, belong to a history that breaks through what we ordinarily call history.

The comparison should therefore turn to a different figure: Constantin Leontiev, who placed his faith not in Russia or its people but in the sacred and hieratic ideal of the Byzantine world. He had no interest in providing a mystical foundation for a worldly theocratic kingdom. 475 Insofar as sacred Byzantium inherited the legacy of the Neoplatonists whose “hieratic” wisdom we invoked at the beginning of this study, Sohrawardî's purpose lends itself to comparison with Leontiev's wholly spiritual and ascetic purpose.

For neither man is a people, in itself, what matters most; what matters is the sacred idea that inhabits and governs it. What the sacred idea of Byzantium was to Leontiev, the idea of ancient Iran's theosophical wisdom was to Sohrawardî. Here, too, we could see at work the principle of freedom embodied by Iranism in Khomiakov's drama of the philosophy of history.

No one was more revolutionary and more traditionalist at once than Sohrawardî. He declared that he had no predecessor; yet it was through him, and beginning with him, that the “Eastern” tradition, the ishrâqî tradition, came into existence as a link between the spirituality of ancient Iran and that of Islamic Iran.

It was therefore not without irony that I recently read a criticism directed at a fellow scholar for classifying Sohrawardî among the Sufis. The objection was that Sohrawardî was a Hellenizing philosopher with no connection to any “regularly constituted” Sufi tarîqat, or spiritual order.

Yet the name “Hellenizing philosophers” is generally given to precisely those whom Sohrawardî excludes from the “royal road,” because they were philosophers and nothing more. He himself, then, cannot be one of these “Hellenizing philosophers.” As for making membership in Sufism depend on some unspecified certificate, document, or formal initiation, such a canonical and bureaucratic view is a Western obsession, alien to Sohrawardî's “Easterners.” Sohrawardî did not merely point to the “regular” tradition with which he was connected: he brought it to life.

Spiritual lineage is something witnessed in a person's life. It cannot be proven by archival documents, but by the way of being, living, and thinking that a person takes as a model. There has been, and still is, in Iran an entire Sufism outside Sufism: a spiritual tradition that does not bear the name, sometimes refuses it, and prefers the words ’irfân and ’orafâ’, referring to mystical knowledge and those who possess it. There are “regularly constituted” Shiite Sufi orders.

But there are also others that have never left, and never will leave, traces in any historical archive. That does not in the least prevent their “members” from being Sufis in the true sense of the word. Sohrawardî received the spiritual legacy he left to his followers from an authority infinitely higher than any “regularly constituted” order. The tarîqat of the Ishrâqîyûn, in turn, has no archives.

Sohrawardî left it to his followers to discover his spiritual legacy on the “royal road,” on one condition alone: that they set out upon it. Their commitment depends not on external formalities but on an inward calling. He expressly recalls this calling as he concludes the Book of Eastern Theosophy, in the “testament” addressed to those who will carry on his work.

This testament is prepared for by the closing pages of the book, which I shall now briefly describe. They confirm that the Book of Eastern Theosophy was not intended as a theoretical treatise, not even a treatise on angels. Its purpose is practical: it must be used as an instrument of meditation and spiritual realization. Theological and theosophical “theorems” correspond to psycho-spiritual energies capable of sustaining that realization and receiving it as a gift.

There is a relationship between the appearances of angels and the intensity of the mystic's spiritual life, a relationship that makes each person's experience uniquely his own. The penultimate chapter of Book V, just before the “Testament,” begins an experiential verification of the books that precede it. It is introduced by two “psalms” whose lyrical inspiration briefly interrupts the course of the final part of the work.

But the author warns us that anyone wishing to know the hidden meaning of these psalms must learn it from the person he calls the “Upholder of the Book” 476—a figure who will be mentioned again in the Testament's final lines. We hesitate, therefore, to press the matter further.

Yet their secret must be very close to that of the Book of Hours (wâridât wa taqdîsât), two of whose “psalms” we translated and discussed above (Chapter III, section 5). Their otherworldly resonance announces the events of ecstasy, always on the point of occurring. It harmonizes with the Manichaean sound of other psalms by Sohrawardî: “Draw the litany of Light upward; deliver the people of Light; lead the Light toward the Light.”

Of the two psalms, or “inspired utterances” (wâridât), that appear at the end of the Book of Eastern Theosophy, I shall quote the opening of the first: 477 “The wanderers who knock at the gateway of the lofty halls of Light, in uprightness and steadfastness of heart, behold, the angels of God come to meet them and draw them toward the Orient of Lights. They greet them with the greetings of the world of the Malakût; they pour over them Water rising from the spring of Beauty, so that they may be made pure.” When this lyrical surge subsides, the exposition resumes with a description of the experiences of those who follow the spiritual path (§ 272).

The commentators, Qotboddîn Shîrâzî and Shahrazôrî, take this opportunity to remind us 478 that the author personally verified not only every theoretical problem discussed in the book but also every genuinely illuminative state he mentions. These states refer to experiences he actually underwent: the fifteen kinds of light and sudden radiance that shake the mystic, from the beginner's stage through the intermediate stage to the first degree of spiritual perfection; the secondary phenomena that accompany them, such as sounds; their seemingly contradictory character, both painful and delightful; the inward vision of one's being brought to white heat; and so on.

All this is described concisely, in a vocabulary of striking precision. Comparison is unavoidable with similar experiences—visions of Lights—described by Najmoddîn Kobrâ (d. 1220), ’Alâoddawleh Semnânî (d. 1336), and Sayyed Mohammad Nûrbakhsh (d. 1464). “When the divine Lights have multiplied upon a human being, they clothe him in the robe of power and majesty, and souls allow themselves to be guided by him” (§ 277). The word Xvarnah does not appear.

But we have already observed, in discussing these lines, that these are the very terms Sohrawardî uses elsewhere 479 to describe the investiture with the royal Xvarnah bestowed upon the life of the mystic: the pilgrim falls beneath the assault of the archangelic Lights—and rises again as a king. This transformation of one's being through the sudden radiance of the Xvarnah, the Light of Glory, corresponds to the Event personally experienced by the mystic in the Malakût, the spiritual kingdom. We have seen how much importance Sohrawardî attaches to the person and ecstasy of Hermes. These lines are like an echo of the Ars Regia, the Royal Art of the Hermetic philosophers.

Finally come the solemn words of the spiritual testament (already discussed above, Chapter I, section 2). Before silence returns, they remind us that this book cannot be studied like any other book. Its aim is not merely to communicate knowledge, but to bring about a real event in the soul—the very event Sohrawardî describes in his initiatory tales: crossing the mountain of Qâf, reaching the mystical Sinai, in short, traveling the “royal road.”

“Brothers, I bequeath to you, as my testament, the observance of God's commands, renunciation of the things He forbids, the complete turning of your being toward God, our Lord, the Light of Lights, abstention from every action and word that is not your concern, and the rejection of every suggestion of the devil. I entrust this Book to your care. Watch over it; protect it from the profane, who are unworthy of it.

“By God, let it take my place—be my ‘caliph’—among you. I finished composing it at the end of the month of Jomâdâ II in the year 582 (16 September 1186), on the day when the seven planets were gathered in the sign of Libra, toward the close of the day. Hand it on only to someone worthy of it, someone who has demonstrated a firm knowledge of Peripatetic philosophy while keeping a heart filled with love for the divine Light.

“Once that condition is fulfilled, before beginning to study the book, the seeker must undertake a forty-day spiritual retreat, abstaining from all meat, eating only the bare minimum, setting aside every concern except meditation upon the Light of God, and following everything prescribed by the Upholder of the Book. When the appointed period before beginning the study of the book has passed, let him then immerse himself in that study” (§§ 278–280).

The Shaykh al-Ishrâq's overriding concern as he completes his book is therefore that it should be placed only in the hands of someone seeking the “royal road”: someone who has passed through the entire course of Peripatetic philosophy, yet whose heart holds a love strong enough to carry him beyond it and free him from the closed circle of theoretical and outwardly apparent certainties.

The commentators say that only those who long to enter the path of direct experience leading to the Orient of Lights may be admitted to the “community of the Book of Eastern Theosophy” (ahl hadhâ'l-kitâb). Those words have a curious affinity with the Quranic expression ahl al-Kitâb, the communities of the Book, as though the Ishrâqîyûn regarded the Book of Eastern Theosophy as itself a book “sent down from heaven.” The “Upholder of the Book” is mentioned again; he will be mentioned once more at the very end.

As for the forty-day retreat prescribed in a few words by the Shaykh as preparation for studying the book, the commentators supply the details.

First, the seeker must attend to the medical care and cleanliness of the body; choose a hermitage sheltered from human noise and concerns, a place of prayer lit only by a subdued light; follow a vegetarian diet; and break the fast only after the evening Prayer, with food that is modest in quantity but delicately prepared—white bread, grains, seasoned greens, almonds, walnuts, and sesame oil. The person on retreat should use carefully chosen perfumes both on the body and in the place of prayer.

Through dhikr, the remembrance of God, whether entirely inward or spoken aloud, the mind should remain occupied day and night with the presence of God, the Angels, and the Archangels of the higher heavenly hierarchies. Elsewhere, in the Creed of the Philosophers, the Shaykh suggests that meditation may be aided by melodies sung softly, the contemplation of suitable images, and so forth. 480 The seeker should spend long periods contemplating the self, “the soul,” as though it had already left behind the dimensions of ordinary time and space and recovered the immaterial nature (tajarrod) of its pure essence.

Sohrawardî himself had many visions of this kind. They led him to defend the power of Imagination as a way of knowing, and the reality of the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world: visions of beings from the spiritual world appearing in forms whose beauty surpasses every other beauty. 481

Qotboddîn Shîrâzî sums the matter up in words identical to Shahrazôrî's: “If the soul perseveres long enough in contemplating itself, behold, a flash of light bursts upon it. This is a light flowing from the archangelic Intelligence upon the soul, an exquisite light that passes like a flash of ecstasy. The Shaykh [Sohrawardî] has described in detail the experience of the different suprasensory lights. Next comes a light that sets the physical organism ablaze [to inward sight]; then a light that wipes away, that abolishes, every awareness in the soul except awareness of its eternal Beloved.

“And this is the ultimate mystical degree.” In another context, this degree appears as the third of the states of mystical consciousness: first, there are you and I; then, I and not you; finally, you and not I. 482 It is toward this ultimate degree that the pilgrim travels along the royal road. That is why Sohrawardî concludes his Creed of the Philosophers with these words: “They have the overflowing portion and the highest rank in this world and the world beyond.

“Blessed is the one who has known himself before dying and has attained for himself in this world a degree that, having made him happy in the abode of passing things, will be his joy in the abode of what endures forever.” 483

And the testament of the Book of Eastern Theosophy ends with these lines: “Whoever studies this book deeply will recognize that the ancients and the moderns alike have missed something that God has allowed my tongue to express. This book was inspired in my heart all at once by the Holy Spirit, on a wondrous day, although it took me no fewer than several months to write it, because of the difficulties caused by my travels. It deals with a matter of the utmost gravity. If anyone denies that this is so, he will not escape the wrath of God, for God is mighty and has the power to exact retribution (3:3).

“But let no one aspire to know the secrets of this book without turning to the person who is a caliph possessed of the knowledge of the Book (13:43 and 27:40).”

These lines are full of allusions that the commentators help us bring to light. The “something” missed by ancients and moderns alike is the way of the “Eastern” theosophers, the Ishrâqîyûn: the royal road, the middle way that unites and encompasses the philosophers' theoretical and outward knowledge and the inward attainment of spiritual realization. It is something that neither the philosophers of Islam—al-Fârâbî, Avicenna, and others—could reach through philosophy alone, nor the Sufis through spiritual discipline alone.

That is why the book concerns so grave a matter, and why anyone who denies either its gravity or its author's claim exposes himself to divine retribution. This testament is entirely in keeping with the hierarchy of sages established in the book's prologue (above, Chapter II, section 3), with its reference to the unbroken and hidden succession of sages.

At the summit of that hierarchy stands the mysterious figure of the mystical Pole, always present in this world even when entirely unknown to humankind. We had noticed that not a word would need changing for a Shiite reader to recognize here the Twelfth Imam, “invisible to bodily eyes, present in the hearts of his faithful.”

Indeed, the Shaykh al-Ishrâq's testament directs his followers to the mysterious “Upholder of the Book.”

Let us recall again that this is the title above all others that the Imams of Shiism have claimed for themselves. They are the “Upholders of the Book” because they possess both its outward and its inward meaning, the complete art of interpretation that makes the Imam the “speaking Quran.”

This meeting of Shiite and ishrâqî language is not accidental. Certainly, even non-Shiite Sufism knows of a hidden succession of spiritual Poles. According to Semnânî, for example, the lineage begins before the Prophet of Islam, passes through Mohammad and then the Imams down to the twelfth, and afterward continues through those whom Sufism recognizes in each age as the “Pole of Poles.”

Although this succession represents a displacement of the Shiite idea of the cycle of walâyat, the cycle of spiritual guardianship, it differs from that idea radically: it does not recognize the Twelfth Imam as still present in the world or as permanently holding the position of “Pole of Poles” (Qotb al-aqtâb).

Nor is it the same as the lineage recognized by Sohrawardî, which includes only some of Sufism's “Poles,” because its spiritual ancestry lies elsewhere. We also know that there is general agreement on this point: Ishrâq stands in relation to philosophy as Sufism stands in relation to Kalâm, dialectical, rational, outward-looking theology. The relationship is analogous; Ishrâq and Sufism are not identical.

Nevertheless, the title “Upholder of the Book,” which Sohrawardî gives to his successors, is literally the title borne by the Shiite Imam in relation to the Quran, with the difference that here it refers to the Book of Eastern Theosophy.

Let us turn back, then, to the diagram in which the Shaykh al-Ishrâq sketched the ancestry of the Ishrâqîyûn (above, Chapter I, section 2). There is indeed the idea of a succession, but no document recording it in the archives of a “regularly constituted” association. The matter is “too grave” to be reduced to that. Sohrawardî's project was probably intended to reach far into the future. This is already suggested by the idea of a community of Ishrâq possessing its own “inspired Book,” gathered around its Qâ’im, the one who “possesses the knowledge of the Book.” The model is the Shiite conception.

Yet so far as we know, only Shamsoddîn Shahrazôrî, at the end of his commentary, claimed for himself the title “Upholder of the knowledge of the Book.” 484 What happened after him? Must we suppose that the succession of “Upholders of the Book of Ishrâq” also entered the ghaybat, the state of concealment? In any case, we can still trace a succession of at least some great figures who illustrate the later fortunes of the Book of Eastern Theosophy and its considerable influence in Iran.

2. The Later “Eastern” Tradition in Iran and India

Given the present state of our knowledge and our examination of the texts, we must limit ourselves to a number of landmarks. They are important ones, certainly.

But the influence of the ishrâqî idea upon Iranian thought as a whole cannot be assessed in detail until many texts still surviving only in manuscript have become accessible. The Anthology now in preparation will contribute to that knowledge. 485

The first name to be placed in the line descending from Sohrawardî's Ishrâq, the line of the “Platonists of Persia,” is that of Shamsoddîn Shahrazôrî. 486 Strangely enough, we know almost nothing about the life of this philosopher, who himself devoted an entire book to the lives of philosophers, both those who lived before Islam and those who appeared within Islam. He is so completely identified with his work that the work alone offers us a few details about the man.

Foremost among his writings are two extensive commentaries on works by Sohrawardî: the Book of Elucidations Inspired by the Tablet and the Throne (Talwîhât) and the Book of Eastern Theosophy. We do know from another source that a young disciple named Shams shared the Shaykh al-Ishrâq's imprisonment in Aleppo. We would like this to have been Shamsoddîn Shahrazôrî himself, Sohrawardî's enthusiastic biographer and commentator.

Yet we cannot even say with certainty that Shahrazôrî had personal contact with Sohrawardî. If he had, why would he have been so hesitant in writing the Shaykh's biography, especially concerning the date of his death? Moreover, he would have had to live an exceptionally long life.

Among his other writings is a monumental encyclopedia entitled Treatises of the Divine Tree and the Theosophical Secrets. 487 It is a Summa of all the philosophy produced within Islam down to his own time, and we can only hope that an editor will soon undertake its publication. The work was completed in 680/1282. Admittedly, this monument, the labor of a lifetime, may have been finished near the end of the author's life.

But a note by a copyist working from the author's original suggests that Shahrazôrî was still alive in 687/1288, a century after Sohrawardî's death. It seems more likely, then, that Shahrazôrî was in contact with Sohrawardî's immediate disciples. His allegiance to Sohrawardî's Ishrâq was all the deeper for having followed a kind of spiritual conversion after an earlier period of reserve.

Another of his books, Hill al-romûz (Solution of the Enigmas), seems to show no trace of Ishrâq at all.

Elsewhere we have described the style and structure of the two great commentaries on Sohrawardî's works and explained why, despite the silence maintained by later commentators on the matter, Shahrazôrî seems to us to come first chronologically. The prologue to his commentary on the Book of Eastern Theosophy bears no dedication. It praises no prince or distinguished person who might have commissioned the work.

There is no hint, then, of a desire to please a patron. The commentary seems entirely inspired by the devotion of mind and heart, given without reservation to an ideal figure. Its only praise is a eulogy of Sohrawardî, following a lament for the decline of the higher sciences and the fading traces of the path followed by the ancient sages, those who had truly experienced theurgic wisdom.

When the Shaykh al-Ishrâq appeared, Shahrazôrî declares, “he undertook to renew what the cycles and ages of time had corrupted, to bring back into view what they had erased ... to raise to life what was dead and abolished.” Philosophy had been completely overwhelmed by Peripatetic thought. The purpose of this book was different. It spoke to the “Solitary Ones” and the “Unique Ones,” individuals set apart from the multitude; that is why it was neglected at first.

“Yet now this eminent man's hour of full noon has come.” Journeys and changes of place have made it possible for men capable of understanding the work to meet one another. Having cleared their hearts of commonplace philosophy, they find themselves increasingly drawn to this singular book. Interest in it grows, “for neither we ourselves nor anyone else have ever encountered a more complete book on theosophical knowledge and the knowledge that initiates into the mysteries.” 488 Such, then, was the wholly disinterested motive that led Shahrazôrî to write his commentary.

One final detail is both significant and revealing. In the preceding pages we have noted Sohrawardî's rather mysterious references to the person who would be the “Upholder of the Book,” or the “Upholder of the knowledge of the Book”—that is, the Book of Eastern Theosophy. This “Upholder” would represent Sohrawardî among those who, in the future, might form something like an Order of the Ishrâqîyûn.

We have also noted that Shiite terminology gives this same title to the Imam as the “Upholder of the Holy Book.” Now Shahrazôrî, unlike the other commentators, does not hesitate to claim the title envisaged by Sohrawardî. His commentary ends with this solemn declaration: “The Upholder of the knowledge of the Book in the present age declares: here ends what, through divine help and inspiration, we have been able to accomplish in commenting upon this sublime book.”

The responsibility and standing Shahrazôrî thus claimed seem to imply an investiture whose origin and meaning remain shrouded in mystery for us. The life of Qotboddîn Shîrâzî, another great commentator on the Book of Eastern Theosophy, can be traced with much greater precision through the written record. 489 He came from Fârs and was born at Shîrâz in 634/1237. His father, Ziyâoddîn Mas’ûd ibn Maslak, originally from Kazerûn, was both a physician and a Sufi Shaykh.

From earliest childhood, then, the future “eminent scholar” (’Allâmeh) was acquainted with scientific learning and the spiritual life. Throughout his life he traveled widely, always seeking scientific and spiritual knowledge; he is recorded as having visited Khorassan, Anatolia, Syria, and Iraq. Among his celebrated teachers were Nasîroddîn Tûsî, the renowned Shiite astronomer and philosopher, and the great mystic Sadroddîn Qonyawî, a disciple and stepson of Ibn ’Arabî. His writings, taken together, have an encyclopedic scope.

Just as Shahrazôrî composed the still-unpublished philosophical encyclopedia mentioned above, so Qotboddîn Shîrâzî produced an encyclopedia embracing the whole system of the sciences. 490 One story reported by Mîrkhond would cast a shadow over our picture of him. He is said to have developed a quiet but stubborn hostility toward his teacher Nasîr Tûsî, to the point of joining a plot to destroy the distinguished philosopher and astronomer's standing with the Mongol ruler Hûlâgû.

The plot failed, since the observatory in which the ruler was so interested had not yet been completed. It is better, with the good Khwânsârî, to doubt that this story concerns the same Qotboddîn, although Khwânsârî adds: “It is true that this would not have been the first bottle to break in Islam.” 491 Our Qotboddîn died at Tabrîz in Ramadan 710/January 1311, at the age of seventy-six lunar years.

His great commentary on the Book of Eastern Theosophy opens with praise of the Shaykh al-Ishrâq no less warm than Shahrazôrî's. He too recalls the mystical theosophy (hikmat dhawqîya, wisdom known through direct experience) of the ancient sages. This included knowledge of the imaginal world through which the resurrection of bodies takes place. It was a knowledge of the divine mysteries and the eternally subsisting Lights, not to be reached through “philosophical chatter” but through a refining and elevation of the innermost consciousness (taltîf al-sirr). Qotboddîn declares that Avicenna had already recalled this in certain passages of his Ishârât.

Then, after lamenting the Peripatetics' excessive resort to dialectical argument—in words reminiscent of both Sohrawardî and Shahrazôrî—Qotboddîn evokes a theosophical wisdom directed toward inward vision, contemplative seeing (moshâhada). This cannot be attained through definitions or syllogisms, but through the Lights that rise in the Orient of the soul (anwâr ishrâqîya), impressing their image upon it as upon a mirror, taking possession of it as fire takes possession of iron heated until it glows. Such was the state of souls “that have sought the Orient and the illumination of the divine Light.” 492 Yet the Shaykh al-Ishrâq's book has remained a hidden treasure. Qotboddîn intends to make the path easier for the soul that longs to put its teachings into practice.

This purpose led him to write a masterly commentary, completed in 694/1295, when he was sixty years old. We recalled earlier that the great encyclopedia into which Shahrazôrî had incorporated the substance of his own commentaries on Sohrawardî was completed in 680/1282. This seems decisive in establishing the chronological priority of Shahrazôrî's commentary. Furthermore, Qotboddîn's commentary includes long passages that reproduce Shahrazôrî's text word for word. It is true, however, that it also contains many developments absent from Shahrazôrî, 493 and its structure is quite different.

Shahrazôrî proceeds by taking relatively long passages of the text as points of departure, inserting his own explanations between them. Qotboddîn, aware of how difficult Sohrawardî's highly compressed text can be, inserts his explanations within the author's very sentences, opening up passages that are too tightly packed before proceeding to the commentary proper. He enriches this with reminders, quotations, and comparisons, making implicit meanings explicit and gradually clearing away every obscurity.

In short, he becomes the best of guides. That is why his annotated edition of the Book of Eastern Theosophy became the standard textbook for every generation of Ishrâqîyûn. Far more manuscripts of it survive than of Shahrazôrî's commentary, which it seems to have pushed into the background—rather as Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî's writings later eclipsed those of his teacher Mîr Dâmâd.

Among the major commentators on Sohrawardî's work, Ibn Kammûna (d. 683/1284) deserves special mention. He wrote an extensive commentary on a work already discussed here, one whose brevity makes it especially difficult: the Book of Elucidations Inspired by the Tablet and the Throne. The work comprises three books, on logic, physics, and metaphysics. It forms the first part of the trilogy that Sohrawardî intended as an indispensable preparation for studying his great Book of Eastern Theosophy. 494 Ibn Kammûna makes no secret of the difficulties he encountered. Had he not been afraid of disappointing those who had asked him to write the commentary, he would have abandoned the undertaking. He completed it in 667/1268.

Yet this commentary, in turn, contains many pages agreeing word for word with Shahrazôrî's commentary on the same treatise by the Shaykh al-Ishrâq. The question arises once again: which writer came first? Elsewhere, in a more detailed account of the work, we have explained why we believe the answer here too must favor Shahrazôrî. 495 This in no way diminishes the importance of Ibn Kammûna's work. His commentary, whose quotations show a thorough knowledge of Sohrawardî's other writings, remains the indispensable aid to close study of the Book of Elucidations that its author intended it to be.

When preparing our edition of Sohrawardî's text more than twenty years ago, we ourselves had access to the copy of Ibn Kammûna's commentary that had belonged to Qotboddîn Shîrâzî, the commentator on the Book of Eastern Theosophy.

We must now be content to name a succession of figures who serve as landmarks. The philosopher Athîroddîn Abharî (d. 663/1265) agreed with thinkers such as Shahrazôrî that the word “metaphysics” (mâ ba’d al-tabî’a, “what comes after physics”) is appropriate only from our human point of view, because we perceive sensible things first.

Thus the priority given to “physics,” the study of natural things or Naturalia, is a matter of convention, not of the nature of things; it reflects a teaching need. In reality, the principles of natural things come before those same natural things in being and in causation. These principles should therefore be established first, within a discipline better called prephysics than metaphysics. Abharî develops this argument in an entire treatise, the Kashf al-haqâ’iq, in which his account of prephysics faithfully reproduces Sohrawardî's ishrâqî philosophy of the human being's existence after death. 496

As for the writings of the great Shiite philosopher Nasîroddîn Tûsî, mentioned above, it would be interesting to investigate the extent of their debt to Ishrâq. In discussing angelology and the emanation of the Intelligences—which calls into question the famous principle ex uno non fit nisi unum, “from one thing only one thing can proceed”—Mollâ Sadrâ pointed out with great precision what Nasîr Tûsî, in his commentary on Avicenna's Ishârât, owed to Sohrawardî's inward, esoteric application of the laws of optics. 497

Among Ibn ’Arabî's commentators and disciples, ’Abdorrazzâq Kâshânî (d. around 730/1330) paid particular attention to the Hermetic origins of the Ishrâqîyûn. The influence of Ishrâq is especially striking in the great work of Ibn Abî Jombûr, the Kitâb al-Mojlî, composed in 895/1490, barely ten years before Shâh Isma’îl's accession. Together with the great synthesis of Haydar Âmolî (eighth/fourteenth century), this work brought Shiite theosophy and Ibn ’Arabî's theosophy decisively together. 498 Indeed, it is throughout Ibn ’Arabî's writings that we ought to seek connections with Sohrawardî's Ishrâq.

Later (in Book IV) we shall have occasion to show how Sâ’inoddîn Torkeh Ispahânî, an eminent Shiite philosopher of the fifteenth century (d. 830/1426 or 836/1432) and himself a commentator on Ibn ’Arabî's Fosûs, situated the Ishrâqîyûn. His entire body of work, of great importance for the metaphysics of being, remains to be studied.

Jalâloddîn Dawwânî (d. 907/1501), who converted to Shiism after a dream, was also an active commentator on the Shaykh al-Ishrâq. To this prolific writer we owe above all a commentary on the Book of the Temples of Light, to which Ghiyâthoddîn Mansûr Shîrâzî (949/1542) replied with a counter-commentary. 499 Two figures from Tabrîz must also be mentioned. Wadûd Tabrîzî wrote a systematic commentary on the Book of Tablets Dedicated to ’Imâdoddîn, the Seljuk emir of Anatolia.

Earlier in this study we drew upon the pages of that work dealing with the Xvarnah. The commentary was completed in 930/1524. A certain Najmoddîn Mahmûd Tabrîzî, a contemporary of Wadûd, wrote glosses on the Book of Eastern Theosophy. 500 Let us repeat that none of these commentaries should be neglected. They correspond to the studies we publish today in specialized scholarly journals.

This somewhat dry enumeration brings us to the moment when the teaching and spiritual experience of the Shaykh al-Ishrâq reveal themselves as a true center of intellectual life, a meeting place for spiritual worlds that communicate with one another on the plane of gnosis. The Book of Elucidations (Talwîhât) had already been translated into Hebrew.

Now, in the sixteenth century, Sohrawardî's work was to spread its influence into India, while in Iran it contributed to the philosophical revival of the Safavid period. It exercised a profound influence on the circle of thinkers gathered around Emperor Akbar (1556–1605), the Mughal ruler of India, and on his generous project of an ecumenical religion (dîn-e ilâhî, religio divina). Ishrâqî theosophy was one of the sources of this search for a universal religious understanding.

At the time, a vigorous exchange of spiritual ideas developed between Iran and India, with philosophers and Sufis traveling frequently back and forth. Here we shall concentrate on two examples of the fruit borne by Sohrawardî's work in Persian, which was then the language of culture in northwestern India. One belongs to the movement that arose around Shâh Akbar's initiative. The other consists of an entire body of Zoroastrian ishrâqî literature that emerged during the same period, under the influence of the same spiritual milieu.

As we have seen, the Shaykh al-Ishraq, Suhrawardi, wrote some of his works in Persian; in a few cases he even translated his own writings from Arabic into Persian. His great trilogy, however, and The Book of Oriental Theosophy, for which the trilogy serves as a preparation, were written in Arabic. So were the major commentaries mentioned above, which helped bring his thought into the wider intellectual life of Islam.

The first example of the passage of his work into Persian that concerns us here is Mohammad Sharif ibn Harawi, who produced an extensive Persian treatment of the prologue and second part of The Book of Oriental Theosophy. It was fitting that he should concentrate on the five books making up that second part, for it is there that the Illuminationist (ishrâqî) teaching is principally set out. Nor did he confine himself to Suhrawardi's text. He translated much of Qotb Shirazi's commentary into Persian and added reflections of his own 501.

We know little else about the translator himself. He completed his work in 1008 AH/1600 CE, which makes him a contemporary of Mir Damad (d. 1040 AH/1630 CE), the great teacher around whom the school we have called the School of Isfahan would take shape. Mohammad Sharif's prologue also suggests that he knew Indian Sufism firsthand and had actually spent time in India. His undertaking may therefore be connected with the religious questions raised by Shah Akbar's reforms.

Our second example comes from a body of Parsi Illuminationist writing produced by Zoroastrians who had emigrated from Iran to India. About forty years ago, the Parsi scholar Dr. J. J. Modi published an important study of Azar Kayvan, a Zoroastrian high priest who moved with his disciples from Shiraz, or its surroundings, to India around the turn of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries 502. Suhrawardi's writings found devoted admirers among them, so the history of this group is especially revealing for the Shaykh al-Ishraq's later influence in the East.

Earlier, we saw in the outcome of Suhrawardi's great project something like a homecoming of the Hellenized Magi to Iran—though now to an Islamic Iran. With Azar Kayvan's circle, that homecoming extends into a Zoroastrian community, and the circle is complete. This also helps us understand the books written within or around the group. The Parsis of India have called them “semi-Parsi” books, but regarded them favorably enough to undertake their publication.

Let us be clear from the outset: these works have relatively little to offer a specialist in Avestan and Pahlavi philology. For a student of religious philosophy, however, they are immensely interesting. They show Suhrawardi's work being reinterpreted through what these Zoroastrians knew of the Avesta and the Pahlavi texts. How far do their readings of Suhrawardi agree with Zoroastrian belief in its full, traditional form? That is why we recalled the description “semi-Parsi.” Dr. J. J. Modi was exceptionally well placed to judge.

What is certain is that these books contain genuinely Zoroastrian material. Not all the rest can be called Suhrawardian—they also contain substantial Manichaean, Buddhist, and Sufi elements—but a reader familiar with the Shaykh al-Ishraq will still feel on familiar ground on almost every page. Their extraordinary value lies in showing us how, in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, a group of Zoroastrian mystics received the work of a thinker who had expressly set out to “revive the theosophy of the ancient Persians.”

Only a few works seem to have survived from what was apparently a fairly extensive literature, and their rarity makes them hard to obtain. One of the works belonging to this larger body of writing is the Dabestan al-Madhahib—roughly, “The School of Religious Sciences”—a rich source of information about religious life in India at that time 503. Its author, Mobed-Shah, maintained close contact with Azar Kayvan's disciples. It is hardly surprising, then, that he devoted considerable attention to the different branches of Zoroastrianism existing in his day; indeed, on this point he is our only source.

In Chapter XI, on the religion of the philosophers, he divides them into two great families: the Illuminationists (Ishrâqîyûn) and the Peripatetics, followers of the Aristotelian tradition. He observes, for reasons that should now be clear, that the teachings and practices of the Illuminationists correspond exactly to those he had described in his first chapter under the heading “the ancient religion of the Iranians” 504. There, too, we are told that this ancient Iranian sacred wisdom was also the wisdom of the ancient Greeks, up to and including Plato—just as we read in Suhrawardi and his commentators.

The chief work cited as an authority by the author of the Dabestan probably originated within Azar Kayvan's school or its immediate circle. It is called the Dasatir-Nameh, the “Collection of Sacred Books” attributed to the ancient prophets of Iran. In the past, the few Orientalists who examined it generally confined themselves to negative criticism because it did not provide the kind of text they were looking for as philologists. Certainly, anyone hoping to find a surviving fragment of the Avesta or of Pahlavi literature will be disappointed.

But we should ask the book to give us what it actually sets out to give: the reflections of Zoroastrians who, in the spirit of the Shaykh al-Ishraq, pondered a body of traditions that have yet to receive a systematic study. The work presents itself as a “Bible of the prophets of Iran,” consisting of sixteen books attributed to sixteen prophets. It is written in two languages.

Whether one of them is an invented jargon or simply a cipher matters little to us, since it comes with a clear and readable Parsi Persian “translation.” Whether that translation was really written by Sasan V, said to have lived in Iran in the time of Khosrow Parviz and frequently mentioned in this literature, is quite another matter. Historically, “improbable” would be far too mild a word.

Yet the book's contents remain fascinating for anyone tracing the history of Ishraq. The “Book of Mah Abad” and the “Book of Sasan I,” for example, offer a close reflection of Suhrawardi's metaphysics, sometimes expanded with ideas drawn from the theosophy of Iranian Sufism 505.

Much the same can be said of another important work from Azar Kayvan's school. Among the members of the Zoroastrian high priest's community whom the author of the Dabestan knew personally, one figure stands out: Farzaneh Bahram ibn Farshad, known as “Bahram the Younger” (Kuchak Bahram). Mobed-Shah met him at Lahore in 1048 AH/1638 CE. He tells us that Bahram had completed the full course of philosophical and theological studies; that he knew Persian, Arabic, and Hindi, as well as at least one Western language; and that he translated Suhrawardi's works into Persian 506.

Unfortunately, no manuscript of these translations has yet come to light. One substantial work by Farzaneh Bahram, however, Sharestan-e chahar chaman (“The City of Four Gardens”), was published by lithography in Bombay in 1279 AH/1862 CE through the efforts of four Zoroastrian mobeds, or priests. This Persian work proceeds along lines similar to the Dasatir-Nameh and has four parts.

The first three deal with the creation of the cosmos and then with the sacred history of the prophet-kings of ancient Iran, from Hushang to the last Sasanian ruler. The fourth, or “fourth garden,” deals with astronomy, the structure of the cosmos, and geography 507. A long account of Illuminationist theosophy follows the chapter on Zoroaster. This is not an unthinking anachronism: for this Zoroastrian Illuminationist, the chapter on Zoroaster provides precisely the right occasion to state his position toward the Islamic schools and religious groups of his own time.

One more work from the same school deserves mention: Ayin-e Hushang (“The Religion of Hushang,” Iran's primordial prophet). It was published by lithography in Bombay in 1296 AH/1879 CE by the Parsi scholar Mirza Bahram Rostam Nasrabadi, who supplied a lengthy preface. It is a substantial collection of four Persian treatises 508, whose manuscripts came from the imperial library. Even a quick reading reveals the influence of Ishraq.

We can do no more here than draw attention to these little-known books. This Zoroastrian Illuminationist literature calls for a study of its own, which we hope to undertake elsewhere. The author of the Dabestan also mentions other Zoroastrian sages from Shiraz whom he knew personally. Among them were Hakim Ilahi Herbad and Hakim Mirza, both described as Ishrâqîyûn. Both knew the Shaykh al-Ishraq's works thoroughly, and had absorbed his teaching so completely that they made his “Book of Hours”—from which we translated two psalms above, in Chapter III, Section 5—the liturgical ritual of their own religious life 509.

The understanding held by these Zoroastrian Illuminationists in Shah Akbar's time—of philosophy's Iranian origin in its two forms, ecstatic (ishrâqî) and dialectical (Peripatetic), and of the translators who disseminated learning preserved in the treasuries of the ancient Persian kings—ought to be compared with the older traditions preserved in authentic Pahlavi literature. Nor was Suhrawardi's image of the Iranian sage as a Platonist something he invented.

The historian Mas'udi (d. 346 AH/957 CE), discussing Tansar, the chaplain of Ardashir who restored the Mazdean religious establishment in the Sasanian Empire in the third century CE, already describes that eminent figure as a Platonist—or, in the terms of our texts, an Illuminationist. Tansar's own words, in his famous letter, explaining and justifying his way of life were not chosen at random. They correspond exactly to the stages that would later structure Suhrawardi's spiritual discipline 510.

Through the distinguished spiritual figures he met in India, the author of the Dabestan ultimately leads us back to Iran. He tells us that he learned directly from Farzaneh Bahram that among those close to Azar Kayvan's circle, and those granted meetings with the master, was none other than Baha'oddin 'Amili, one of the most eminent figures of Iranian Shiism: the venerable mujtahid, or jurist qualified to exercise independent judgment, who taught Molla Sadra in Isfahan 511.

Thus we find ourselves once more on Iranian soil, following the traces of the “community of the Book of Oriental Theosophy.” We have just seen this mystical community send out branches into India. Although distinct from Sufism, its history is nonetheless intertwined with Sufism's—perhaps most directly with the Nurbakhshiyya order. A distant great-grandnephew of the Shaykh al-Ishraq is said to have succeeded Sayyed Mohammad Nurbakhsh (d. 1464) as head of that order 512.

As for Shiism, we have already noted more than one point of contact between Illuminationist and Imamite theosophy—indeed, something far more substantial than mere points of contact. Their interaction becomes clearer still, as we recalled earlier, when Shiite theosophers recover what they recognize as their own spiritual inheritance within the theosophy of Ibn 'Arabi. The merging of these currents would mark Iran's great intellectual and spiritual flowering under the Safavids, while in India the effects of Shah Akbar's reforms were being felt at the same time, with many Iranian thinkers taking part.

The first name that comes to mind is Mir Damad (d. 1040 AH/1630 CE), the intellectual master of the School of Isfahan, whose influence is still felt in Iran today. Without examining here how far each of his writings agrees with Suhrawardi's positions, let us note a few telling details. In answering a correspondent's question about a difficult passage in Suhrawardi's Book of Oriental Theosophy, Mir Damad shows a profound understanding of the text 513. As for the “Profession of Faith of the Philosophers,” we have elsewhere mentioned a manuscript copied in Mir Damad's own hand, ending with the highest praise for the Shaykh al-Ishraq 514.

Finally, Mir Damad adopted the very name Ishraq as his pen name (takhallos). Readers who turn to the “Ecstatic Confessions” translated later in this work (Book V, Chapter I) will be able to appreciate the affinity between these two shaykhs. We may also recall that one of Mir Damad's pupils, Qotboddin Ashkevari, discerned in the Twelfth Imam the features of the figure whom Zoroastrian teachings about the end of time call the “Saoshyant,” the restorer who will raise the dead.

The full brilliance and range of Suhrawardi's thought become especially apparent, of course, in the work of Mir Damad's most celebrated pupil, Molla Sadra Shirazi. Molla Sadra left an immense body of writing, running to several folio volumes. An entire book would be needed to establish the place of the Shaykh al-Ishraq's writings and ideas within it. Here we shall mention only the Glosses Molla Sadra wrote on The Book of Oriental Theosophy: a work of remarkable depth, scale, and originality in its own right, without which much of Suhrawardi's book would lose its resonance.

We shall give a sample of these glosses later, after attempting to explain Molla Sadra's importance to the spiritual culture of Iran (below, Book V, Chapter II). Molla Sadra frequently uses the words mashriq (“east”) and mashriqî (“eastern”), and it is a pleasure to see his commentators—from Mirza Ahmad Ardakani Shirazi and Molla Isma'il Isfahani to Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i—carefully distinguish their meanings; their analyses invariably lead back to Suhrawardi's use of the words 515.

Later (Book V, Chapter III), we shall also devote several pages to another outstanding master, Qazi Sa'id Qommi. His work is of the greatest philosophical interest because it shows how the Shiite understanding of the Imam intersects with a fundamental Illuminationist idea.

Even after naming two eminent masters such as Molla Hadi Sabzavari and Molla 'Abdollah Zonuzzi, who carried the philosophy of Ishraq into nineteenth-century Iran, we would still have to trace its presence in the writings of another forty or fifty thinkers who have sustained philosophical life in Iran over the past four centuries. Unfortunately, the work of examining those writings—which first requires reliable editions of the texts—has scarcely begun.

3. The Religion of Transfigured Eros

This title for our final section seems to bring together, better than any other, the teachings and intentions of the Shaykh al-Ishraq. It also prepares the way for Book III, which will deal with Ruzbehan and the “Faithful in Love.”

The theme draws together connections we have suggested, sometimes only in passing: the “story” of the gnostic; the earthly self and its heavenly counterpart; the Hermetic figure of Perfect Nature and the Mazdean or Manichaean vision of the angel Daena; the idea of Sophia in Jacob Boehme; the philosophers' Active Intelligence and the Madonna Intelligenza of the Fedeli d'amore; the emergence of the mystical epic; and more. What especially concerns us is how the austere metaphysical theme of the Active Intelligence unfolds, through imagination, into a mystical epic of love.

We can see this again in one of Suhrawardi's tales of initiation.

We must say a little about it in closing, because its dramatic setting contains, in suggestive form, everything we have tried to analyze here. It resonates with so many centuries of Iranian mystical poetry that, if we attempted to set Suhrawardi's themes alongside all their later variations, the task would have no end.

Here we shall concern ourselves only with the metaphysical foundation of the religion and mysticism of love as presented in this last tale. In doing so, we shall briefly return to all the themes we have encountered throughout this book and the questions they have raised.

Our section's title is not accidental. It is inspired by a work of the Russian philosopher Boris Vycheslavtsev, who remains little known for want of translations: his Ethics of Transfigured Eros, a book of the first importance for anyone investigating the role of imagination in spiritual life 516. Vycheslavtsev seeks to ground moral life in the proposition that “images of the imagination possess a power of transfiguration.” His inquiry is part of a broader effort to understand transcensus: the absolute reality of transcendence, which makes it “impossible to remain within the limits of pure immanentism” and can be fulfilled only “in the sphere of the beyond, of metaphysical being.”

Accepting the findings of depth psychology, he holds that imagination alone provides the key to the subconscious because it “raises psychic energy to a higher level.” Sublimation, on this account, corresponds to the spiritual transformation of the human being, to the divinization spoken of in Christian mysticism. By recognizing sublimation as a driving force of the soul, Vycheslavtsev can propose a new ethics, one that moves beyond moralism: “The true ethics of grace is that which is capable of transfiguring and sublimating” 517.

Clearly, this takes us far beyond the pious but ineffective distinction between eros and agape on which so many moral theologians have insisted.
